posts.title: How Revinate accelerated API adoption with Amazon API Gateway
posts.summary: Accelerating API adoption while reducing operational overhead is a challenge that every growing organization faces. For Revinate, a hospitality provider serving over 12,500 hotels worldwide and powering more than 1.25…
posts.content:
Accelerating API adoption while reducing operational overhead is a challenge that every growing organization faces. For Revinate, a hospitality provider serving over 12,500 hotels worldwide and powering more than 1.25 billion guest profiles, Amazon API Gateway became the foundation of their solution.

Revinate empowers hoteliers to connect directly with guests at every touchpoint, driving $24 billion in lifetime direct revenue through an AI-powered Customer Data Platform (CDP) that helps reduce reliance on online travel agencies (OTAs) and deliver data-driven insights.

With the expansion of CDP capabilities, Revinate needed to expose rich guest data through APIs, so that hotel properties and partners can programmatically access guest profiles, reservation data, and other critical hospitality information.

This post explores how Revinate used Amazon API Gateway and the newly released Amazon API Gateway Portal to create a scalable, secure, and developer-friendly API program.

Business need: Evolving API infrastructure to match growth

As Revinate expanded its CDP capabilities and began exposing guest profile and reservation data through APIs, the limitations of managing API infrastructure in-house became clear. Each new partner integration required manual provisioning, custom security configuration, and ongoing maintenance. The team needed an API gateway solution that could scale with growing partner demand without adding operational burden. Rather than building and maintaining a self-hosted solution, Revinate wanted an approach that would open up engineering time, streamline partner integrations, and align infrastructure costs with actual usage. The team identified four key business drivers:

  • Operational efficiency and agility – Accelerate API deployment cycles and reduce time spent on infrastructure maintenance so the engineering team can focus on building features that directly serve customers.
  • Faster partner and developer onboarding – Helping external developers and partners to discover and adopt Revinate’s APIs required a faster, more self-service experience.
  • Growth aligned costs – Infrastructure costs needed to scale proportionately with revenue generation. An on-demand pricing model, where costs flex with actual API usage rather than fixed overhead, was essential to support sustainable growth. Equally important was the ability to attribute API costs per consumer, enabling transparent cost allocation across hotel properties and partners.
  • Enhanced security and compliance – API security controls including authentication, authorization, rate limiting, and threat protection. Meeting compliance requirements and maintaining customer trust demanded strong security without adding complexity to the development workflow or requiring the team to build and maintain custom security infrastructure.

These requirements shaped the team’s evaluation of available solutions.

Evaluating alternatives

When evaluating API gateway solutions, the team translated the business drivers into four core technical requirements. On-demand pricing was essential to align infrastructure costs with actual API usage and enable per-consumer cost attribution. Authentication federation allows integration with Revinate’s existing identity provider, so partners can onboard faster without building custom auth infrastructure. Rate limiting was needed to protect backend services and enforce fair usage across hotel properties and partners as the API program scales. Finally, strong security, including threat protection, audit logging, and access controls, was required to meet compliance requirements for protecting sensitive guest data.

The engineering team evaluated three approaches. Each approach came with distinct tradeoffs across cost, flexibility, and operational burden.

Self-managed API management

Deploying a self-managed API gateway would provide flexibility and avoid licensing fees, but requires ongoing infrastructure management, security patching, scaling, and monitoring. The team would also need to build a custom developer portal from scratch.

Custom-built

Building a proprietary API gateway tailored to Revinate’s exact needs offers maximum control but demands significant upfront development investment and ongoing maintenance. Every capability, including routing, authentication, rate limiting, and documentation, would need to be built and maintained in-house, diverting engineering resources from core hospitality platform features.

Enterprise API management platforms

Enterprise platforms offer comprehensive out-of-the-box features, but introduce vendor dependencies, higher costs, and fixed-term licensing models where costs misalign with revenue growth.

All three approaches shared a common drawback: they would divert resources, whether engineering time, budget, or both, toward capabilities that don’t differentiate Revinate’s product, delaying time-to-market for features that directly serve hotel customers.

The solution: Amazon API Gateway with Developer Portal

Revinate needed the comprehensive capabilities of an enterprise API management platform without the fixed-term licensing, vendor dependencies, and operational overhead. Amazon API Gateway, combined with the newly released Amazon API Gateway Portal, delivered exactly that, aligning with both the technical requirements and business objectives that shaped the evaluation.

Fully managed infrastructure

Amazon API Gateway removes the need to manage underlying infrastructure, so the engineering team can focus on the core hospitality solution rather than API gateway operations.

Native AWS integration

Amazon API Gateway provides native integration with other AWS services, including Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) for backend services and AWS Lambda authorizers for federated authentication with an external identity provider. This allows Revinate to authenticate API consumers against the existing identity provider infrastructure with minimal development effort.

Infrastructure as code with Terraform

The team maintains strict infrastructure-as-code practices, using Terraform exclusively for all production deployments. The AWS provider for Terraform enables defining the Amazon API Gateway configuration, including REST APIs, stages, usage plans, and authorizers as version-controlled code. This approach verifies consistency across environments, enables peer review of infrastructure changes, and provides complete audit trails for compliance requirements. The declarative nature of Terraform enables rapidly iterating on the API Gateway configuration during development while maintaining confidence in production deployments.

Cost-effective pay-per-use model

Amazon API Gateway’s pay-per-use pricing model aligned perfectly with Revinate’s growth strategy. During the initial rollout phase, costs remained minimal and scaled naturally as new API consumers onboarded. Usage plans allow Revinate to track and attribute costs per consumer, providing clear visibility into which hotel properties and partners drive API usage. This per-consumer cost attribution, combined with tiered pricing that scales from tens to hundreds of customers, replaced fixed annual licensing fees that required upfront investment regardless of actual usage.

Managed Developer Portal

The November 2025 release of Amazon API Gateway Portal provided a fully managed, AWS-native Developer Portal that served as the central hub for API discovery, documentation, and governance. This removes months of custom development work that building a comparable solution would require.

Developers can use the managed portal to:

  • Set up a branded Developer Portal in minutes rather than months.
  • Provide hotel property developers with self-service API discovery and interactive documentation.
  • Maintain centralized control over API documentation freshness and access governance.
  • Deliver a professional developer experience that accelerates customer onboarding from weeks to days.

Strong security

API Gateway provides built-in security features that meet stringent requirements for protecting sensitive guest data:

  • OAuth2 client credentials for machine-to-machine (M2M) authentication.
  • Authorization logic using AWS Lambda authorizers integrating with an external identity provider of choice.
  • Request throttling and quota management to prevent abuse.
  • Integration with AWS WAF and Amazon CloudFront for layered protection against common web exploits and DDoS threats.
  • Comprehensive audit logging through AWS CloudTrail for compliance and access tracking.
  • Real-time observability through Amazon CloudWatch metrics and dashboards, with support for streaming to third-party observability platforms.

Architecture overview

The solution uses a modern, scalable AWS architecture designed to serve hotel properties globally. Hotel properties access the platform as API consumers through Amazon CloudFront for edge caching and low-latency responses, with AWS WAF providing comprehensive protection against common web threats and bots. Requests flow through Amazon API Gateway, which serves as the unified entry point for API operations. Lambda authorizers handle authentication and authorization by integrating with an identity provider (IdP) to provide secure, token-based access control for each request. After authentication, API Gateway routes traffic to backend services running on Amazon EKS, providing the flexibility and scalability needed for containerized microservices. The EKS application layer orchestrates requests to the Customer Data Platform.

Figure 1: Architecture diagram showing the end-to-end flow from hotel property consumers accessing the Amazon API Gateway Portal, through Amazon API Gateway, to backend services running on Amazon EKS.

Connecting API Gateway to EKS

A critical design decision emerged: how to securely and efficiently connect API Gateway to backend services in Amazon EKS while keeping traffic within the AWS backbone network using VPC Link. The team evaluated four options:

Option 1: NGINX ingress controller: Route traffic through a Kubernetes-native NGINX Ingress Controller with a Load Balancer service.

Pros: Highly customizable routing, flexible header manipulation, consistent with common Kubernetes patterns.

Cons: Adds extra latency hop, requires manual lifecycle management (upgrades, configs, scaling), non-AWS-native monitoring.

Option 2: AWS load balancer controller: Use the AWS Load Balancer Controller to manage LB resources as Kubernetes Ingress objects.

Pros: Bridges AWS and Kubernetes natively, supports path-based routing, AWS-managed Load Balancer (LB) lifecycle.

Cons: Introduces an additional hop (Amazon API Gateway → LB → service).

Option 3: Target group binding: Directly bind Amazon EKS pods to Network Load Balancer (NLB) Target Groups using the AWS Load Balancer Controller’s TargetGroupBinding feature.

Pros: Removes ingress controller overhead, lowest latency, native AWS integration, cost-efficient (shared NLB across multiple Target Groups), fine-grained control over health checks and scaling.

Cons: More complex initial setup, less Kubernetes-native (more AWS-specific), different applications will need individual NLB.

Option 4: LoadBalancer service: Expose each service directly via a Kubernetes LoadBalancer service (NLB/ALB).

Pros: Most straightforward setup, minimal routing complexity, no ingress controller needed.

Cons: No path-based routing, costly at scale (each service requires its own load balancer), limited observability, requires TLS offloading configuration, different applications will need individual NLB.

The team selected Target group binding because it effectively balances performance, cost-efficiency, and AWS-native integration. By removing the extra hop introduced by traditional ingress controllers, this approach provides direct control over Target Groups and health checks while maintaining sub-second latency at scale.

Security implementation

The API Gateway implementation uses OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with an external identity provider, delivering strong authentication for machine-to-machine (M2M) communication. This approach provides secure, scalable access control as Revinate onboards new hotel properties and partners.

API Gateway enforces usage plans with configurable throttling and quota limits, for fair usage and protection against abuse.

Figure 2: Sequence diagram illustrating the OAuth 2.0 authentication flow using AWS Lambda authorizers.

AWS Lambda authorizers take the caller’s identity as the input and return an IAM policy as the output. This architecture provides flexibility to implement sophisticated authorization logic while maintaining the simplicity of the API Gateway managed infrastructure. The team also deploys and manages the Lambda authorizer functions through Terraform, maintaining infrastructure as code (IaC) standards.

Developer Portal experience

The Amazon API Gateway Portal serves as the central hub for the API operations, providing developers using APIs with a streamlined experience.

Figure 3: User interface flow showing the developer journey through the Amazon API Gateway Portal, including API discovery, interactive documentation with try-it-now functionality, and subscription management.

Developers can:

  • Browse available REST APIs with comprehensive documentation.
  • Test API endpoints directly in the portal with interactive examples.
  • Access code samples and integration guides.

This self-service model reduced burden on support while accelerating customer time-to-value.

Results and benefits

The implementation of Amazon API Gateway and the Developer Portal delivered significant qualitative benefits across operational efficiency, developer experience, and business scalability.

Reduced operational overhead

By choosing a fully managed API gateway, the engineering team avoided the burden of maintaining, scaling, and troubleshooting self-hosted infrastructure. With the fully managed API gateway, the team can focus on core platform innovations that directly benefit hotel customers rather than undifferentiated gateway operations.

Improved developer experience

The centralized Developer Portal transformed the integration experience for hotel properties and partners. Self-service API discovery and interactive documentation reduced onboarding time from weeks to days. Developers consistently praised the professional portal experience and comprehensive documentation.

Accelerated customer onboarding

With the Developer Portal’s self-service capabilities, new customers can discover APIs and begin integration without waiting for manual provisioning or support intervention. This self-service approach positions Revinate to scale API access to hundreds of hotel properties and partners as demand grows.

Enhanced governance and control

The solution centralized control over API documentation, versioning, and access policies, verifying consistency across customer integrations. A single source of truth for API specifications removes documentation drift and reduces integration errors. Managing infrastructure through Terraform verifies changes follow proper review and approval processes.

Cost optimization

The pay-per-use pricing model aligns costs with actual usage and revenue generation. Usage plans and API keys provide per-consumer cost attribution, giving Revinate clear visibility into infrastructure spend by customer. As usage scales, tiered pricing verifies predictable cost growth that tracks with business value, replacing fixed licensing models that require upfront investment regardless of adoption.

Positioned for growth

The API layer, from Amazon API Gateway to the Developer Portal, scales automatically to meet demand without capacity planning or operational intervention. The team can confidently pursue growth targets knowing the API infrastructure will scale automatically.

Enhanced security posture

Amazon API Gateway provides strong security capabilities built into the platform, including centralized authentication and authorization mechanisms, request throttling and rate limiting to protect against abuse, and automatic threat protection through AWS Shield integration. Built-in security capabilities remove the need to build and maintain custom infrastructure while verifying consistent security policies across API endpoints. The centralized approach reduces the attack surface and provides comprehensive audit trails through CloudWatch integration, so the team can maintain robust security without additional operational overhead.

Key takeaways

The successful implementation of Amazon API Gateway and the Amazon API Gateway Portal offers valuable lessons for organizations exposing APIs to external customers and partners:

Managed services accelerate time-to-market – By using fully managed infrastructure and the new Amazon API Gateway Portal, the team avoided months of custom development work and launched the API program faster than would have been possible with self-managed alternatives.

Developer experience drives adoption – The professional, self-service Amazon API Gateway Portal significantly reduced friction in the customer onboarding process, so API access can rapidly scale as new hotel properties and partners onboard.

Infrastructure as code verifies consistency – Using Terraform for all production deployments provided the infrastructure team with version control, peer review, and audit trails while maintaining deployment consistency across environments.

Pay-per-use aligns costs with value – For organizations in growth mode, pay-per-use pricing removes the risk of overcommitting to fixed costs before achieving product-market fit with API offerings.

OAuth 2.0 delivers strong security at scale – Implementing OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow with an external identity provider enables a robust, scalable authentication foundation that grows securely alongside its expanding customer base.

Native AWS integration reduces complexity – For organizations already running on AWS, API Gateway’s native integration with services like EKS, Lambda, and CloudWatch minimizes architectural complexity and operational overhead.

Future enhancements

posts.title: Automating agentic AI Well-Architected reviews with the AWS Agentic AI Lens
posts.summary: Smarsh used the AWS Well-Architected Framework's Agentic AI Lens to review its first agentic workload. Because the lens is not yet selectable in the console, the team encoded it as a Claude skill that assessed all 150…
posts.content:
In regulated industries, there’s no room for a move fast and break things approach, especially when AI agents are handling sensitive customer communications data. In this post, we show how Smarsh, a leading archiving and compliance platform for communications intelligence, used the AWS Well-Architected Framework’s Agentic AI Lens to conduct a rigorous, evidence-based review of its first agentic workload. The Agentic AI Lens is available today as prescriptive guidance, though it is not yet selectable as a lens in the AWS Well-Architected Framework.

To operationalize the review, Smarsh built a custom skill for Claude, Anthropic’s AI assistant. The skill assessed the workload against all 150 best practices in the lens, pulling evidence directly from the workload’s GitHub repository and producing a comprehensive review workbook in hours rather than days. In this post, we walk through the skill’s architecture, the assessment methodology, how the team validated the skill itself, and how the resulting findings strengthened Smarsh’s engagement with its AWS account team.

About Smarsh

Smarsh is a recognized global leader in electronic communications archiving and digital communications governance. For over 20 years, the multinational software as a service (SaaS) company has enabled more than 7,000 organizations, from small businesses to large multinational financial institutions, to capture, retain, monitor, and analyze communications across 100+ channels, including email, mobile, voice, video, chat, and AI assistants, at scale. The company’s enterprise archive business runs on Amazon Web Services (AWS), and its next generation of AI capabilities are being built on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. Smarsh uses AgentCore’s runtime, gateway, registry, and identity capabilities to power these solutions. A 2025 AWS Partner of the Year Award winner, Smarsh holds a deep partnership with AWS.

Prerequisites

To follow along with the approach described in this post, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with access to Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Familiarity with the AWS Well-Architected Framework and its lens model.
  • A GitHub repository containing your agentic workload’s source code, infrastructure definitions, and documentation.
  • Access to Claude (Anthropic’s AI assistant) with the ability to install custom skills.

The challenge: A lens you can read, but not run

Smarsh operates in a highly regulated industry where compliance and security are paramount. Every agentic solution must pass a Well-Architected review before it reaches an end customer. So when a Smarsh architect set out to review the company’s first multi-agent workload, the natural choice was the AWS Well-Architected Framework’s Agentic AI Lens. That workload is an intelligent agent review system for compliance alerts built on the runtime, gateway, registry, and identity capabilities of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

The Serverless Applications Lens and other lenses can be added directly in the AWS Well-Architected Tool. The Agentic AI Lens, by contrast, existed only as published documentation: 150 best practices across 41 questions and six pillars, each with a risk level and a desired outcome, but with no way to run the review natively on the console. That left two apparent options: a multi-day manual effort in which every reviewer structured the assessment differently, or waiting for console support. Smarsh chose a third: make the lens executable, in a way every future workload could reuse.

Solution architecture: The lens as data, the reviewer as a skill

Smarsh packaged the review process as a Claude skill: a versioned bundle of instructions, reference data, and executable scripts that Claude discovers through a frontmatter description and loads on demand. Progressive disclosure keeps the token cost near zero until a review is actually requested. The skill has three components:

  • lens_data.json – All 150 best practices from the published lens documentation, extracted into a structured JSON dataset: best-practice ID, pillar, review question, title, risk level (90 High, 59 Medium, 1 Low), and desired outcome. Risk levels were cross-validated against the lens appendix to catch extraction errors. This dataset is the single source of truth, and the skill is instructed never to invent or renumber items.
  • assessment-guide.md – A five-value status rubric (Compliant, Partially Compliant, Non-Compliant, Not Applicable, and Not Reviewed), an evidence-gathering checklist, per-pillar signals to look for, and a set of honesty rules. The checklist covers README and architecture docs, decision records, infrastructure as code, continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) workflows, and test and evaluation suites. Every status must cite evidence found in the repository, items with no signal are marked Not Reviewed rather than guessed, and the same underlying fact must produce a consistent status wherever it appears across pillars.
  • build_report.py – A deterministic Python script (openpyxl) that renders the model’s assessment into a formatted workbook. The generator validates its input, so unknown best-practice IDs or invalid statuses abort the build and hallucinated items cannot silently ship. The output includes per-item status with data-validation dropdowns and conditional formatting. It also provides columns for cited evidence, gaps, and remediation, plus a summary sheet whose pillar counts and high-risk exposure tracker are live COUNTIF formulas rather than hardcoded numbers.

The assessment contract between the reasoning and the rendering is in a single JSON document:

{
  "AGENTSEC08-BP01": {
    "status": "Partially Compliant",
    "evidence": "Two-stage input validation (JSON Schema + Pydantic); 5 MB payload cap; typed prompts.",
    "gap": "No prompt-injection screening on message content.",
    "remediation": "Add injection screening; treat communication text as untrusted data in prompts."
  }
}

Running a review is a one-line request: point Claude at a repository and ask for a Well-Architected review. From there, the skill drives the following workflow:

  1. Claude loads the skill and reads the frontmatter description to understand the review scope and methodology.
  2. The skill pulls the lens_data.json dataset containing all 150 best practices across six pillars.
  3. Claude gathers evidence read-only from the target repository: README, architecture docs, infrastructure-as-code, CI/CD workflows, and test suites.
  4. The skill assesses all 150 items against the gathered evidence, applying the five-value rubric and honesty rules from assessment-guide.md.
  5. Claude calls build_report.py to generate the formatted workbook, validating row counts and flagging blank statuses.
  6. The skill returns an executive summary of the top high-risk gaps.
  7. Human reviewers validate findings, feed a remediation backlog, and surface open system questions for a focused AWS deep dive.

Figure 1: From published lens documentation to an evidence-backed review workbook

Testing the tester: Evaluating the skill before trusting it

Smarsh evaluated the skill before relying on its output. The team built two synthetic fixture repositories: a moderately mature LangGraph-style workload and a deliberately rough proof of concept, complete with hardcoded credentials and a runaway-cost incident in its history. The team ran reviews both with and without the skill. Each run was graded against eight verifiable expectations per fixture: all 150 lens items present, no blank statuses, evidence cited for every definitive status, honest calibration, and fixture-specific findings such as the hardcoded credential being flagged. With the skill, runs passed 16 of 16 expectations. Baseline runs without it passed only 8 of 16, producing ad-hoc 18–39 item checklists with no lens traceability. The eval set ships inside the skill, so regression testing continues as the skill evolves.

What the first review found

Against the real workload, the skill read the repository’s architecture and authentication documentation, AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) infrastructure definitions, GitHub Actions workflows, registry and gateway design records, and test suites. The skill then assessed all 150 items in hours. The workbook showed a credible mix of strengths and gaps. Strengths included per-agent AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) execution roles scoped to named runtime Amazon Resource Names (ARNs) and SigV4-signed Model Context Protocol (MCP) calls through AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The workbook also recorded schema-validated inputs with typed error contracts, exported decision audit trails, and continuous quality monitoring through AgentCore online evaluations. High-risk gaps included the gateway ingress authorizer running with authentication disabled under a documented risk acceptance, no prompt-injection screening on bad actor-influenced message content, rate limiting recorded as a TODO, and no automated cost controls. Each gap was tied to the lens item, the evidence, and a recommended remediation.

Next, the Smarsh architect brought in the engineering team. Together they triaged the findings, validating statuses against what the team knew, accepting or challenging results right in the workbook, and ranking the remediation backlog. Engineering’s input reshaped the review: several items collapsed into one anomaly-detection epic, and a single finding was upgraded once the team pointed to evidence the repository had overlooked. Dependency scanning was already running on every pull request.

Sharper questions, better AWS engagement

Triage surfaced a class of gaps no repository can answer: system-semantics questions about the AWS services themselves. Rather than booking a general architecture review, the team built a focused agenda for its AWS Solutions Architects, mapping each question to the checklist item it would close. The agenda covered:

  • The durability and consistency of AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, as a session checkpoint store.
  • The retry and idempotency semantics of the InvokeAgentRuntime API.
  • Break-glass patterns for halting agent invocations.
  • Amazon Bedrock Guardrails patterns for screening untrusted content.
  • Penetration-testing rules of engagement for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.
  • Amazon GuardDuty and AWS CloudTrail coverage for agentic-runtime threat detection.

The deep dive became a working session with a definition of done.

Why AWS

The security and compliance posture of Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, spanning runtime, gateway, registry, identity, and evaluation capabilities, meets the bar Smarsh’s regulated customers expect. The AWS Well-Architected Framework already anchors how Smarsh evaluates workloads. Extending it to agentic AI through the published lens, and pairing automated reviews with AWS Solutions Architect expertise to close the hard gaps, is a natural continuation of how the two teams work together.

Results and expected outcomes

These numbers reflect Smarsh’s first internal uses and the outcomes the team is tracking toward.

  1. Review effort – A complete 150-item, evidence-cited draft in hours instead of a multi-day manual effort, with human time refocused on validation and prioritization.
  2. Comparable reviews – Every workload produces the same standardized workbook, which Smarsh expects to translate into faster security approvals and improved time-to-market for agentic solutions.
  3. Sharper use of AWS expertise – Instead of broad discussions, AWS engagements became itemized working sessions, each mapped to a specific best-practice gap.

What’s next

  1. Publish the skill internally as the standard evaluation tool for Smarsh agentic workloads. It has been contributed to the company’s internal AI-SDLC plugin marketplace and has already been run against a second, architecturally different agentic repository.
  2. Bake reviews into the software development lifecycle so well-architected checks run continuously during development, not as a one-time gate at the end.
  3. Enforce governance by making the review workbook required evidence in Smarsh’s project milestone and gate process before agentic workloads reach production.
  4. Expand the lens-as-data pattern to other AWS Well-Architected lenses and additional repositories, eventually covering the broader application portfolio.

Conclusion

The gap Smarsh hit, prescriptive guidance published faster than console tooling can absorb it, is one many customers will meet as agentic AI best practices evolve. The answer generalizes: treat the lens as data, encode the reviewer’s discipline as a skill with enforced honesty rules, validate the tool with its own evaluation suite, keep humans on judgment, and let findings drive precise conversations with AWS. A review that once implied days of manual effort is now a repeatable capability the whole organization can run, before, not after, an agentic workload meets a regulated customer.

To get started:

  • Explore the AWS Well-Architected Framework and the Agentic AI Lens documentation.
  • See the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation for building agentic workloads.
  • Contact your AWS account team to schedule a Well-Architected review of your own agentic workloads.

We’d love to hear how you’re approaching Well-Architected reviews for your own agentic workloads. Share your experience in the comments, or reach out to your AWS account team to get started.

About the authors

posts.title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
posts.summary: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Haiyu Lu, Shuo Gu, Yang Yang (Tony), Jingwen Ren, Tianchen Ji, Qing Zhang, Wentian Guo, Haocheng Wu, Siqi Zeng, Yunchen Pu, Liang Wang, Chonglin Sun
  • This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval.
  • In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system).
  • For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook.

Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. 

Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale.

Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval

The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. 

Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. 

Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture 

Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs.

New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale 

The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline.

Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits 

With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motivated a joint collaboration with NVIDIA.

Each of these challenges drove a corresponding advance.

Unlocking Retrieval Performance Through Model-System Co-Design

Next-Gen Retrieval Model Architecture — Retrieval Mixture-of-Experts 

The latest iteration of Meta Andromeda introduces three synergistic architectural innovations that bring large language model (LLM)-inspired mixture-of-experts (MoE) into the retrieval (see Figure 1). With this highly expressive yet inference-efficient architecture, a new retrieval performance-efficiency Pareto frontier has been established: model performance approaches ranking-level in a typical retrieval-then-ranking system, at approximately 300x fewer inference-time FLOPs than the 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval model.

On the user modeling side, we transitioned from a single user tower to an ensemble of specialized user towers as experts. This captures diverse, time-evolving, and contextualized user interests by integrating a vast array of high-fidelity signals: sequential ad engagement events, user-cohort representations, LLM-derived semantic features, and cross-surface co-engagement signals.

In the candidate ads tower, we employ a joint encoding strategy that incorporates real-time serving context, ensuring that downstream interaction models receive context-aware representations.

In the interaction overarch layer, the interaction model evolved from dense neural networks into an MoE attention-based gating network that dynamically routes candidates across the most relevant user experts, delivering near-ranking-level performance at a fraction of the FLOPs.

A defining property of the new architecture is that its performance is co-designed with the underlying hardware execution model. Model inference throughput has reached over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200 GPU, and this efficiency allows model capacity to grow further, through richer feature interactions, additional expert sub-networks, and deeper architectures, without a proportional increase in GPU cost. Each incremental model advancement translates into greater advertiser value.

Co-Designing the Model and System Onto a Single GPU Pipeline

The 2026 Meta Andromeda pushes the model-system co-design to the next level with two innovations — a single GPU kernel fusing both model and system workloads per user-ad interaction and a strategy to co-locate per user request logics with per user-ad GPU kernels in a single GPU box. To this end, a highly optimized and fully fused GPU pipeline is built to host the entire end-to-end Meta Andromeda workflow.

Fused Kernel

At a high level, Meta Andromeda’s inference time per user-ad workload is a compact sequence of operations across model execution and system logics — gathering embeddings, executing user-ad interaction models, and scoring. The ~300x FLOPs reduction in the retrieval MoE gating architecture creates the necessary headroom and is less resistant to fully fuse both model execution and non-model system workloads into a single GPU kernel, compared to the 2024 launch where only operations within the model execution were fused. Consequently, the fused kernel now runs at over 10 billion ads per second on a single GH200.

This matters because retrieval workloads are fundamentally memory-bandwidth bound. At billions of ads per second, even a small intermediate tensor per ad multiplies into terabytes per second of high bandwidth memory (HBM) traffic. The memory workload of these intermediate tensors, not arithmetic, becomes the dominant bottleneck in multi-kernel retrieval pipelines.

The fused kernel eliminates this bottleneck entirely. Rather than dispatching multiple small GPU kernels for model and system operations, it executes the entire per user-ad computation in one pass. Intermediate results stay in GPU registers and thread block shared memory and are never materialized to HBM, achieving high utilization of the GPU’s peak memory bandwidth rather than wasting it on redundant intermediate traffic. 

Co-Location Strategy

Measured in isolation, the per user-ad fused kernel runs at multi-billion ads per second on a single GPU. However, per-user request operations such as the index matching (i.e., enforcing advertisers’ targeting rules) and top-K selection run on separate local CPU hosts and communicate with the fused GPU kernel scoring service on remote accelerators through the network connection. At multi-billion ads per second throughput, this traffic alone saturates the network link, making the network bandwidth become the bottleneck rather than GPU compute.

The co-design response was to collapse the system architecture to match the model architecture: co-locate index matching, scoring, and top-K selection on the same GPU. Instead of shipping large candidate lists across hosts, the system sends a compact request payload — user features and a targeting query — to a single GPU server, which runs the entire retrieval pipeline locally and returns only the final top-K results. This reduces network traffic by ~100x and shifts the system back to a GPU-compute-bound regime.

Moving index matching onto the GPU is not straightforward. Ads index matching evaluates complex advertiser-defined targeting logic across tens of feature categories, and must support real-time index updates as ads are created, modified, or expired throughout the day. Supporting this on GPU required redesigning the index structure for GPU-parallel execution while preserving the full fidelity of production targeting semantics.

A Single GPU Pipeline for Meta Andromeda

Combining the aforementioned two innovations, the fully co-located single GPU pipeline processes over one billion ads per second on a single GPU server while scoring every eligible ad in the candidate pool. This is a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models, and as the next section describes, significant headroom remains.

GPU-Accelerated Retrieval: The Meta-NVIDIA Collaboration

With the production pipeline running at over one billion ads per second, a natural question follows: How close is the system to the ceiling of the current generation hardware, and how much headroom remains for future model growth? In early 2026, Meta and NVIDIA launched a joint collaboration to answer this question — systematically optimizing each component of the retrieval pipeline to push throughput toward hardware limits. NVIDIA contributed optimized GPU kernels, and Meta integrated and benchmarked the full pipeline. Each component achieved 2x to 5x speedup over the baseline.

Interaction Network (Retrieval MoE Gating Network)

The optimized gating kernel improved by 5.3x, from 2.4 billion to over 10 billion ads per second, reaching ~85% of the GPU’s peak HBM bandwidth. At this throughput, the execution time / latency of the gating mechanism is just as fast as what a simple dot-product scoring kernel achieves on the same hardware — while the model is substantially more expressive. This is the co-design validation: the additional model complexity is essentially free on Tensor Core hardware. INT8 quantization achieved a further up to 2x throughput increase over the optimized FP16 kernels, with accuracy on par with 16-bit precision.

Index Matching

Through targeted GPU kernel optimizations, index matching throughput improved over 2x, reaching over 100 billion ads per second — an order of magnitude higher than the scoring network. This headroom means index matching can be re-run across multiple retrieval pathways without becoming a bottleneck.

End-to-End GPU Pipeline

Beyond individual kernels, the collaboration profiled the full retrieval flow and identified that data movement between pipeline components — not computation — accounted for a significant fraction of end-to-end latency. By co-designing data layouts across index matching and scoring to eliminate unnecessary indirection, the team removed this overhead. With all optimizations applied, the full pipeline benchmarks at multiple times the current production throughput on a single GPU server, with further gains expected as additional optimizations integrate into production.

Continuing Work on Next-Generation NVIDIA Platforms

Building on the Hopper results above, we are extending our optimization and co-design work to Grace Blackwell. Here, we are focusing on platform design optimizations that enable different CPU-to-GPU compute ratios, which our work so far suggests is an important factor for Andromeda-like workloads. We are evaluating how sensitive end-to-end application performance is to these ratios, using Grace-class CPU performance and Blackwell-class GPU performance for their respective parts of the workload.

More broadly, we are exploring how these findings extend to the next platform generation, where greater flexibility in CPU+GPU execution, resource ratios, and coupling could bring more of these architectural improvements to bear on Andromeda-like workloads.

These results confirm that the co-designed retrieval pipeline is not yet at its ceiling. With quantization unlocking further scoring throughput and index matching operating at an order of magnitude above the scoring network, the architecture is positioned to absorb significantly more model complexity — deeper interaction networks, richer feature spaces, and additional retrieval pathways — without proportional infrastructure growth.

The Path Forward for Ads Retrieval

The advances described here follow a single principle: The largest gains come from designing model, system, and hardware as one integrated stack, rather than optimizing each in isolation. The retrieval MoE gating architecture delivers near-ranking-level expressiveness at no additional serving cost. Fusing the entire retrieval pipeline onto a single GPU eliminates network and memory bottlenecks. And pushing the pipeline towards its hardware ceiling confirms substantial headroom remains.

Looking ahead, the co-design principle that drove these results applies equally to next-generation model architectures and hardware platforms, with the demonstrated headroom enabling continued scaling without proportional infrastructure growth.

For people who use Meta’s products, this translates directly into better ads that are more relevant to them, delivered within the same latency budget. For advertisers, it means better customer matches and more conversions. For Meta, it means increased business from advertisers and lower costs, as each GPU now evaluates more ads per second. As the volume of eligible ads continues to grow, driven by Advantage+ automation and generative AI creative tools, Meta Andromeda’s co-designed architecture scales to meet it.

posts.title: Publishing LMS courses with a Kiro SCORM pipeline
posts.summary: See how to use Kiro, an agentic AI, to automate converting raw training material into compliant SCORM packages that are ready to upload to a learning management system (LMS).
posts.content:
Publishing a Shareable Content Object Reference Model (SCORM) course to a learning management system (LMS) is rarely as straightforward as writing the course. The LMS needs SCORM packages to adhere to a standard format for successful import and launch. Producing one by hand means restructuring slides into modules and hand-editing SCORM manifests. The packaging mechanics pull authors away from developing the course content itself.

This post shows how to use Kiro, an agentic AI with an integrated development environment (IDE) and a CLI, to automate the conversion of raw training material into compliant SCORM packages. Testing with a small course included in the sample produced a SCORM package in a few minutes.

Solution overview

Kiro structures course content and guides the author through the publishing workflow. Figure 1 shows the end-to-end pipeline from raw material to upload-ready package.

Figure 1: Kiro course publishing pipeline overview

An author places raw training material (slide decks, playbooks, and written docs) in a course folder, and Kiro runs two pipeline stages. Course Development includes planning and authoring lessons. Course Build includes linting the lessons, building the SCORM package, and validating the SCORM package. The output is a SCORM 1.2 .zip ready to upload to your LMS. You drive the whole pipeline from a Kiro conversation. Start by loading your material into a course folder, ask Kiro to build the course, and it hands back the upload-ready .zip file.

The Kiro building blocks this pipeline uses

Kiro is an agentic AI available as an IDE and a CLI (kiro-cli). This pipeline is built from three Kiro primitives:

  • Steering – Markdown files that give Kiro persistent context (.kiro/steering/) about your workspace. Steering loads automatically. always files load in every session, fileMatch files load when you touch files they govern, and manual files load on demand.
  • Specs – Specifications (.kiro/specs/) that formalize the development process for features or bug fixes.
  • Hooks – Automated triggers (.kiro/hooks/) that run prompts or shell commands when events occur in the IDE, such as creating a file, saving a file, or ending a session.

The LMS content publishing pipeline

The following sections walk through the steps a course goes through and the parts that carry them out.

How a course gets built

For a new course, Kiro works through six steps with you in conversation:

  1. Add source material to courses/<name>/ (slide decks, Word, PDFs, playbooks, Markdown docs).
  2. Plan – Kiro reads the source and creates the course.yaml manifest.
  3. Author – Kiro converts the source into a lesson.md per module.
  4. Lint – Check the authored lessons for structural problems such as missing frontmatter, broken image paths, or a knowledge check with no correct answer.
  5. Build – Render the lessons into one index.html and compress the SCORM package.
  6. Validate – Confirm the .zip file is a well-formed SCORM 1.2 package before it goes to the LMS.

The course manifest

Each course starts as a single manifest, course.yaml, that declares its modules, source material, and SCORM build configuration. Kiro creates the manifest at step 2, after you upload your source content and ask it to build a course.

course:
  title: "Build a SCORM Course from Markdown"
  short_name: "sample-course"
  short_description: "A three-module example course."
  default_language: en-US
  total_duration_minutes: 30
modules:
  - id: module-1
    title: "The Authoring Pipeline"
    target_duration_minutes: 10
  # ...
scorm:
  version: "1.2"
  output: scorm/dist/sample-course.zip
  passing_score: 100
  min_page_dwell_seconds: 5

A few notable settings you can customize:

  • min_page_dwell_seconds sets the minimum time a learner must spend on a page before the Next button unlocks.
  • target_duration_minutes sets each module’s expected completion time, shown to learners on the course home page.
  • total_duration_minutes sets the course-level expected completion time, shown to learners and reported to the LMS.
  • passing_score sets the score a learner must reach for the LMS to mark the course complete (written into the SCORM manifest as the mastery score).

Steering is where the pipeline’s knowledge lives

Steering is where this pipeline keeps everything Kiro needs to know. Steering files hold three kinds of knowledge:

  • Lessons learned – The SCORM knowledge accumulated from actually building and running courses.
  • Authoring conventions – How to break source material into modules and lessons, plus writing-style guidance so each lesson.md reads as polished, learner-facing content.
  • The repository contract – The uniform courses/<name>/ layout every course follows, so the same shared scripts work for every course.

Each steering file loads in one of the three modes from earlier: always, fileMatch, or manual. Every session picks up only the guidance it needs. The steering files in the sample repository are listed in the following example, grouped by their inclusion mode:

.kiro/steering/
# always - loaded in every session
product.md          what the pipeline is for
pipeline.md         the six-step build sequence and commands
structure.md        repo layout and the courses/<name>/ contract
tech.md             toolchain and required versions
# fileMatch - loaded when matching files are edited
scorm-invariants.md   invariants for scorm/src, build output, and course.yaml
# manual - deep guides, pulled in on demand
course-planning.md          plan modules and course.yaml
source-intake.md            convert raw source into lessons
lesson-authoring.md         write each lesson.md
scorm-authoring.md          build and package the SCORM zip
assessment-authoring.md     author an optional course assessment

Hooks automate the repetitive steps

Hooks run automatically as Kiro or the author works, so common checks don’t depend on someone remembering a command:

  • Lint on save – Editing any lesson.md or course.yaml re-lints that course immediately.
  • Validate on package creation – A new SCORM .zip file appearing under scorm/dist/ is validated the moment it’s built.
  • Steering reflection – After each turn, Kiro proposes updates to the steering guidance to capture best practices worth keeping for future course development.

Spec-driven development of new features

The repo includes a feature spec kept as a reference for how the pipeline was built. The page-dwell-gating spec added the feature that enforces a minimum time a learner must spend on a page before proceeding. After you understand the pipeline, you can extend it the same way, using the spec-driven development process in Kiro.

Walkthrough: Building a course

The following walkthrough takes you from an empty repo to an upload-ready SCORM package.

Prerequisites

  • Access to Kiro (IDE or kiro-cli).
  • Node.js 20+, Python 3.11+, and the zip command, with permission to install package dependencies (Kiro installs the project’s npm and pip packages during setup).
  • Raw training material to convert (slide decks, playbooks, and written docs).

Open the repo

Open the repository in Kiro. The workspace steering under .kiro/steering/ loads automatically, so Kiro already knows the pipeline commands, the repo layout, and the SCORM constraints.

Build the sample course

Building a course is a single prompt. In the Kiro chat panel, enter:

“Build the sample course.”

Kiro runs lint, build, and validate, and replies with the path to the upload-ready .zip file: courses/sample-course/scorm/dist/sample-course.zip.

Turn your own material into a course

For a new course, add your source material to courses/<name>/ and enter the following prompt:

“Plan and build a course from <name>.”

Kiro walks through planning course.yaml, authoring one lesson.md per module, and packaging.

Verify before you publish

You’ve already seen Kiro lint, build, and validate the package, and an included test checks the course’s progress tracking. The last check is a visual one. Serve the built course locally over HTTP to see it for yourself before uploading:

cd scorm/build    # the unzipped build output (same content as the .zip file)
python3 -m http.server 8080 # then open http://localhost:8080 in a browser

This serves the full built course locally. Figure 2 shows the course home page as a learner would see it.

Figure 2: Local preview of the sample course home page

The home page displays the course title, a short description, and a card for each module showing its number, estimated duration, a brief summary, and a link to start.

The final step is to upload the .zip file to your SCORM 1.2-compliant LMS to confirm end to end. Learning management systems vary. If you run into an issue, ask Kiro to help you troubleshoot it and learn the specifics of your LMS.

Cleaning up

There are no cloud resources to tear down because the pipeline runs entirely as local scripts and a Kiro session against your own repository. If you built the bundled sample course only to try the pipeline, you can safely delete courses/sample-course/scorm/dist/ and courses/sample-course/scorm/build/. Both are build output.

Conclusion

In this post, you saw how to turn raw training material into LMS-ready SCORM packages with Kiro. Authors stay focused on the course while Kiro handles the packaging. Because the pipeline lives in the repo as Steering, Specs, and Hooks, that expertise is version-controlled and reusable across every course and team.

To get started, clone the aws-samples repository, drop your source material into a course folder, and ask Kiro to build the course. To learn more, explore Kiro.

About the author

posts.title: Vessel-specific voyage optimization with machine learning: Manta on AWS
posts.summary: Manta Marine Technologies closes the gap between seemingly identical ships by training machine learning models on each vessel's own operational history. Learn how Manta delivers vessel-specific voyage optimization on…
posts.content:
Voyage performance varies even between seemingly identical ships, and models built on vessel-type averages often miss the mark. Manta Marine Technologies (Manta) closes that gap with machine learning (ML) models trained on each vessel’s own operational history. In this post, we show how Manta delivers vessel-specific voyage optimization with machine learning on Amazon Web Services (AWS), helping shipowners reduce fuel consumption and improve voyage efficiency.

Differences in hull condition, trim, draft, machinery condition, loading patterns, and operational practices mean that when operators build models on vessel-type averages, those models often can’t capture how a specific vessel performs. For shipowners, this gap translates directly into unnecessary fuel consumption and cost.

Manta takes a vessel-specific approach. The company trains machine learning models on each vessel’s own operational history and combines them with forecast weather and ocean conditions. To support this approach at scale, Manta built its data infrastructure on AWS. Manta’s solution uses services such as Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2), Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), and Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS).

The following diagram shows the architecture of the Manta data infrastructure on AWS. The system receives vessel data and environmental forecasts in a secure, multi-Availability Zone environment. Manta’s solution processes this data, stores it, and uses it to train and run machine learning models.

Figure 1: Architecture of Manta’s data infrastructure on AWS

In the diagram, vessel data and environmental forecasts enter an Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) deployed across multiple Availability Zones. Inside the VPC, Manta uses Apache Airflow on Amazon EC2 to orchestrate data pipelines and machine learning workloads as Amazon ECS tasks on EC2 capacity, with a separate Auto Scaling group and capacity provider for each instance type. AWS Lambda serves as the entry point for requests from client applications. The system stores data in Amazon RDS and Amazon DynamoDB, and manages container images in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR). For security and configuration, the architecture includes AWS Secrets Manager and AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. The Airflow scheduler also drives the retraining loop: as new voyage data accumulates for a vessel, it launches a training task on the appropriate instance type, and the updated model is used for that vessel’s subsequent voyage optimizations. Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) provide monitoring and alerting across all layers.

The challenge: Predicting how a specific vessel performs

Manta’s goal is voyage guidance that continuously learns from each vessel’s behavior and improves over time. This requires infrastructure that processes large volumes of operational vessel data—up to 3 billion data points in a single training run. The infrastructure also combines historical performance with weather and ocean forecasts. Manta’s solution must also run machine learning workflows, deliver guidance globally, and support continuous model improvement as new voyage data arrives.

The solution: A cloud-native data infrastructure built on AWS

Manta runs its data infrastructure as a cloud-native solution on AWS, deployed across multiple Availability Zones within an Amazon VPC.

At the core of the infrastructure, workflow orchestration with Apache Airflow runs on Amazon EC2. Airflow runs on a persistent EC2 instance because the orchestration layer needs a long-running server process. Airflow submits all compute work to Amazon ECS through the ECS operator, so every extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipeline, model training run, and voyage optimization runs as an ECS task. Manta runs those tasks on EC2 capacity rather than AWS Fargate because EC2 gives the team direct control over instance type, including GPU instances and specific chip generations. Manta defines one capacity provider, one Auto Scaling group, and one launch template per instance type instead of sharing a single pool. Model training and voyage optimization use different instance types. Per-instance-type capacity gives granular control over how each workload scales, running less urgent jobs on Spot capacity and time-sensitive jobs On-Demand. The infrastructure also uses AWS Lambda as the entry point for requests from client applications. A Lambda function triggers the corresponding Airflow directed acyclic graph (DAG) or returns already-processed results from the database. Manta manages container images in Amazon ECR, with separate images for Graviton and x86-64 instances, GPU workloads, orchestration, and machine learning operations. Manta stores data in Amazon RDS and Amazon DynamoDB.

For observability, Manta uses Amazon CloudWatch for monitoring and Amazon SNS for alerting. Manta keeps non-sensitive application and infrastructure configuration in AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store. For sensitive values such as database connection credentials, Airflow application secrets, and authentication tokens for third-party services, Manta uses AWS Secrets Manager. Those secrets are encrypted, and access to them is restricted through IAM permissions. Manta gives each system component its own AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, scoped with least privilege so that each component holds only the permissions its task requires. The company also encrypts data with AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS).

Because the infrastructure runs in the cloud, Manta continuously improves its models as new voyage data becomes available. Each completed voyage contributes operational data to future model training, and an Airflow scheduler retrains each vessel’s model periodically, based on how much new data that vessel has produced. This creates a learning cycle that makes recommendations increasingly relevant for that specific vessel.

Why AWS

With AWS, Manta has the scalability to support growing fleets and increasing data volumes. The company stores historical vessel performance data, processes weather and ocean forecasts, and trains and operates its machine learning models. It also delivers voyage recommendations to fleets operating worldwide and scales compute capacity on demand as workloads grow.

Cost efficiency is also a key factor. Manta runs its ETL pipelines, model training, and voyage optimization workloads on AWS Graviton-based instances. For one ETL pipeline that processes large datasets, Manta observed approximately 25–30 percent better price performance after moving to Graviton-based instances. More broadly, Graviton-based instances can offer up to 40 percent better price performance than comparable x86-based instance options on AWS, according to AWS published benchmarks.

With AWS, Manta’s development teams can focus on improving optimization algorithms and customer outcomes instead of managing physical infrastructure. Manta defines its solution as infrastructure as code using the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) and AWS SDK for Python (Boto3). With this approach, the team can change the architecture quickly and verify through continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) that nothing has broken. It can also reproduce identical development, staging, and production environments.

That reproducibility also changes how the team experiments. Manta’s engineers develop and validate machine learning and data engineering work on their own machines, against large samples of vessel data pulled from the system. The only cost of an experiment is then retrieving the data. Because that work runs in the same container images the system uses in production, a validated algorithm reaches the full fleet without re-engineering and without infrastructure to provision. When an experiment outgrows a local machine, the team runs it at full scale on AWS instead of scoping it down. They submit the same container to the instance type the workload needs, whether that means GPU capacity or many parallel CPU tasks. Experimentation stays cheap when it can be and unconstrained when it needs to be. Scaling a validated result to every vessel is then a scheduling decision rather than a project.

The results: Guidance built around how each vessel actually performs

Through Manta’s solution, ship operators receive voyage-specific guidance built on the vessel’s own historical performance and relevant external data such as atmospheric and oceanic weather data. The system’s continuous improvement loop refines this guidance as new voyage data arrives, with each vessel’s model retrained as its own operational history grows.

Fleet managers gain guidance designed around how each vessel actually performs, rather than vessel-type averages or industry benchmarks. Pairing vessel-specific data with decades of maritime operational expertise helps customers run greener and more profitable operations.

Based on internal voyage simulations conducted across its active fleet, Manta expects fuel savings of approximately 2–4 percent per vessel. The company anticipates further gains as its models improve and new capabilities are added.

Conclusion

Manta built a cloud-native data solution on AWS to deliver vessel-specific voyage optimization. Apache Airflow on Amazon EC2 orchestrates data pipelines and machine learning workloads across EC2, Amazon ECS, and AWS Lambda. Manta stores data in Amazon RDS and Amazon DynamoDB and enforces security through least-privilege IAM roles and AWS KMS. Graviton-based instances keep the solution cost efficient as data volumes grow. Every completed voyage feeds a learning cycle that makes guidance increasingly tailored to each vessel.

To learn more about Manta’s voyage optimization solution, visit the Manta Marine Technologies website. For more information about the AWS services used in this solution, see Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, and Amazon RDS in the AWS documentation.

For related reading, see Using machine learning to predict vessel time of arrival with Amazon SageMaker and How potential performance upside with AWS Graviton helps reduce your costs further.

About the authors
