posts.title: How Anchorage Digital and Turnkey verify code with AWS Nitro Enclaves
posts.summary: Anchorage Digital and Turnkey built verifiable infrastructure on AWS Nitro Enclaves so crypto wallets can cryptographically verify which code parsed a transaction. This post covers the architecture, the…
posts.content:
This post is co-written with Prasanna Gautam from Anchorage Digital and Arnaud Brousseau from Turnkey.

In crypto, trust is a liability. A wallet often delegates computation to a third party to parse a transaction, evaluate a policy, or manage key material. Each time, it raises a question: how do you know the service ran the code it claims to have run? Contractual trust, network perimeter security, and reputation don’t provide a cryptographic answer. Verifiable infrastructure built on AWS Nitro Enclaves does.

Anchorage Digital is home to America’s first federally regulated digital asset bank. Turnkey is a verifiable key management infrastructure provider whose platform secures millions of wallets. Together, they built that cryptographic answer on top of AWS Nitro Enclaves. Their collaboration produced VisualSign, an open source, cross-chain transaction parser that runs inside Nitro Enclaves and returns results with attestation-backed proof of what software produced them. The immediate application protects users from phishing attacks by making complex transactions human-readable, and the architecture is a blueprint for verifiable infrastructure that extends well beyond blockchain.

This post describes the architecture and design decisions behind the system, including why AWS Nitro Enclaves are foundational to the trust model. It also shows how the same pattern applies to any high-trust workflow, not only Web3 or crypto.

The problem: Blind signing and phishing in Web3

Cryptocurrency phishing attacks exploit a basic limitation of wallets: they can’t natively parse the full semantics of complex transactions. Blind signing is the approval of a transaction whose full effects the wallet can’t display, and it’s what attackers depend on. A user interacting with a decentralized finance (DeFi) protocol might receive a request to sign a transaction, but the wallet displays only a raw hex payload or a partial summary. Attackers craft malicious transactions that look benign at the surface level but contain hidden operations: token approvals to attacker-controlled addresses, unexpected contract interactions, or fund transfers disguised within multi-step operations.

The industry has attempted to make transactions readable with simulation services and transaction decoders. These approaches typically require the wallet to trust a third-party service without a way to verify which code the service ran or that the result came back unmodified.

A transaction parser needs two guarantees:

  • Correctness: The parsing logic is the exact, unmodified code that was audited and approved.
  • Integrity: The parsed output hasn’t been tampered with between the parser and the wallet.

The solution: VisualSign on Turnkey Verifiable Cloud, powered by AWS Nitro Enclaves

VisualSign Parser is an open source Rust codebase developed by Anchorage Digital. It converts raw blockchain transactions into structured, human-readable JSON. As of this writing, it supports Ethereum and its layer 2 networks (L2s), including Arbitrum, Optimism, Base, and Polygon. It also supports Solana, Sui, and Tron, with additional chains in development.

Consider a Uniswap Universal Router transaction: the uniswap-v2swap.input fixture in the visualsign-parser test suite is 2,470 characters of raw hex. VisualSign turns it into a clear hierarchical breakdown: a Permit2 approval, a V2 swap with specific token amounts and minimum outputs, a fee payment, and a WETH unwrap. Each step lists explicit addresses, amounts, and expiration dates.

Turnkey Verifiable Cloud

The collaboration between Anchorage Digital and Turnkey began after Turnkey published its whitepaper in January 2025. The whitepaper details how Turnkey uses AWS Nitro Enclaves to secure wallets and private keys at scale. Turnkey has detailed this implementation and AWS architecture in the post Building secure, verifiable blockchain key management on AWS Nitro Enclaves at Turnkey.

Anchorage Digital now uses Turnkey Verifiable Cloud (TVC) to outsource computation verifiably. Rather than running transaction parsing logic in its own infrastructure, Anchorage Digital deployed VisualSign Parser within Turnkey-deployed AWS Nitro Enclaves.

Anchorage Digital and Turnkey documented the full verification workflow in the Wallet Integration Guide so that other wallet providers can use VisualSign Parser in the same way.

With VisualSign Parser, crypto wallets, typically limited in their ability to run complex logic, can verifiably parse complex cryptocurrency transactions. This helps prevent phishing attacks that rely on users approving signatures for malicious transactions without understanding them.

Beyond VisualSign, TVC supports running any high-trust workflow inside verifiable, isolated infrastructure, including policy evaluation, compliance checks, and transaction classification. You can now build with cryptographic proof instead of relying on trust for your most sensitive operations.

Architecture: How VisualSign runs inside AWS Nitro Enclaves

The following diagram shows how a parsing request travels from the wallet client to the enclave and back, and where attestation enters the flow.

Figure 1: End-to-end VisualSign flow

The flow works as follows:

  1. A wallet client sends a raw transaction payload to the Turnkey API.
  2. The Turnkey API forwards the request to any AWS Nitro Enclave-supported EC2 instance running QuorumOS. QuorumOS is the open source operating system Turnkey uses to run enclaves, and the VisualSign Parser binary.
  3. The parser converts the raw transaction into structured, human-readable output.
  4. The enclave signs the response with an ephemeral P-256 key and requests an AWS Nitro attestation document from the Nitro Hypervisor.
  5. The wallet client verifies the attestation and signature, confirming the response came from the expected software running in a genuine Nitro Enclave.

Anchorage Digital doesn’t need to trust Turnkey: ephemeral key signatures and AWS Nitro attestation documents prove that enclaves are provisioned with the correct software. The attestation document contains Platform Configuration Registers (PCRs), which are cryptographic measurements of the enclave image, kernel, and application. The wallet client compares PCRs and other attestation fields against the values derived from reproducible builds. Reproducible builds compile the same source code into byte-identical binaries every time, regardless of who runs the build or where. Because the binary is always identical, its PCR measurements are deterministic, so the trusted values stay constant across rebuilds and verification policies never need to be updated. Reproducibility allows any party to independently verify that the enclave runs the expected QuorumOS version, as well as the exact, unmodified VisualSign Parser code.

Why AWS Nitro Enclaves

AWS Nitro Enclaves provide several properties that are essential to this architecture:

  • Hardware and software-based isolation – Nitro Enclaves use the same Nitro Hypervisor technology that provides CPU and memory isolation for Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances to isolate the vCPUs and memory for an enclave from a parent instance. The Nitro Hypervisor ensures that the parent instance has no access to the isolated vCPUs and memory of the enclave.
  • No persistent storage or external networking – Enclaves communicate only with the parent instance over a local vsock channel. No persistent storage, no network interface, no DNS, no metadata service.
  • Cryptographic attestation – Attestation is a feature unique to AWS Nitro Enclaves. The Nitro Hypervisor produces signed attestation documents that include PCR measurements of the enclave image, signed by the AWS Nitro Attestation PKI, proving the enclave’s identity to external services.
  • No operator access – No single AWS, Turnkey, or Anchorage Digital operator can access customer data within the enclave.

These properties make Nitro Enclaves well-suited for workloads where the computation itself must be verifiable: not only the inputs and outputs, but the guarantee that a specific, known program produced the result.

Advancing Go tooling for Nitro Enclave verification

Attestation verification in production is difficult to implement correctly. The attestation document specification is a CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Sign1 structure whose payload carries an X.509 certificate chain, PCR measurements, and optional fields such as UserData and PublicKey. Correct verification means parsing CBOR, validating the COSE signature, and walking the certificate chain back to the AWS Nitro root certificate. It also means checking expiration and comparing PCR values, with clear error handling at each step.

awsnitroverifier: A purpose-built Go library for Nitro attestation

Anchorage Digital built and open-sourced awsnitroverifier, a Go library for validating AWS Nitro Enclave attestation documents with complete chain-of-trust verification. The team designed it to address the gaps they encountered while building the VisualSign verification workflow. The library implements built-in PCR validation and separates parsing errors from validation failures, instead of leaving that to the caller. Handling it in the library makes the cause of an error easier to determine. The library’s clear two-tier error handling separates malformed input (err != nil) from validation failures (result.Valid == false). Each validation failure includes a specific, actionable error message (PCR mismatch, expired certificate, chain verification failure) rather than a generic “verification failed.”

The library also gives direct access to the UserData, PublicKey, and Nonce fields, the root certificate fingerprint, and chain trust status to validate the Nitro Enclave used for the request. The library comes with tests covering the verification package. Developers also have the option to write continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) tests without having to spin up a Nitro Enclave by using offline/test mode. There’s also an included migration guide for users currently using nitrite, a widely used open-source AWS Nitro Enclave Go attestation library.

visualsign-turnkeyclient: End-to-end verification built on awsnitroverifier

On top of awsnitroverifier, Anchorage Digital built and open sourced visualsign-turnkeyclient, a Go client that performs end-to-end verification of transactions parsed in Nitro Enclaves. The awsnitroverifier library handles the low-level attestation document validation. The Turnkey client adds the application-level workflow.

You can adopt the verification levels in increasing order of complexity:

  1. Basic P-256 signature verification – Confirms that a key inside Turnkey’s infrastructure signed the response.
  2. Boot attestation with PCR validation – Uses awsnitroverifier to verify the enclave image and configuration match expected values.
  3. Complete manifest verification – Full QuorumOS manifest validation including the specific application binary hash.

This layered approach separates a focused attestation library from an application-level client, so you can build non-blockchain use cases on Nitro Enclaves by excluding blockchain-specific dependencies.

Beyond blockchain: Verifiable compute for any high-trust workflow

VisualSign is a blockchain product, but the infrastructure underneath it isn’t. Turnkey and Anchorage Digital built that architecture on reproducible builds, enclave-hosted computation, and attestation-gated access. It’s a general-purpose pattern for any scenario where you need cryptographic proof that a specific program processed specific data. Without the blockchain specifics, the architecture provides a verifiable compute building block.

The core pattern: Attestation-gated access

The key insight from Anchorage Digital’s implementation is that an enclave attestation document can serve as an access credential. Rather than granting access to sensitive resources based on network identity, API keys, or operator trust, the system grants access based on proof of what code is running. The principle is keeping the computation away from the sensitive data and using attestation to bridge the gap.

At Anchorage Digital, hardware security modules (HSMs) protect sensitive key materials. The VisualSign Parser runs in a separate Nitro Enclave, and the HSM grants access based on verified attestation, not based on trusting the network, the operator, or the host machine. The Anchorage Digital engineering team’s philosophy is that this pattern applies to any application that handles sensitive information or uses third-party libraries. The goal is to keep the computation away from the sensitive data. The following diagram shows the generalized form of the pattern. An untrusted input enters an enclave-hosted application, the enclave returns a signed bundle with an attestation document, and the HSM releases key material only after that attestation is verified.

Figure 2: Generalized attestation-gated access pattern

Several non-crypto workflows fit this pattern. A financial institution can run sanctions screening or anti-money laundering (AML) checks inside a Nitro Enclave built from a reproducible image. This produces cryptographically verifiable proof that the exact audited screening software processed the data. A healthcare provider can run a diagnostic model against patient data inside an enclave that has no persistent storage and no network access. Attestation confirms that the approved model binary ran, and the model operator has no path to copy the data out. Any application that relies on third-party libraries for sensitive operations can run that code inside an enclave with a pinned, reproducible build.

This architecture also supports an organizational separation of concerns that maps naturally to team expertise. As Anchorage Digital describes it: “someone with expertise in evaluating blockchain transactions uses first-party blockchain tools to vet them, while the team managing sensitive data focuses on verifying correct validation and applying policies.”

In practice, Anchorage Digital splits ownership of the system between two teams:

  • Blockchain domain experts build and maintain the VisualSign Parser using first-party blockchain tools and deep protocol knowledge. They understand Ethereum opcodes, Solana instruction formats, and DeFi protocol semantics.
  • Security and infrastructure teams focus on attestation verification, HSM policy enforcement, and access control around sensitive key materials. They understand PCR validation, certificate chains, and key management.

Neither team needs to operate in the other’s domain. The blockchain team doesn’t need access to key materials. The security team doesn’t need to understand Solana’s account model. The Nitro Enclave attestation serves as the machine-verifiable contract between the two teams that says, “This exact code ran, and here’s the proof.”

Conclusion

In this post, we showed how Anchorage Digital and Turnkey use AWS Nitro Enclaves to run the open source VisualSign Parser inside an attested enclave, so wallets can cryptographically verify which code parsed a transaction. The collaboration between Turnkey and Anchorage Digital started with a specific problem: making crypto transactions human-readable with cryptographic proof of correctness. What they built applies well beyond blockchain. The architecture pattern of reproducible builds, enclave-hosted computation, and attestation-gated access can serve as a general-purpose building block for verifiable compute.

To get started building verifiable applications, the VisualSign ecosystem and its underlying verification tooling are fully open source. Follow the documentation to spin up AWS Nitro Enclaves for your sensitive workloads that require cryptographic attestation. Use the awsnitroverifier Go library to implement AWS Nitro Enclave attestation validation. For blockchain applications, the VisualSign Turnkey Client and Wallet Integration Guide handle end-to-end attestation validation and wallet integration.

If you want to run your own workloads on Turnkey Verifiable Cloud, TVC is in private beta as of this writing. To get a more in-depth understanding of how Turnkey architected this solution, refer to the post Building secure, verifiable blockchain key management on AWS Nitro Enclaves at Turnkey.

posts.title: How the fastest-growing enterprises on Stripe scale globally
posts.summary: Despite slower global economic growth and greater geopolitical fragmentation, the fastest-growing enterprises continue to look beyond their home markets and are investing in tools and workflows that make expansion…
posts.content:
We analyzed more than 100 of the fastest-growing enterprises on Stripe and found that they processed their first cross-border transaction on Stripe 24x faster than the enterprise baseline. Despite slower global economic growth and greater geopolitical fragmentation, these enterprises continue to look beyond their home markets—and are investing in tools and workflows that make expansion faster and more repeatable.

To identify the fastest-growing enterprises on Stripe, we used a composite score that measures month-over-month payment volume growth, year-over-year performance, and recent momentum since 2025. We compared this cohort—which spans more than 10 industries across financial services, manufacturing, retail, technology, and others—against a broader set of more than 1,000 enterprises of a similar scale. We define an enterprise as an organization that has been active on Stripe for at least six months and that meets our internal benchmarks, including employee size and revenue.

Here’s what we learned about where enterprises find international demand, how they adapt payments to local preferences, and how they manage the accompanying fraud risk of expanding into new markets.

The fastest-growing enterprises have an outsized presence in emerging markets

Mature economies remain important sources of customer spending, but more of the world’s economic growth is expected to come from emerging economies. These markets are projected to grow by around 4% in 2026, compared to 1.5% for mature economies. And by 2035, emerging markets are expected to account for 65% of global economic growth. 

Surprisingly, the fastest-growing companies on Stripe already see outsized spend in emerging global markets. Compared with the enterprise baseline, they achieved 1.6x the share of cross-border payment volume in Brazil, India, and Argentina. 

They also reach customers across a wider range of markets. During its first year on Stripe, the median fastest-growing enterprise processed payments from customers in 25 countries—more than six times as many as the enterprise baseline. 

This suggests that a geographically diverse approach to expansion can help increase growth. Rather than following the traditional approach of sequential country-by-country expansion or a gradual test-and-learn approach, the fast-growing cohort expands to many mature and emerging markets in parallel.

The fastest-growing enterprises add more ways to pay with less work

Serving customers across so many countries means accommodating a wide range of payment preferences. A checkout that offers only one payment method—or omits the methods customers use locally—can reduce conversion by up to 15%. 

The fastest-growing enterprises are investing in a more localized payment experience. The median enterprise from the cohort offers 2x more local payment methods than the enterprise baseline. 

We also saw a pattern in how these enterprises manage their wider range of payment options. Adding a new payment method traditionally requires businesses to integrate, configure, and test it, then maintain it over time. Enterprises in the cohort are shortening that process, making it easier to add payment options as customer preferences evolve. 

For example, Facile.it—a price comparison service in Italy and a member of the fast-growing cohort—uses Stripe Checkout to add new payment methods in 80% less time than its legacy system required. 

Anthropic, a member of the cohort, also used Stripe Checkout to improve its checkout flow and offer a wider range of payment methods. It allowed Anthropic to easily offer payment options, such as credit cards, digital wallets like Apple Pay and Cash App Pay, and local payment methods that would appeal to the company’s increasingly international user base.

These examples show how the right infrastructure can help enterprises support rapid international growth without rebuilding their checkout for every new payment method or market.

The fastest-growing enterprises take a more targeted approach to fraud rules

Broader international reach can expose businesses to a wider variety of fraud patterns, which often differ by region and payment method. That risk exposure showed up in our analysis. In the first half of 2026, the fastest-growing enterprises saw an attempted fraud rate nearly 1.8x higher than the enterprise baseline. 

To help combat this fraud, more than half have implemented at least one custom fraud rule within Stripe Radar, our AI-powered fraud prevention product. This makes them more likely than the enterprise baseline to customize their fraud controls.

However, if we only analyze enterprises that use custom rules, the fastest-growing cohort maintains fewer rules per business than the baseline. This suggests a more deliberate approach to fraud management, with fast-growing enterprises relying on Radar’s default fraud models and adding targeted custom rules only where needed—rather than building extensive customized rule sets. 

How Stripe can help 

Enterprises use Stripe to expand into new markets and operate with less complexity. Stripe’s global selling solution brings together localized checkout, payments performance, money movement, tax compliance, and fraud prevention into one platform, so you can adapt to local customer preferences and regional risks for every new market.

Reach customers in more markets

  • Quickly launch a localized, optimized checkout experience across web and mobile with Stripe Checkout, including built-in support for 195+ markets, 135+ currencies, and 34 languages.
  • Automatically localize prices in 150+ markets, increasing cross-border revenue by an average of 17.8% with Adaptive Pricing.
  • Expand your customer base by offering relevant global and local payment methods, with built-in support for one-time payments, stablecoins, subscriptions, AI-powered fraud detection, localized currency presentment, and cross-border payments—all through a single integration. 
  • Launch in new markets faster without setting up local entities using Stripe Managed Payments, Stripe’s merchant of record solution that simplifies global selling.

Manage risk as you expand globally

  • Intelligently apply authentication to riskier transactions and as required by local regulations with adaptive 3DS, reducing fraud without adding unnecessary friction for legitimate customers.
  • Reduce fraud across supported payment volume globally, including bank debits, stablecoin payments, digital wallets, real-time payments, and cash vouchers, with Radar.

Learn more about how Stripe can help you go global faster, or contact us.

posts.title: Python Typing Survey 2026: AI Tools and the Shifting Checker Landscape
posts.summary: The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more…
posts.content:
.entry-header
  • The 2026 Python Typing Survey received 1,794 responses. 
  • Type hint use changed little across three years, but checker selection changed sharply. 
  • Among respondents who reported which checkers they use, half selected more than one, and missing library type information was the most common difficulty.

For the third consecutive year, we asked Python developers how they use and experience Python typing: the language features, specifications, and tools used to describe and check types in Python code. We run the survey to learn what is working and what library maintainers, tool builders, documentation authors, and standards contributors should tackle next.

Most respondents were experienced Python developers: 76.4% had used Python for at least five years. The clearest change was the shift in checker choice, while missing library type information remained the most common difficulty.

Key Takeaways From the 2026 Python Typing Survey

This year’s findings show several recurring opportunities:

Broader and more accurate type information would help users of data-science packages: Dynamic frameworks pose a different challenge because current type systems cannot express some runtime behavior. Possible directions include new typing features and checker support tailored to individual libraries and frameworks.

Tool builders could focus on editor feedback and an initial checker run that requires little configuration: Error messages could link to short explanations and examples. Typing documentation can assume Python experience. Projects using multiple checkers would benefit from clear explanations of intentional differences between them.

Better callable syntax remains a practical area for standards work, especially if improvements keep common typing tasks straightforward.

AI usage remains an open question: The findings on AI leave an open question about which interactions between AI tools and type checkers help developers. Further empirical study could inform future designs.

AI Tools Now Write Types and Respond to Checker Errors

The share of respondents who selected “Makes AI-generated code more accurate/reliable” rose from 18.5% in 2025 to 38.4% in 2026. AI tools wrote type hints for 42.5% of 1,517 respondents, while 32.6% wrote types to improve AI-generated code. Respondents also used AI to fix or explain type errors. Across all four activities listed for AI tool use in typing, 61.0% of respondents reported they used at least one of these options.

Some respondents said their AI coding tool runs the checker and then fixes the errors. Of the 1,517 developers who answered how they run a checker, 24.4%, said an AI coding tool invoked their checker. Among the 370 respondents, 61.6% also used AI to fix checker errors. The rate was 19.3% among everyone else.

Some respondents described AI-generated types that are too broad and agents that suppress checker errors:

“I fix AI coded type hints because AI often gets lazy and uses object for everything.”

“Lazy coding agents that spam #type: ignore comments everywhere.”

When asked how useful types are for better AI-assisted coding, 29.8% of 1,551 respondents chose “I’m not sure.” The uncertainty rate for AI-assisted coding was nearly four times the 7.7% rate for runtime guarantees, the next-highest of the six benefits. We still need empirical evidence about which interactions actually help.

The Pyrefly team is already studying how AI coding tools and type checkers work together. At the 2026 Python Typing Summit, the team presented Type Checking in Agentic Workflows.

Library Gaps Lead Overall; Occasional Users Struggle With Complexity

Missing type information in third-party libraries was the leading difficulty, selected by 65.1% of 1,486 respondents. Another 44.6% said the type system could not describe everything their code does.

Developers can still have a poor experience after a library ships dedicated stubs. Among 156 people who wrote their own answer, 22 described dynamic constructs, decorators, metaprogramming, or framework behavior. Ten described arrays, dataframes, or scientific typing, and at least eight described annotations that were inaccurate, incomplete, or too broad. Respondents repeatedly named Django, SQLAlchemy, Pydantic, NumPy, pandas, and Polars.

“Django does so much black magic it’s a wonder a type checker works at all.” — survey respondent

Library maintainers need annotations that capture how frameworks and data-science libraries behave. The Pyrefly team has been working with Quansight to improve third-party library typing, including contributions to pandas-stubs and NumPy.

Frequency of use changed which problems stood out. Among developers who used type hints rarely or sometimes, 41.6% found the type system too complex or verbose. The rate was 14.5% among developers who used type hints often or always. Missing library typing affected 36.2% of the lower-frequency group and 70.0% of the higher-frequency group.

“I use the straightforward parts and avoid the parts that are difficult to understand.” — survey respondent. 

Years of typing experience showed a different pattern. Complexity was reported by 18.2% of respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 16.0% with three to six years, and 21.0% with seven or more. Newer typing users were often regular users and experienced Python developers: Of the 396 respondents with zero to two years of typing experience, 306 (77.3%) used type hints often or always and 345 (87.1%) had used Python for at least three years.

Guidance for developers who are new to typing should assume Python experience and show how to add types to an existing repository. Occasional users need a useful first check with little configuration and easy-to-understand errors. As we change the type system, we should aim to support more patterns without making common tasks harder.

Better Callable syntax is one practical place to start. It was the most selected missing feature, chosen by 45.7% of the 1,486 respondents who answered the question. The selection rate was similar for respondents who reported complexity and the rest of the sample.

Newer Checkers Gained Ground Quickly

Frequent type hint use remained between 85.5% and 88.0% across the three surveys: 88.0% in 2024, 85.9% in 2025, and 85.5% in 2026. A different group answered each year, but the overall rate remained consistent.

Checker choice was far less stable. When the 2024 Python Typing survey asked what feature was missing from the Python type system, one response now reads like a preview of the changes captured in this year’s results:

“A faster Mypy. Its lack of speed led to ecosystem fracturing and other type checkers don’t support Mypy plugins and behave differently in general.” – survey respondent

By 2026, developers had several newer open-source checkers to choose from. Speed or performance topped the reasons for choosing a checker, at 56.5%. Using the same list of checkers in both years, 49.9% selected two or more in 2026, up from 46.0% in 2025.

Developers Mix Checkers Across Their Workflows

Of the 700 respondents who selected Mypy, 297 also selected its editor plugin. Another 314 selected a different named checker integration without selecting the Mypy plugin.

Most Pyrefly respondents also selected another checker: 220 of 264, or 83.3%. In the free-text responses, developers described why their teams divide work between checkers:

“Because my team members use different IDEs, we use multiple type checkers for development, but rely on Mypy for linting (local and CI).” — survey respondent

“Locally we primarily use Pyright because it’s the only option we’ve tried that fully understands all the more niche typing patterns within our codebase. In CI/CD, we do a Pyrefly run and only run Pyright on files where Pyrefly fails, to improve performance of the check.” — survey respondent 

Among the 1,486 developers who answered the question about difficulties, 33.3% reported inconsistencies between checkers. Among the 738 respondents who selected multiple static checkers and answered the difficulty question, 315 (42.7%) reported inconsistencies between checkers.

IDE Support Remains Central as Typing Help Moves Away From Stack Overflow

Readability or documentation was the most selected reason to use type hints, chosen by 93.6% of 1,571 respondents. Editor support also ranked highly: 84.8% of the 1,494 people who gave it a numeric rating chose 4 or 5. About 39% of the 103 developers who supplied their own reason mentioned completion, navigation, hover information, or editor error messages.

“Drastically improves IDE tooltip/autocomplete.” – survey respondent 

Real-time editor feedback was widespread: 82.9% of 1,517 respondents ran a type checker in an editor. VS Code was the most selected editor or IDE, at 59.3%.

Where developers look for help has changed as well. From 2024 to 2026, Stack Overflow use fell from 46.4% to 22.9%, while large language model (LLM) chat rose from 26.0% to 41.7%. Python typing documentation rose from 56.2% to 65.9%. Checker-specific documentation ended at 60.5%, up from 52.2% after a dip in 2025. General Python documentation fell from 66.7% to 62.2%.

As developers move from Stack Overflow to typing- and checker-specific documentation, the quality of those sources matters more. Error messages should link to short, relevant explanations and examples. Links to documentation would also give LLM chat tools better information to work with.

Survey Results and Raw Data

Download the full results and data from the Python Typing Survey 2026.

Acknowledgements

The survey ran from August 5 through September 2, 2026. It was developed with support from the Pyrefly team at Meta, the PyCharm team at JetBrains, the Python team at Microsoft, the ty team at Astral/OpenAI, and community contributors on discuss.python.org. We shared it through Reddit, X, Mastodon, newsletters, the Python typing forum, LinkedIn, Bluesky, Discord, Slack, and type-checker project websites and social accounts. We lightly edited quotations for spelling, grammar, and punctuation. We thank everyone who responded, shared the survey, reviewed the data, or contributed to the Python typing community.

posts.title: Data governance with annotations in Amazon S3
posts.summary: Attach governance context such as classification, retention, residency, and PII flags directly to your Amazon S3 objects with S3 annotations. This post walks through the end-to-end pattern and the handful of S3…
posts.content:
If you run data governance in Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), the context that matters most probably lives somewhere other than S3. Think of how an object is classified, which retention policy applies to it, where the data may reside, and whether it holds personally identifiable information (PII). You typically keep that context in a separate database, one system away from the objects it describes.

Amazon S3 annotations closes that gap. You can attach the governance context directly to the S3 object, without rewriting the object. A single object version can carry up to 1,000 annotations. Each one is a UTF-8 payload between 1 byte and 1 MB, in a format such as JSON, XML, YAML, or plain text. That’s room for a complete governance record rather than a few key-value pairs.

Annotations give you five properties that are hard to get from a separate metadata store:

  • Context that travels with the data – S3 stores annotations with the object version rather than in a separate system. When you copy or replicate an object, S3 moves the annotations with it, so a classification or residency label accompanies a disaster-recovery copy.
  • Context you can revise in place – Updating an annotation doesn’t rewrite the object or change its ETag, so a record’s classification can be corrected, or a generated label promoted from proposed to reviewed, as the context is validated.
  • Governance answers without reading the data – A consumer with read-only annotation access can answer a question such as “which objects hold PII and have an expired retention policy” per object through the annotation APIs, or across the bucket through an S3 Metadata annotation table.
  • Context stays readable in any storage class – Even when an object is archived in a cold storage class, its annotations stay directly readable. You can retrieve the governance context for an object in Amazon S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or S3 Glacier Deep Archive without restoring the object first. You pay S3 Standard rates for annotations regardless of the parent object’s storage class.
  • SQL at scale – An S3 Metadata annotation table, which is an Apache Iceberg table, makes the same context queryable with Amazon Athena or any Iceberg-compatible engine across a large object population.

This post walks through the pattern end to end, then the handful of S3 behaviors that determine whether the design is correct. Each behavior comes with the documented rule and a working example: an annotation payload, an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policy statement, or an AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) call.

Prerequisites

To follow along and adapt the examples, you need the following:

  • An AWS account with an S3 bucket that has versioning enabled.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal with permission to configure bucket policies and annotation actions.
  • The AWS CLI installed and configured.

Familiarity with S3 annotations concepts, object versioning, and IAM identity-based policies is assumed.

The governance record

Consider a governed bucket where each object is a business record such as a contract, policy document, or customer record. You build an enrichment pipeline that reads each new object and records a governance annotation. That annotation captures the classification, the applicable retention policy, the jurisdiction and data residency, a PII inventory, and a short rationale. Annotations aren’t limited to governance context. The same mechanism can attach other object context, such as a short content summary or a processing date. In this pattern, the annotation is written after the upload completes, through the annotation API operations. The same process backfills objects that predate the pipeline, through the separate path shown in the architecture section.

A PutObjectAnnotation call writes exactly one uniquely named annotation on a given object version, and an object version can hold up to 1,000 annotations. How you distribute a governance record across them is a design choice. With granular annotations, you can update one aspect of the context without rewriting the rest, keep an accidental overwrite scoped to a single field, and query finer-grained units in an S3 Metadata annotation table, which you optionally enable for richer queryability. A single annotation that holds the whole record keeps each write and each read to one operation, and keeps the record internally consistent. There’s no partial state across several names to reconcile. This post uses one annotation, named governance-context, because the record here is authored and consumed as a unit.

The payload looks like the following.

{
  "schema_version": "1.0",
  "classification": "confidential",
  "retention": {
    "policy": "contracts-7y",
    "effective_date": "2026-06-01",
    "expires_on": "2033-06-01",
    "status": "active"
  },
  "jurisdiction": "EU",
  "data_residency": "eu-west-1",
  "pii": {
    "present": true,
    "categories": ["name", "email", "national_id"]
  },
  "rationale": "Signed customer contract containing personal data of EU data subjects; classified confidential under the 7-year contracts retention policy.",
  "generated_by": "enrichment-process",
  "generated_at": "2026-06-29T10:15:00Z",
  "review_required": true
}

When a record is reviewed or reclassified, the enrichment process updates the annotation in place with PutObjectAnnotation. The classification changes without rewriting the object or changing its ETag. That in-place update is itself replicated, so a later re-classification on the source keeps a cross-Region copy’s context current without recopying the object. This works as long as the replication role carries the annotation-replication permission described later in this post.

Objects that predate the pipeline need the same context. A backfill pass annotates existing object versions in bulk with the same PutObjectAnnotation call, so the write path covers new objects as they arrive while the backfill path brings the existing population up to the same standard. Both paths appear in the architecture that follows.

On the read side, a consumer with read-only annotation access answers the governance question by listing and retrieving annotation context. There are no object reads and no separate governance database.

At scale, you activate an S3 Metadata annotation table with a bucket metadata configuration that names an IAM role S3 assumes to read your annotations. S3 then provisions and maintains a table in Amazon S3 Tables, a capability of Amazon S3, backed by Apache Iceberg, that you query with SQL. The role trusts the metadata.s3.amazonaws.com service principal. That turns the same question into one Athena statement across a large object population. S3 populates the table asynchronously, and the initial backfill can take minutes to hours depending on how many objects and annotations the bucket holds. Query results reflect annotations as of the most recent table refresh, which typically happens within about an hour, so treat them as eventually consistent rather than real time.

SELECT object_key, object_version_id
FROM "s3tablescatalog/aws-s3"."b_amzn_s3_demo_governance"."annotation"
WHERE name = 'governance-context'
AND json_extract_scalar(text_value, '$.pii.present') = 'true'
AND json_extract_scalar(text_value, '$.retention.status') = 'expired';

Reference architecture for the pattern

The pattern sits inside an event-driven system with S3 at the center, shown in Figure 1. It carries four paths. A write path enriches new objects, a maintenance path keeps context current, a backfill path annotates existing objects, and a read path serves consumers from annotation context alone.

Figure 1: Event-driven architecture for authoring, maintaining, backfilling, and reading S3 annotation governance context.

The numbered steps in Figure 1 trace the four paths:

  1. A producer uploads an object to the governed S3 bucket with PutObject.
  2. S3 emits an object-created event to Amazon EventBridge. When you route through Amazon EventBridge rather than invoking AWS Lambda directly from S3, you can filter on event attributes such as prefix or object size. You can also route the same event to multiple targets without changing the bucket configuration. A direct notification or an Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) queue is a reasonable simpler choice if you don’t need that routing.
  3. Amazon EventBridge invokes the enrichment Lambda function.
  4. The function calls the Amazon Bedrock enrichment agent to classify the object and extract retention, jurisdiction, and PII context. The agent returns the structured context to the function (dashed return arrow). Have the function validate that the output parses as JSON and conforms to your schema before it writes anything. Models often wrap JSON in a Markdown code fence, and an annotation payload must be the raw structured document.
  5. The function writes the context to the object with PutObjectAnnotation. The write emits an s3:ObjectAnnotation:Put event notification that downstream consumers can subscribe to, which fits the event-driven design.
  6. On a schedule, Amazon EventBridge Scheduler re-invokes the enrichment function to re-assess and update annotations in place.
  7. To annotate objects that predate the pipeline, S3 Batch Operations invokes a backfill Lambda function.
  8. The backfill function writes context with PutObjectAnnotation.
  9. A consumer asks the Bedrock consumer agent a governance question, and the agent returns a grounded answer (dashed return arrow).
  10. The consumer agent lists and retrieves the relevant annotations with ListObjectAnnotations and GetObjectAnnotation. S3 returns annotation context only, never the object body (dashed return arrow).
  11. For queries across many objects, the consumer agent queries Athena.
  12. Athena reads the S3 Metadata annotation table, which S3 maintains automatically from the object annotations (dashed “maintains” relationship).

The scheduled update in step 6 needs one guard: a conditional write on the object’s ETag. Pass the ETag with the --object-if-match CLI parameter, which maps to the x-amz-object-if-match request header.

An ETag is the identifier S3 returns for an object version’s content. The function reads it when it fetches the object and passes it back on the write. If the object was overwritten in the meantime, the ETag no longer matches and the annotation write fails. That guards against overwriting context that belongs to a version the function never evaluated.

The behaviors that decide your design

The plumbing is straightforward. The behaviors in this section are where teams most often get a governance design wrong. Each behavior appears in the documentation, and each has a governance implication that becomes clear only when you trace it through. One principle predicts most of them:

An annotation is caller-authored context bound to a specific object version. S3 stores it and moves it, but it doesn’t interpret or validate its meaning. The annotation’s lifecycle follows the object version’s lifecycle.

Two consequences follow. Because an annotation is bound to an object version, versioning behavior governs whether your context stays or disappears: delete markers, version-specific deletes, and overwrites all change what remains attached. And because S3 doesn’t interpret the content, a classification your agent writes is only as trustworthy as the process that produced it. For each behavior, ask what the annotation is bound to, and what the object version’s lifecycle does in that situation.

Deletion is scoped to the object version

A common governance requirement is to delete a data subject’s records on request. The annotation is bound to a specific object version, so it disappears only when that version disappears. Deleting the object and assuming its context goes with it is correct only in a non-versioned bucket.

In a versioned bucket, a DELETE request without a version ID creates a delete marker and leaves the underlying version, along with its annotations, in place. The object no longer appears in a ListObjectsV2 response, so it looks gone. It’s still returned by ListObjectVersions, and the PII context you recorded still exists on that prior version.

To actually remove the annotations, delete the specific version.

aws s3api delete-object \
  --bucket amzn-s3-demo-governance \
  --key contracts/acme-msa.pdf \
  --version-id <VERSION_ID>

To expire noncurrent versions on a schedule instead, apply an S3 Lifecycle configuration such as the following. It permanently deletes noncurrent versions 30 days after they become noncurrent.

{
  "Rules": [
    {
      "ID": "expire-noncurrent-governed-records",
      "Filter": { "Prefix": "contracts/" },
      "Status": "Enabled",
      "NoncurrentVersionExpiration": { "NoncurrentDays": 30 }
    }
  ]
}

A lifecycle rule expires versions on a time schedule. It can’t read annotation values. If you want an object’s classification or retention status to trigger expiration or deletion, your own automation has to read the annotation and issue the delete. If the trigger you need is an event rather than a value, such as a contract closing or an audit completing, Object Lock event holds handle that natively and you don’t need to build the automation.

Don’t rely on a plain delete for a right-to-be-forgotten workflow in a versioned bucket. Decide up front whether you will issue version-targeted deletes or expire noncurrent versions, make that the only supported path in your tooling, and test it against a real object. The failure mode is silent. Version-targeted deletion is also permanent, so tooling that deletes the wrong version destroys data that is recoverable only from a separate backup.

Object Lock freezes annotations

Governance buckets frequently use S3 Object Lock, and annotations count as modifications to the object version, which Object Lock blocks. While a version is under an active Object Lock retention, PutObjectAnnotation and DeleteObjectAnnotation are both denied with AccessDenied and the message “object protected by object lock retention,” in both Governance and Compliance mode. Reading annotations still works, so consumers are unaffected. What you can’t do is add or update a governance annotation on a version whose retention has already started.

That makes sequencing a design rule: Annotate the object first, then apply the retention period. An annotation written before the lock survives and remains readable, but it’s frozen until retention expires. If your agent re-assesses classifications over time, plan the retention duration and the enrichment cadence together. Where retention starts on a future event rather than at write time, there’s no known end to that frozen window when you annotate, so write the complete governance record before the hold goes on.

The retention mode also changes the right-to-be-forgotten path. In Governance mode, a version-targeted delete of a locked version is denied unless the caller holds s3:BypassGovernanceRetention and passes --bypass-governance-retention. That workflow therefore needs the permission and an approval step around it. In Compliance mode, no one can delete the version, including the root user, until retention expires, so a request may not be satisfiable before then.

Event holds add a third case. A version under an event hold is protected while the hold is in place. Releasing the hold starts the retention period rather than ending protection, so releasing it moves a deletion request further away rather than closer. IAM and bucket policy condition keys govern who may set or release a hold and can enforce minimum and maximum durations, which is where the approval gate belongs.

Object Lock and annotations do different jobs. Object Lock enforces retention, including event-based retention through event holds. The annotation records which policy applies and why, which is context Object Lock doesn’t store. One protects the object, the other explains the decision.

Multipart copies drop annotations unless you opt in

Governance labels are only useful if they stay attached as data moves. For a CopyObject request (objects up to 5 GiB), S3 copies annotations along with the object by default.

For larger objects copied with multipart upload, annotations aren’t copied unless you opt in. Multipart upload is what the AWS CLI and SDKs use through their transfer managers above roughly 8 MB. The default is easy to overlook, because the behavior changes with object size rather than with the command you run. A copy that carries its labels on a small object silently drops them once the object crosses the multipart threshold, with no error or warning. With the multipart opt-in, the SDK writes the annotations after the copy completes, so the destination object exists briefly without all its annotations.

aws s3 cp \
  s3://amzn-s3-demo-governance/contracts/acme-msa.pdf \
  s3://amzn-s3-demo-governance-dr/contracts/acme-msa.pdf \
  --copy-props all

When you call CopyObject directly, the x-amz-annotation-directive header gives explicit control. COPY includes the source annotations on the destination object, and EXCLUDE omits them. Reach for EXCLUDE when you deliberately want a reduced-sensitivity copy.

Set this once as a default rather than deciding per call. Standardize on the copy-props opt-in in every annotation-dependent copy path. Confirm it with a test that copies an object larger than the multipart threshold, because a small-object test would pass while hiding the problem.

Annotation deletion and overwrite are irreversible

Object versioning gives you a safety net. Annotations don’t have one. There’s no delete marker and no version history for an annotation, even in a versioned bucket, so after you delete one it’s gone. The same is true of an update: writing a new payload to an existing annotation name overwrites the previous content in place. That makes an accidental overwrite as destructive as a delete.

Treat annotation deletion as a deliberate, gated action rather than routine cleanup. Restrict s3:DeleteObjectAnnotation to a dedicated administrative role, with an approval step. If a record’s context might be needed for an audit, subscribe to the s3:ObjectAnnotation:Put and s3:ObjectAnnotation:Delete event notifications, or use the S3 Metadata journal table, to keep an audit trail of annotation changes, so that removing the annotation doesn’t erase your only copy of the governance decision.

posts.title: Recommended resilience testing in the next generation of AWS Resilience Hub
posts.summary: The next generation of AWS Resilience Hub introduces recommended resilience testing: four pre-configured, AWS FIS-powered tests that validate how your service detects and recovers from failures across Availability…
posts.content:
Organizations that have defined resilience policies and assessed their applications face a common next step: verifying those applications behave as expected when failures occur. Designing fault injection experiments manually requires deep expertise. You need to know which faults to inject, which resources to target, and how to judge whether the outcome counts as success. Many teams do not know where to start, and experiments built by hand can drift out of date as architectures evolve.

Recommended resilience testing in the next generation of AWS Resilience Hub addresses this. It’s a new capability that helps you validate how your services respond to and recover from failure scenarios. The tests are pre-configured and powered by AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS).

Recommended resilience testing uses what AWS Resilience Hub already knows about your service, including its resources, dependencies, and resilience policy. With this information, AWS Resilience Hub automatically creates FIS experiments, injects faults, and evaluates the results against your success criteria and recovery time objective (RTO). It uses that evaluation to determine a pass or fail outcome. What used to be manual experiment design becomes an out-of-the-box test with built-in success evaluation based on your policy. Each test run auto-generates a report, accessible through the Resilience Hub console.

Customers frequently ask which failure modes to test for and what prescriptive testing guidance we can offer. AWS Resilience Hub answers this by providing four tests at launch, selected based on your service’s architecture and resilience policy.

Availability Zone: recovery – Validates your service can detect and recover from an Availability Zone impairment. The test injects the symptoms of a power interruption in a single Availability Zone, affecting compute, networking, storage, and database resources within that AZ. It confirms your service detects the impaired AZ, continues operating in the healthy AZs, and returns to a healthy state within your defined RTO. It can also help surface single-AZ dependencies you might not be aware of.

Dependency validation – Validates how your service responds when its dependencies within the AWS Region are impaired. If you have enabled dependency discovery, the discovered soft dependency with the highest query volume is pre-selected by default. You can adjust the selection to target individual dependencies or specific groups. The dependency validation test blocks dependencies within the Region to see how your service behaves when they are unavailable. It can help you validate that your service remains healthy when soft dependencies are impaired, and surface dependencies you might not have known were hard. You can also include known hard dependencies to understand their impact and confirm your service detects and responds when they are unavailable. We recommend starting with a single soft dependency and expanding from there.

Multi-Region: isolation – Validates your service can operate independently from a Region when connectivity to another Region is unavailable. The test blocks connectivity between the two Regions, including network traffic, cross-Region data replication, and selected dependencies. This test applies to both active-active and active-passive architectures, and is also a useful precursor to the Multi-Region: recovery test.

Multi-Region: recovery – Validates that your service can recover and serve clients within your defined RTO after a Region is impaired. The test introduces failures into dependencies in the selected Region. Through success alarms, it confirms that your service recovers within your defined RTO in the recovery Region and remains healthy for the duration of the test. You perform the recovery action yourself, such as triggering a failover or executing an Amazon Application Recovery Controller (ARC) Region switch plan.

Each test works at three levels. A test template is the pre-configured recommendation, specifying the fault actions, target resource types, and parameters. A test is your configured instance of a template for your service, with your success alarms, stop conditions, and settings. A test run is a single execution that scopes to your current resources and produces a pass/fail outcome with results and a report. You can run the same test quarterly, monthly, or on demand. To get to that pass/fail outcome you can use success criteria in the test.

Choose success criteria that reflect your service’s health and customer experience, such as order success rate or end-to-end availability, rather than the state of individual resources. The impaired resources are expected to be unhealthy. What you are validating is whether your service as a whole absorbed the failure. Combined with your resilience policy, these criteria determine the pass/fail outcome.

For recovery tests (Availability Zone recovery and Multi-Region recovery), the test passes when all success criteria return to a healthy state within the RTO defined in your policy and hold until the test ends. This validates not just that your service recovered, but that it recovered fast enough to meet your stated objectives.

For sustained tests (Dependency validation and Multi-Region isolation), the test passes when all success criteria hold their thresholds from fault injection through the end of the test, proving your service remained healthy throughout the impairment.

You can also select additional alarms for observability only, such as watching the impaired Region degrade. These appear in results and reports without affecting the outcome.

Deep dive: Dependency validation

Of the four recommended resilience tests, dependency validation was one of the most requested capabilities by our customers, and for good reason. Modern applications depend on dozens of services, and understanding which of those dependencies your application can function without is the key to building a resilient application. The dependency validation test determines whether your application continues to work when a given dependency becomes unavailable.

How dependency validation works

The dependency validation test blocks connectivity to your selected dependencies within an AWS Region to observe how your service behaves when they are unavailable. It validates that your service remains healthy when soft dependencies are impaired and surfaces dependencies you might not have known were hard. You can also include known hard dependencies to understand their failure impact.

This is a sustained test. Unlike recovery tests that measure whether you meet your RTO, the dependency validation test passes when all success alarms remain in OK state from the moment faults are injected through the end of the test.

Dependency discovery

You can define dependencies in two ways:

  1. Turn on dependency discovery. This uses DNS query log analysis with a 35-day look-back window and continuous polling to automatically identify the AWS services, internal endpoints, and third-party endpoints your service calls. Dependency discovery surfaces dependencies you might not be aware of, including unexpected cross-Region calls, critical third-party dependencies, and infrequently accessed services that could cause failures during incidents.
  2. Manually enter DNS endpoints directly when configuring the test.

After you define your dependencies, we recommend classifying each one as a soft or hard dependency.

ClassificationWhen to useExampleWhat the test validatesSoftYour service degrades but continues operating without this dependencyAnalytics API, notification service, feature flags, recommendation engineApplication handles absence gracefully. Test should passHardYour service fails if this dependency is unavailablePrimary database, authentication service, credential exchangeApplication detects failure and handles it gracefully. Test might fail (this is expected and informative)

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure you have at least one service created and assessed in the next generation of Resilience Hub. You would also require an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) service role for the next generation of Resilience Hub to assume when running a resilience test. This role can either be created in the next generation of Resilience Hub console or you can specify an existing one.

Configuring the test

From your service dashboard in the next generation of Resilience Hub, choose the Testing tab. You will see four recommended resilience tests. Select Dependency validation, and then choose Edit test configuration.

The configuration page walks you through six sections:

1. Basic settings

Test duration: The length of time fault actions run. Set any value from 1 minute to 12 hours (default: 30 minutes). After the duration, the test takes a few additional minutes to evaluate success before it ends.

Dependency Region: The AWS Region where your service is deployed that you want to test for dependency failures.

2. Dependencies to block

This is where the distinction between soft and hard dependencies directly drives your test.

Default behavior:

The discovered soft dependency with the highest query volume is pre-selected. If no dependencies have been classified as soft, none are pre-selected.

  • Discovered dependencies: A selection box pre-populated with dependencies found in your service in the selected AWS Region. You can choose up to 10 dependencies to test.
  • (Optional) Additional dependencies: Expand this section to include hard dependencies or dependencies not listed in the primary selection. If you didn’t run any dependency discovery, you can use this field to enter a DNS address that will be blocked as a dependency.

Best practice: Start with a single soft dependency and expand from there, progressively building confidence in your application’s failure handling before including hard dependencies.

3. Test actions (fault actions)

The next generation of Resilience Hub uses AWS FIS actions to block connectivity to your selected dependencies, automatically targeting resources discovered in your service. The fault actions inject 100 percent packet loss at the compute layer, dropping traffic to the selected dependencies:

Fault actionWhat it doesaws:ssm:send-commandDrops traffic from Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instances to the selected dependenciesaws:ecs:task-network-packet-lossDrops traffic from Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) tasks (EC2 and AWS Fargate) to the selected dependenciesaws:eks:pod-network-packet-lossDrops traffic from Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) pods to the selected dependencies

When the test starts, it matches actions to resources discovered in your service. If no resources match an action’s target type, that action is skipped. This means the test automatically adapts to your compute environment, whether you are running on Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS, or a combination.

Additional setup required: The setup for these actions depends on your compute type. You need an AWS Systems Manager Agent container in your Amazon ECS task definition, a Kubernetes service account for Amazon EKS pods, or AWS Systems Manager Agent installed on your Amazon EC2 instances.

4. Test alarms

Alarms determine whether the test passes or fails. Select alarms discovered from your service that reflect service performance and customer experience. For example, order success rate for an ecommerce service or transactions processed for a payments system.

  • Success alarms: The next generation of Resilience Hub uses these to validate whether your service passed or failed the test. Choose alarms that measure your service’s health across the AWS Region.
  • (Optional) Additional alarms: Tracked during the test run and shown in the report, but don’t affect the test outcome. Use additional alarms for observability to monitor how these alarms behave during the dependency impairment.

How to pass: The test passes if all success alarms remain in OK state until the test actions end.

Success criteria and additional alarms share a limit of 5 per configuration update.

5. Stop conditions, reports, and logs

Stop conditions: Amazon CloudWatch alarms that act as guardrails. If breached, they stop the test automatically to protect your workloads. Choose up to five alarms. They must be in the account where the test runs and the AWS Region where the faults are injected.

(Optional) Reports: If you configure an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket as a report destination on your service, the next generation of Resilience Hub generates a report after each test run that includes the test configuration, alarm status, timeline, and results.

Logs: Optionally send test logs to an Amazon S3 bucket or Amazon CloudWatch Logs for deeper analysis. The next generation of Resilience Hub doesn’t charge for sending logs, though ingestion and storage charges apply.

6. Test permissions

The test requires an IAM role to grant access to AWS services and resources. For single account setups, you need one execution role. For multi-account setups, you need an orchestrator role in the account running the test and a target role in each account containing targeted resources. You can create the role directly from AWS Management Console with required permissions pre-configured or use an existing role. Once saved, the role is used by default for future runs.

Note: Updating test settings might change required IAM permissions. Required permissions vary based on the trust policy, fault actions, and test options selected. Always review the IAM role instructions to confirm correct permissions.

Running the test: What success and failure look like

The value of the dependency validation test becomes clear when you compare results across dependency classifications. We walk through two test runs on the same service with the same success alarms: one blocking soft dependencies, one blocking hard dependencies.

Test run: Soft dependencies blocked — PASSED ✅

Dependencies blocked:

  • Payment Gateway.
  • Notification Service.

Success alarms:

  • canary-heartbeat-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors service health check availability.
  • canary-order-flow-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors end-to-end order processing.

Figure 1: Soft dependency test run with both success alarms holding in OK state for the full test duration

What the results show: Both alarms remained in OK state (solid green) from the moment test actions started through the end of the test. The application continued functioning normally without Payment Gateway and Notification Service. The order flow kept processing. The heartbeat kept responding. The service handled the absence of its soft dependencies gracefully, exactly as designed.

What this proves: These dependencies are correctly classified as soft. Your application can tolerate the loss of these dependencies, suppressing notifications without impacting the customer-facing order flow.

Test run: Hard dependencies blocked — FAILED ❌

Dependencies blocked:

  • Amazon Cognito.
  • AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS).

Success alarms:

  • canary-heartbeat-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors service health check availability.
  • canary-order-flow-canary-failure-us-east-2: Monitors end-to-end order processing.

Figure 2: Hard dependency test run with the order-flow alarm entering alarm state while the heartbeat alarm stays healthy

What the results show: The heartbeat canary stayed green throughout. The application did not become unavailable. But the order-flow canary transitioned to alarm state (red) immediately after faults were injected and remained there until the test ended. Without Amazon Cognito (authentication) and AWS STS (credential exchange), the application couldn’t complete the business-critical order flow.

What this proves: Amazon Cognito and AWS STS are correctly classified as hard dependencies. The test confirms that their absence impacts critical functionality, but importantly, it also shows the failure was contained. The application did not cascade into a complete failure. It continued responding (heartbeat passed) while the specific business flow that required authentication failed gracefully.

Interpreting results: A decision framework

Test results aren’t simply pass or fail. A passing test can still surface a misclassified dependency, and a failing test can confirm that a dependency is genuinely critical. What matters is reading the outcome against how you classified the dependency, so you know whether your architecture behaved as intended and what to do about it.

The following decision framework helps you interpret the results of each test, understand what they mean, and decide what to do next.

ScenarioExpected OutcomeWhat it meansWhat to do nextSoft dependency blocked → test passesYesGraceful degradation is working. Classification is accurate.No action required. Your architecture handles this failure correctly.Soft dependency blocked → test failsNoThe dependency might be misclassified as soft when it’s actually hard. Or your degradation logic has a gap.Review application behavior. Reclassify as hard, or fix the degradation path.Hard dependency blocked → test failsYesConfirms the classification. Critical functionality is impacted without this dependency.Verify the failure is graceful (no cascading failures, no data corruption, no hung connections). Consider whether you can add retry/fallback to reclassify as soft in the future.Hard dependency blocked → test passesNoThe dependency might be misclassified. It could actually be soft. This could also indicate the dependency isn’t being called as intended.Investigate whether your application is more resilient than expected, or whether the dependency is not being exercised. Reclassify if appropriate or fix the application logic.
