posts.title: Meta Networking at the 2026 OCP Global Summit: Open Innovation for Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across AI Networks
posts.summary: At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark, and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Ravindra Sunkad, Omar Baldonado

At the 2026 Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit, Meta shared the networking innovations that are directly supporting our latest AI models, including Muse Wonder and Muse Spark, and our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster. 

Highlights

  • IcePack & IceCube: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack with 102.4T switch blades (128×800G, Broadcom Tomahawk 6C and NVIDIA Spectrum-6 variants), running FBOSS. 
  • Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF) for scale-out: Meta’s multi-plane scale-out fabric where each GPU connects to eight network planes. 3-tier → 2-tier Clos, NIC-level packet spraying, and a combined host+switch control plane. Built with NVIDIA and shared with our cloud partners.
  • Scale-across: BAG, our petabit-scale super-spine joining buildings, campuses, and regions in our gigawatt-scale Prometheus cluster, plus SRv6 regional backbones on FBOSS + SAI.
  • Ethernet for scale-up: Tahan, the Ethernet scale-up switch for MTIA 300 based on Broadcom Tomahawk5; a preview of 72 accelerators per rack on 102.4T silicon; and ESUN progressing from 1.0 → 1.1.
  • OSPA: a new OCP initiative co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba to standardize the switch platform layer. v1.0 spec submitted to OCP.
  • MetaRoCE: our RDMA transport for AI networks, now going open source.

We shared insights into key networking-related initiatives through talks from many of the Meta network and hardware teams. Those talks and their slide decks are now available to everyone! 

Keynote and Executive Sessions

Concrete to Code: Engineering AI Infrastructure at Gigawatt Scale (video)
AI has changed the shape of infrastructure. Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure at Meta, shares how Meta is designing, building, and operating at a scale that requires rethinking the network, the facility, and the systems that hold it all together.
Speaker: Santosh Janardhan, Head of Infrastructure, Meta

Betting on the Network: Meta’s Case for Full-Stack, Open AI Networking (video)
AI progress now depends on the network as much as on compute. The path forward is a full-stack, open approach built in the open ecosystem rather than behind proprietary walls.
Speaker: Omar Baldonado, Senior Director, Data Center & AI Networking, Meta

Breaking the Walls: Open Scale-Across for the AI Era (video)
Training compute is compounding faster than infrastructure can scale. This talk lays out why open scale-across networking is needed to connect AI capacity across data centers and regions.
Speakers: Vipul Deokar, VP, Core Network Infrastructure, Meta; Rakesh Chopra, SVP, Silicon & Systems Architecture and Engineering Fellow, Cisco; Tom Williams, VP, Marketing, Cisco

Switch Platforms, Optics, and Interconnect

Meta 102.4T Ethernet Switch (video)
IceCube is Meta’s 102.4T switch that goes into our liquid-cooled Icepack rack. Icecube and N-IceCube are based on a 2OU, hybrid liquid/air-cooled, PHY-less design and incorporate either the Broadcom Tomahawk 6C or NVIDIA Spectrum-6 ASICs with 128x800GE of non-blocking capacity.
Speakers: Rongchun Zhou, Network Hardware Engineer, Meta; Reza Niazmand, Network Technical Program Manager, Meta

Integrated Optics at Scale: From 51.2T CPO Validation to Meta’s 102.4T (video)
A look at why integrated optics matter for rack-scale AI — power, density, disaggregation, and reliability — and what Meta learned validating 51.2T co-packaged optics that could carry over to 102.4T.
Speakers: Granthana Rangaswamy, Hardware Engineer, Meta; Siamak Amiralizadeh, Optical Engineer, Meta; Xu Wang, Hardware Engineer, Meta

Operating Linear Pluggable Optics at Hyperscale (video)
At AI scale, the per-module retimer DSP is a repeated tax in power, heat, and cost across millions of links — but removing it moves equalization and triage onto the host. This talk answers whether linear optics can match retimed reliability at fleet scale.
Speakers: Amin Yekani, Optical Engineer, Meta; Qing Wang, Optical Engineer, Meta

Large-Scale Deployment of 800G AECs in Meta Data Centers (video)
The economics of AI networking are set at the short-reach link. This session covers Meta’s large-scale deployment of 800Gb/s active electrical cables and the component quality work behind it.
Speakers: Jingyu (Kevin) Yu, Component Quality Engineer, Meta; Abhijit Chakravarty, Quality Head, Optics & Interconnects, Meta

Beyond Pluggables: Building the NPO Ecosystem for Scaling AI
A look at what it takes to build a near-package optics (NPO) ecosystem capable of supporting AI scaling beyond what pluggable modules can deliver.
Speaker: Nan Ge, Technical Sourcing Manager, Meta 

FBOSS and Open Platforms

Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — A Unified Network Switch Platform Reference Design (video)
While SAI has made data plane software portable, the switch platform layer remains proprietary and fragmented, adding months of duplicated bring-up work per platform. This talk introduces OSPA, which proposes a unified, multi-vendor reference design for that layer, and the 1.0 specification that has been contributed to OCP.
Speakers: Tao Ren, Tian Fang, and Xu Wang, Meta; Guohan Lu, Individual; Ying Xie, Microsoft; Yiyuan Huang and Zhiping Yao, Alibaba

NVIDIA SDK + FBOSS: Building Production-Ready AI Network Fabrics (video)
How NVIDIA’s Spectrum-X switch, SDK, SAI implementation, and simulator come together with FBOSS, Meta’s network operating system, to build production AI fabrics. The talk covers the CI/CD and test-driven workflow that made rapid joint integration possible.
Speakers: Parvez Shaikh, Meta; Harish Krishnamoorthy, Alan Elder, and Tom Zhu, NVIDIA

Open, AI-Ready FBOSS: From Platform Bring-up to Solution Qualification (video)
A tour of the FBOSS software stack — routing, forwarding, platform services, and board support — and how a config-driven approach can more quickly and easily take a platform from board bring-up to qualified status for the OCP ecosystem.
Speakers: Srikrishna Gopu, Software Engineer, Meta; Benoit Sigoure, Software Engineer, Nexthop AI

Experiences With Scale-Out and Scale-Across

High Performance at Scale and Reliability by Design: Operating Meta’s Largest AI Clusters (video)
What it takes to operate Meta’s largest AI clusters reliably, walking the full training stack from GPUs and scale-up fabrics through FBOSS, drivers, communication libraries, and the scheduler.
Speakers: Jose Leitao, Production Engineering, Meta; Guille Cobo, Network.AI, Meta

Scaling AI Infrastructure Across DC and Beyond: Meta’s Journey with BAG (video)
An overview of Backend Aggregation (BAG) — its purpose, architecture, and performance benefits — with lessons from deployment in Meta’s Prometheus cluster. The talk also covers the engineering challenges of platform fit, distance management, reliability, and capacity planning, especially given the quickly evolving AI ecosystem.
Speakers: Jalpa Patel, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Hany Morsy, Network Engineer, Meta

SRv6 Powered Backbone Networks (video)
This talk delves into why Meta chose SRv6 for a new layer of its backbone, how the data plane and control plane work in production on FBOSS (including using shallow buffers at WAN distances), and the accelerated timeline from concept to deployment in a matter of months.
Speakers: Jasmeet Bagga, Software Engineer, Meta; Andrey Golovanov, Network Engineer, Meta

Bridging On-prem and Cloud: GPU Networking at Meta Scale (video)
A look at how Meta uses cloud GPU capacity, and what lessons Meta brings from its on-premises deployments into clouds to make them highly performant and reliable for AI workloads.
Speakers: Adi Gangidi, Technical Lead, Meta; Carmen Au, Software Engineering Manager, Meta

Scale-Across Networking Panel (video)
A cross-industry panel on what scale-across AI clusters demand from routing and optical transport equipment. Panelists compare approaches across hyperscalers, silicon, and systems vendors.
Panelists: Jeff Rahn, Meta; Tad Hofmeister, Google Cloud; Yawei Yin, Microsoft Azure; Xiguang (Henry) Wu, Broadcom; Vijay Vusirikala, Arista Networks (moderator)

Scale-Up and ESUN

Tahan: An Open, Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch for MTIA (video)
We introduce Tahan, an Ethernet-based scale-up switch for our rack-scale MTIA 300 AI system. This talk walks through Tahan’s bandwidth and latency characteristics and scale-up feature set, demonstrating Ethernet’s strengths in scale-up and moving toward ESUN for future scale-up designs.
Speakers: Vimal Vasudevan, Technical Program Manager, Meta; Ashutosh Grewal, Software Engineer, Meta

ESUN: Open Ethernet for the AI Scale-Up Era (video)
We partnered with the community last year to launch ESUN: Ethernet for Scale-up Networking. This talk covers progress since the last OCP Global Summit, with the 1.0 specification released earlier in the year and the upcoming 1.1 specification.
Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Network Technologist, Meta; Pratik Marolia, AI System Architect, Microsoft

Validation Methodologies for the ESUN Ecosystem (video)
A validation methodology for the ESUN ecosystem, situating scale-up within the broader set of AI scaling domains — scale in, up, out, across, edge, and above.
Speakers: Manoj Wadekar, AI Systems Technologist, Meta; Venkat Pullela, CTO, AI Infrastructure, Keysight

Test Methodology for Multi-Accelerator Copper Scale-up Interconnect (video)
In a copper scale-up domain, thousands of connections per rack mean roughly 10 bad links even at 99.9% yield — and blind-mate cartridges leave no per-link serviceability. At Meta, we look at this as a statistical problem rather than a set of isolated debugging problems. This talk shares our test methodology.
Speakers: Yao Rong, Systems Engineer, AI Systems, Meta; Karthik Ganesan, AI/HPC System Performance Engineer, Meta

RDMA Transport

MetaRoCE: Rethinking RDMA for AI (video)
The network is now in the critical path for AI clusters, with all-reduce and all-to-all performance gated by the slowest node across hundreds of thousands of accelerators. This talk covers the MetaRoCE transport specification.
Speakers: Arvind Srinivasan, Meta; Sandeep Nagaraja, Meta; Balakrishnan Raman, AMD

MetaRoCE in Software (video)
Meta is making its MetaRoCE software implementations available in open source, starting with a user-space version on GitHub (libsoftmetaroce) with a DPDK-based version coming soon.
Speakers: Ashkan Nikravesh, Software Engineer, Meta; Yiorgos Nikolaidis, Software Engineer, Meta

You can watch all of the recorded talks from the event on the 2026 OCP Global Summit website.

A huge thank-you to every presenter from our Meta network and hardware teams and to our great partners across the industry who made this possible!

posts.title: Trends from Money20/20 2026: The rise of “hidden” financial services
posts.summary: As fintech products become increasingly capable, the infrastructure behind them fades into the background. Three trends from Money20/20 show how stablecoins, agents, and always-on money are changing financial services.
posts.content:
Onstage at Money20/20 USA this week, Airtm Chief Product Officer Arshi Singh made the case that financial infrastructure works best when customers don’t have to think about it. “If we expect our user to understand the stablecoin infrastructure, then we are not doing our job right,” she said.

Speakers from Robinhood, Citi Treasury and Trade Solutions, the Solana Foundation, and other companies reinforced that idea throughout the event, which brought more than 11,000 payments, fintech, and business leaders to Las Vegas. Customers need access to useful financial products without requiring them to understand—or manage—the infrastructure underneath. That can mean using a stablecoin wallet inside a familiar application, setting clear limits on what an AI agent can buy, or accessing financial services outside banking hours.

Making those products easy to use requires enterprises and fintechs to use the right infrastructure behind the scenes. Three trends at Money20/20 showed what that looks like.

The next 100 million stablecoin users might never download a crypto wallet

Stablecoin adoption might not depend on persuading consumers to download a crypto product. Instead, businesses are embedding stablecoin wallets into the mobile apps, websites, and other products people already use. In most cases, users won’t need to understand the infrastructure underneath. 

Amira Valliani, head of payments growth at the Solana Foundation, described two emerging models: dedicated crypto wallets that give users access to a wide range of assets, and “hidden” or white-labeled wallets embedded inside another product. These hidden wallets might support stablecoin payouts, for example, without presenting users with an explicitly crypto-branded experience.

“I don’t know about a single feature that will bring on 100 million users,” said Valliani. “But I do think what’s going to happen is we’re going to have a few killer integrations that bring on the next 100 million users.”

A mobile-device manufacturer, for example, could add stablecoin-powered international money transfers to the wallet app already available on its phones, rather than ask customers to adopt a separate financial app. This can help make an existing product more useful, increase engagement, and add financial capabilities without becoming a traditional bank.

As stablecoin wallet functionality becomes more integrated throughout the existing financial ecosystem, consumers increasingly associate the experience with the application they use, rather than the infrastructure behind it. "I think crypto basically just fades into the background,” said Nitesh Nath, founder and CEO of DFlow. “[The wallet and application] become the same thing.”

Companies that simplify the underlying complexity can have an advantage. Customers want to be able to sign up quickly, access funds right away, and complete transactions without learning the language of crypto. By building these capabilities into familiar products, fintechs can reach new users without requiring them to adopt a separate crypto product—or even know that a stablecoin wallet is involved.

Always-on money is creating new financial products

Around-the-clock settlement with stablecoins allows fintechs and financial institutions to design credit, investment, treasury, and earnings products that respond to demand in real time, including outside traditional banking hours.

Citi Treasury and Trade Solutions offered its vision for helping institutional clients fund activity across markets with different operating calendars. Ryan Rugg, global head of digital assets for Citi Treasury and Trade Solutions, described a broker-dealer that wanted to buy US equities during Chinese New Year, when banks in Singapore were closed for the holiday. Traditionally, the company would have had to forecast its needs and send money to the US in advance. With tokenized deposits, it could move the funds when they were needed.

Always-on payment rails can also support new lending models. Valinor Digital used stablecoins to create a financing facility that lets prediction-market businesses access capital in real time, including overnight and on weekends. 

“The economy doesn’t shut just as the banks do,” said Valinor Digital Cofounder and CBO Lily Yarborough. The facility gave borrowers access to capital when demand arose, while giving lenders an opportunity that would have been difficult to serve on a traditional banking schedule.

Consumer fintechs are using the same infrastructure in different ways. Robinhood used on-chain lending markets to let customers earn potentially higher returns on their stablecoins than through its traditional cash product. Airtm uses stablecoins to help digital workers outside the US and Europe receive earnings from companies in those markets, then connects those funds to local options for saving, spending, and withdrawing. 

This 24/7 money movement can reduce the need to forecast and prefund accounts, align financing with real-time demand, and make financial services available across more hours and markets. This helps financial products to operate on the schedules of the businesses and people they serve.

Agentic payments require machine-readable consumer intent

A payment credential can show that an agent has access to a consumer’s funds, but it can’t show what the consumer authorized the agent to purchase. Businesses need a structured record of the consumer’s instructions, such as what the agent can buy, how much it can spend, and when the permission expires.

However, natural language instructions leave room for interpretation. For example, a consumer might request a cheap pair of headphones that will arrive quickly.  The agent still has to define “cheap,” “quickly,” and even “headphones.” The agent might make a reasonable inference from the customer’s spending history and still complete a purchase the customer did not intend.

Rather than asking consumers to manage the payment mechanics themselves, payment providers are building those boundaries into the transaction. Shirley Zhou, product lead for Link at Stripe, described a process in which an agent submits a spend request specifying the amount, seller, and purpose of a proposed purchase. The buyer can approve the request before the agent completes the purchase, with the spend request information also informing fraud models. Link’s wallet for agents also offers free purchase protections when an agent uses Link to complete an eligible purchase on their behalf. For qualifying Link transactions, accidental damage, lost items, price drops after they buy, no-fee returns, and return guarantees are covered. 

Other financial companies are developing ways to carry consumer intent through the agentic transaction. American Express, for example, described a model where the issuer receives the customer’s purchase instructions earlier in the transaction lifecycle and can set controls based on what the customer asked for. Permissions for longer-running tasks may also need to remain visible, adjustable, and revocable. A buyer could authorize several purchases within a set budget, ask an agent to monitor an item for a price drop, or allow it to act until a specified date.

The financial infrastructure for these agentic payments remains largely out of sight, while the consumer retains control over the decisions that matter.

How Stripe can help

Customers increasingly want products that help them make better use of their money. Delivering those experiences means connecting traditional and stablecoin rails, preserving customer preferences across agentic channels, and maintaining trust as AI takes on more responsibilities tied to personal finance. 

Stripe brings these capabilities together in one stack. Businesses can embed wallets, issue cards, enable payments, and move money between fiat and stablecoins without exposing users to the underlying complexity. 

Stripe also supports OUSD, Open Standard's recently launched stablecoin for global money movement and settlement across payment networks. With more than $800 million in circulation, OUSD allows businesses to receive, hold, send, and spend funds with Stripe Treasury; build and operate a global card program with Stripe Issuing; and pay recipients worldwide with Stripe Global Payouts. 

Stripe’s agentic commerce solution can also help businesses make payments available to agents while preserving details they’ve spent years honing, like authorization, fraud controls, and branded checkout.

To learn how Stripe can support your stablecoin or agentic commerce strategy, contact us.

posts.title: Automate medical coding with Step Functions and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
posts.summary: Learn how to combine deterministic orchestration with bounded agentic reasoning using AWS Step Functions and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness. This medical coding workflow escalates cheapest-first: a safety…
posts.content:
With AI agents, you can automate medical coding while keeping the workflow deterministic, auditable, and subject to human approval. The key is division of labor: the workflow engine owns sequencing and approval gates, while agents reason within individual, bounded steps. Handing the entire workflow to an agent would make the runtime path a property of the model’s reasoning, which is difficult to review and replay.

Medical coding makes this concrete. Teams must translate free-text clinical terms like “migrane” (a typo) or “flutters in my chest sometimes” into standardized codes before they can analyze or report the data. The target vocabularies include controlled medical dictionaries such as MedDRA for adverse events and WHODrug for medications. This work is safety-critical because a coding error can send an adverse event to the wrong safety signal. Yet it’s mostly repetitive work, with skilled coders reviewing terms one by one. The opportunity is to code the confident cases automatically and route only the ambiguous ones to a human.

In this post, we show you how to combine deterministic orchestration with bounded agentic reasoning using AWS Step Functions and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness integration, a managed capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We walk through a medical coding workflow that escalates cheapest-first: a safety block-list, then exact matching, then an AI agent only for the terms that need judgment. We also explain the design decisions that keep the model bounded. The complete sample, including infrastructure code and a seeded test dataset, is available in the aws-samples GitHub repository.

Note that MedDRA is a registered trademark of the International Federation of Pharmaceutical Manufacturers and Associations (IFPMA), managed by the MedDRA Maintenance and Support Services Organization (MSSO). WHODrug is maintained by the Uppsala Monitoring Centre (UMC). Both are proprietary, licensed dictionaries. Deploying against them requires a valid subscription. The sample dataset contains generated study identifiers and verbatims with a de minimis illustrative set of dictionary entries, and no patient data. The AWS services used in this sample, including Amazon Aurora and Amazon Bedrock, are HIPAA-eligible when used under a signed AWS Business Associate Addendum (BAA). Before processing protected health information, see the HIPAA Eligible Services Reference and the AWS HIPAA Compliance overview.

Solution overview

The design follows one principle: spend the cheapest, most deterministic mechanism that can code a term with confidence and escalate only when it can’t. A large language model (LLM) agent is powerful but expensive and non-deterministic, so it isn’t the default. Even then, the workflow, not the model, owns every routing decision. The agent might choose which medical code and how confident it is. It doesn’t decide what happens next. A compliance reviewer can read the state machine definition and understand the execution path independent of any agent’s runtime reasoning.

The solution uses AWS Step Functions to orchestrate the coding decision, AWS Lambda for the deterministic steps, and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness for the agentic step. An Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, exposes the agent’s tools. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL-Compatible Edition (Serverless v2) with the pgvector extension serves as a single store for the reference data and its embeddings, so there is no separate vector store to synchronize.

Figure 1 shows the architecture.

Figure 1: Medical coding workflow solution architecture

Each Step Functions execution codes one verbatim: a deterministic direct lookup, an agentic semantic search that runs only on a miss, score-threshold routing on the agent’s confidence, and a write-back onto the same study record. The state machine is deliberately a standard workflow. Executions are exactly-once, and the queryable history is a per-term audit trail. For a regulated coding process, answering “why was this term coded this way, by what, and when” is a requirement. Error paths in this sample end with the term left open, so every record gets a terminal status. In production, send errors that survive the retries to a Fail state instead. The execution then shows as failed in Amazon CloudWatch, and you can redrive it after fixing the cause.

The write-back step stores every symptom entry’s full medical family tree, not just an isolated code. For example, a symptom like ‘muscle spasms’ links all the way up to its overarching category, ‘musculoskeletal and connective tissue disorders’. Safety teams can then roll up signals at any level, not just the lowest one. Additionally, the agent logs a one-sentence explanation for its decision. This makes sure that if similar symptoms (like cramps) end up categorized differently across studies, teams can trace the exact study context that caused the variance. They don’t need to guess based on a generic confidence score.

Figure 2 shows the coding decision flow in Unified Modeling Language (UML) activity notation.

Figure 2: Medical coding decision flow with the three terminal outcomes in UML activity notation

Note: This sample is for demonstration purposes only and is not intended for clinical use. Before using this pattern in production, validate it against a known-correct dataset and measure coding precision and the incorrect autocode rate.

Walkthrough

The walkthrough follows one verbatim through the state machine, focusing on the architectural decision each stage encodes.

Prerequisites

Before you begin, make sure that you have the following:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create Step Functions state machines, Lambda functions, an Aurora PostgreSQL cluster, Amazon Bedrock AgentCore resources, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles.
  • Access to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in a supported AWS Region. The harness uses Claude Sonnet 5 (us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5), and the dictionary search uses Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 (amazon.titan-embed-text-v2:0). Both models are enabled by default, but Anthropic models require a one-time usage form before first use, which you can submit from the Amazon Bedrock playground. For model availability by Region, see Supported models by AWS Region in Amazon Bedrock.
  • Node.js 24+, the AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) CLI, and a bootstrapped target account.

Estimated cost

The largest cost is the Aurora Serverless v2 cluster. It keeps a minimum capacity of 0.5 Aurora Capacity Units (ACUs), so it’s billed for every hour it runs, even when idle. For current rates, see Amazon Aurora pricing. To stop the charges, delete the stack as described in Clean up.

Step 1. Resolve the deterministic cases first

The first task state invokes a Lambda function that makes two checks, in a deliberate order. It first checks a terms-not-to-autocode block-list. These are real dictionary terms, like “HAEMORRHAGE,” that are too broad to auto-assign because the code changes depending on where the bleeding occurred. A hit ends the workflow with the term left open for a human. Because this runs before any model call, it’s a hard control: a safety rule placed ahead of the model cannot be prompted away, and costs nothing to enforce.

The same function then runs a case-insensitive exact match against the dictionary and a curated synonym list (“Hypothyroid” maps to “Hypothyroidism”). A match is accepted only if it resolves to exactly one distinct code. On the sample workload, five of twelve cases finish here: one safety block and four auto codes at score 1.00, each for the cost of an indexed query. More than a third of the workload never reaches the agent at all.

Step 2. Declare the coding agent in the workflow definition

We use an agent for this step because deciding when to pull in study context is judgment, not a fixed rule. In our test run, the agent called the study-info tool only for ambiguous terms and skipped it for a clear typo and for gibberish input. That kind of judgment is hard to encode as a threshold, and the agent can take on new tools later without a workflow redesign. This is also why the agent sits last in line, after two cheaper, deterministic checks.

Only on a miss does Step Functions invoke the agent, using the AgentCore harness optimized integration. The harness resource declares only the model. The system prompt, tools, and allowed tool names are supplied per invocation from the task state. The agent’s full contract is therefore readable in the workflow definition, and there is no container to build or operate. The following abbreviated excerpt shows the shape. See the sample for the full definition. The InvokeHarness Task state has a hard 15-minute execution cap regardless of TimeoutSeconds, so a term needing many tool round-trips could hit it. The sample’s two-tool, single-turn design stays well under that limit.

CodingAgent:
  Type: Task
  Resource: arn:aws:states:::bedrockagentcore:invokeHarness
  Arguments:
    HarnessArn: "${CodingHarnessArn}"
    RuntimeSessionId: "{% $uuid() %}"
    Messages:
      - Role: user
        Content:
          - Text: >-
              {% 'Code this verbatim term: "' & $verbatim & '". Dictionary='
              & $dictionary & ' version=' & $dictionaryVersion
              & ' study=' & $study & '.' %}
    Tools:
      - Type: agentcore_gateway
        Name: gateway
        Config:
          AgentCoreGateway:
            GatewayArn: "${GatewayArn}"
    AllowedTools:
      - "@gateway/search-dictionary___search_dictionary"
      - "@gateway/study-info___get_study_info"
    SystemPrompt:
      - Text: |-
          You are a clinical medical-coding expert...

The agent has exactly two tools, exposed as Model Context Protocol (MCP) tools through an AgentCore Gateway. search_dictionary embeds the verbatim with Amazon Titan Text Embeddings V2 and runs a pgvector similarity search. It searches the verbatim exactly as given, because the misspelling is the signal. get_study_info returns the study’s free-text protocol description. It exists because similarity search can return several clinically plausible candidates it can’t separate on text alone. A human coder breaks that tie using knowledge of the study. This tool gives the agent the same context and nothing else: it returns prose only, not codes.

The clearest illustration is the same verbatim coded in two different studies. “cramps” returns an identical candidate list in both. Only the study description differs. In an oncology study that monitors muscle spasms as adverse events of special interest, the agent coded it to “muscle spasms.” In a reflux study where abdominal cramping is expected and musculoskeletal events aren’t an endpoint, it coded the same verbatim to “abdominal pain.” In this run, the oncology result scored 0.92 and was autocoded, and the gastrointestinal (GI) result scored 0.85 and went to a coder for review. In both cases the agent’s job was to bring the right candidate to the top with a reason a coder can check. That’s how a coder who knows the protocol would decide.

Step 3. Route on coding confidence, not retrieval similarity

The most important design decision is what the threshold routes on. Routing on retrieval similarity, the distance between the two embeddings, is measurably wrong. Table 1 illustrates this with an example.

VerbatimSelected termRetrieval similarityAgent confidencemigraneMigraine0.370.97flutters in my chest sometimesCardiac flutter0.650.75

Table 1. Retrieval similarity and agent confidence for sample terms (one run, Claude Sonnet 5)

Table 1 shows the problem. The typo “migrane” looks very different from “Migraine” as text, so its similarity score is low, but the right code is obvious. “Flutters in my chest sometimes” shares more words with “Cardiac flutter,” so its similarity score is higher, but the right code is less certain. Similarity ranks these two cases the wrong way round, and no threshold can fix that. So instead, the agent reports how confident it is in its own choice, using three bands set in the system prompt. It reports 0.95 to 1.00 when the match is clear, 0.70 to 0.94 when the verbatim is vague or the agent needed study context to choose between candidates, and below 0.70 when nothing fits. For example, “cramps” in the GI study could mean muscle cramps or stomach cramps. The agent checked the study description to choose, and reported 0.85, in the middle band. The bands describe the model’s confidence. The 0.90 autocode gate is a separate, fixed rule in the workflow, applied by the Choice state that comes next.

ScoreThreshold:
  Type: Choice
  Choices:
    - Condition: "{% $agentScore >= 0.9 %}"
      Next: WriteBack
    - Condition: "{% $agentScore >= 0.7 %}"
      Next: MarkForReview
  Default: MarkOpen

Note that the routing number is authored by the model. The block-list runs before any model call, and the thresholds are auditable configuration in the state machine definition. The write-back checks the code exists, and anything below the autocode gate reaches a human. Note also that the agent is instructed never to abstain. For gibberish it still returns the top candidate at low confidence, and the gate discards it. The agent scores the candidate, and the workflow decides what happens to it.

Step 4. Write back with a fabrication guard

The terminal task persists the outcome onto the same study record: status, code, hierarchy, score, and a status_changed_by marker that distinguishes machine coding from human action. Before writing, it checks that the chosen code exists in the target dictionary and version. The prompt tells the agent not to invent codes, and this check enforces it. It matters because the agent reads free-text study metadata, which is the kind of input that invites copying a plausible number out of a protocol description. A code that fails the check leaves the term safely open, with the reason recorded. This check has one limit. It can’t tell whether the code was one of the search results, because the workflow only gets the agent’s final response, not what the tools returned. To verify that, look at the agent’s tool calls in AgentCore Observability, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

Deploy and test the solution

The sample deploys with three commands and seeds twelve verbatims that exercise every branch:

npm install && npm run build
npx cdk deploy
npm run seed

Each verbatim runs as one Step Functions execution (the repository README shows the exact CLI calls). The following table shows a live run:

VerbatimRouteScoreOutcomeHAEMORRHAGEblock-listn/aopen (safety block)Dislocated shoulderexact match1.00autocodedHypothyroidsynonym match1.00autocodedibuprofenexact match (WHODrug)1.00autocodedFULVESTRANTexact match, derivation-only1.00autocodedmigraneagent0.97autocoded (Migraine)nexiuumagent0.95autocoded (NEXIUM)cramps (oncology study)agent + study context0.92autocoded (Muscle spasms)cramps (GI study)agent + study context0.85review (Abdominal pain)flutters in my chest sometimesagent0.75review (Cardiac flutter)heart races when I stand upagent0.80review (Tachycardia)asdfghjklagent< 0.70open

Table 2. Score and outcome for sample terms (same run as Table 1)

Derivation-only (FULVESTRANT row): a WHODrug ingredient-level exact match, where the write-back updates only the generic-name derivation and ATC hierarchy fields. No new dictionary term is assigned.

The agent skipped the study-info tool for the unambiguous typo and the gibberish and called it only for the ambiguous cases. Every execution’s graph is inspectable in the Step Functions console, and AgentCore Observability records the agent’s tool calls and token usage in Amazon CloudWatch.

Note: Across repeated runs of identical inputs in this sample, the selected code was stable every time, but the confidence score moved within a band. Cases that land near the 0.90 autocode gate can therefore autocode on one run and route to review on another. In our testing, the oncology cramps case scored between 0.75 and 0.92 over six runs. It was autocoded twice and sent to review four times, and Muscle spasms was selected every time. Assert your tests on the selected code, not the exact score, and set your own autocode threshold with margin below 0.90 rather than directly on it.

Scaling beyond one verbatim: This walkthrough codes one verbatim per execution so each decision stays straightforward to inspect. To code a full study, wrap the workflow in a Step Functions Distributed Map state that reads verbatims from an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) manifest, and set MaxConcurrency based on your account’s Amazon Bedrock quota. To size MaxConcurrency, divide your model’s tokens-per-minute quota by the tokens one agent run burns (model calls * (input tokens + 10 * output tokens) for Sonnet 5). Then multiply by the runtime duration in minutes, divide by the share of verbatims that reach the agent, and apply a safety margin. In our testing, 12 concurrent executions against a cluster that had scaled to zero failed 8 of 12 while still reporting SUCCEEDED, which is why the sample keeps a 0.5 ACU minimum and retries the resume errors. Most verbatims resolve in the two deterministic steps, so only a small share ever reaches the agent. For the quotas that apply to your model, see Quotas for Amazon Bedrock.

Clean up

To avoid future charges, delete the deployed resources with npx cdk destroy. All sample data is reseedable, so nothing needs to be retained.

Recognizing the pattern

posts.title: Stripe survey: Four trends reshaping how SaaS platforms compete in the AI era
posts.summary: AI is creating more SaaS competition, and platforms are feeling the pressure. A Stripe survey of 200 platform leaders shows how they plan to evolve pricing, grow revenue, and retain customers.
posts.content:
AI is making software faster and cheaper to build, lowering barriers to entry and intensifying competition for SaaS platforms. That growth is clearly visible on Stripe, where the number of new platform businesses has increased more than 180% year over year.

We surveyed 200 platform leaders across North America and Europe, half of whom use Stripe, and found that 57% are concerned about losing customers to AI-driven competitors. Leaders are reworking how they build products, set prices, and retain customers to protect margins and make their products harder to displace.

Our survey identified four ways SaaS platforms are adapting: 

  1. Deploying AI internally and in customer-facing products
  2. Testing usage- and outcome-based charges alongside subscriptions
  3. Rebalancing their revenue mix around how their customers operate
  4. Offering embedded finance products to strengthen retention

1. Platforms are pursuing AI efficiency and AI products in parallel

Platforms are applying AI on two fronts: inside their own operations and in the products they sell. Internally, 81% have used AI to accelerate research and development over the past 12 months, and 58% are rebuilding workflows around agents. At Granum, for example, agents automate tasks across customer-facing teams, helping support staff handle 23% more tickets and onboarding specialists serve 34% more customers.

On the product side, 79% have added AI features to existing products over the past 12 months. Canva recently took that approach with Canva AI 2.0, a conversational, agentic workspace within its design suite.

These investments are already paying off. Forty-five percent of platform leaders say their AI investments have lowered operating costs. At GoodLeap, those costs have fallen even as payment volume has increased.

2. Seat-based pricing is losing ground, but not going away

Platforms adding AI are testing pricing tied to usage and outcomes as they look for ways to cover inference costs. Forty-four percent plan to make multiple pricing changes in the next 12 months.

Seat-based pricing will remain part of the mix, but fewer platforms expect it to be their primary model, falling from 16% in 2026 to 11% in 2027. Horizontal platforms are moving away from seats faster. By 2027, just 7% expect seats to remain their primary pricing model, compared with 14% of vertical SaaS.

The key difference is how closely growth has been tied to customer headcount. Horizontal platforms have traditionally grown by selling more seats to larger customers. But fewer seats may be needed as agents take on work that people used to do. Vertical SaaS platforms typically sell only a handful of seats to each merchant, but they’re still tied to people using the software.

Seat-based pricing still gives SaaS platforms a predictable base. One in four plan to keep per-seat fees, then charge separately for agent work based on credits, usage, or outcomes. Zendesk, for example, now charges for resolutions alongside its subscriptions. Another 7% plan to treat agents like seats, charging a base fee plus a license for each agent. The range of approaches suggests that no single metric captures every kind of agent work.

3. Horizontal and vertical platforms are split on leading revenue models

Our survey found a split in expected revenue models by platform and customer segment. Among horizontal platforms serving midsize and enterprise businesses, just 3% expect  embedded finance—including payments, financing, financial accounts, and card issuing—to generate the largest share of revenue in 2027. That figure rises to 34% among vertical platforms serving micro and small businesses. That reverses for usage and hybrid pricing: 60% of the horizontal cohort expect these models to lead revenue, compared with 22% of the vertical cohort.

The gap likely comes down to merchant needs. Small businesses are more likely to want payments and working capital built into the software they already use. Vertical platforms can offer these services because they sit close to the transaction. Larger businesses usually have their own payments and financing infrastructure. But they also need more software to run their complex operations, so software fees can make for a steadier revenue source for horizontal platforms.

4. Embedded finance is emerging as a core retention strategy

Beyond its revenue potential, embedded finance can help platforms retain customers. Sixty percent of platforms say it will be very important or mission-critical to retention over the next 24 months.

Embedding payments and financial services deepens merchant relationships and makes a platform harder to replace. Payments also generate proprietary transaction data, which more than half of surveyed leaders named as a top competitive advantage. Platforms can use payments data to offer financing and let merchants manage more of their finances in one place.

More platforms on Stripe are following that playbook. As of September 2026, the number of active platforms offering Stripe Capital nearly doubled year over year.

Hear from SaaS leaders

Stripe helps more than 19,000 platforms onboard new merchants, accept payments, and grow revenue. Join SaaS leaders across verticals at our SaaS Platform Summit on Tuesday, November 3, in San Francisco to learn how they’re updating their pricing, products, and business models for AI.

Methodology

Stripe surveyed 200 C-suite and director-level leaders at SaaS platforms across North America and Europe in March 2026. Respondents represented startups operating for one to two years, early-stage companies operating for three to five years, established companies operating for six to 10 years, and mature companies operating for more than 10 years. The sample was evenly divided between vertical and horizontal SaaS platforms. Half of the respondents were businesses on Stripe.

posts.title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
posts.summary: Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Carl Hu, Justin Johnson, Parish Aggarwal, Kaushik Rangadurai, Senthil Manickavelu, Tianwei Zhang
  • Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers.
  • GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. 
  • Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers.

GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders, GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. 

GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal.

GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. 

Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases:

  • Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement.
  • Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers.
  • LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. 
  • Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent.

Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields:

  • Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift1 in conversions.
  • Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. 
  • A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture.

1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026.

Introducing GenRecs Tokenization

Pre-trained multimodal models read each ad, product, and page, including its text and images, and encode the items into an embedding that carries world knowledge. The tokenizer combines that content signal with representations learned from how people engage with the items, then quantizes the result into a short sequence of discrete tokens. Similar items share tokens, much as related words share roots. For example, there’s overlap between two running shoe ads from the previous season to the current season, so the new campaign immediately benefits from everything the model has already learned about the previous season’s products.

At the heart of GenRecs Tokenization is a three-stage pipeline that:

  • Encodes each item into a semantic embedding space.
  • Decomposes that embedding into independent subspaces.
  • Quantizes by mapping each subspace to an entry in a codebook. 

Maximizing ads recommendation quality requires diverse combinations of these stages depending on entity and feature semantics. For example, for many ad representations, GenRecs Tokenization uses prefix n-grams that combine a learned encoder, residual decomposition,  learned vector codebooks, and token parametrization. 

Token Quality Predicts Ranking Accuracy

Independently of downstream ranking gain, tokenizer model quality can be evaluated against intrinsic measures like:

  • Cluster purity: The items that share a code tend to share a category, giving the model a cleaner signal per token;
  • Distribution balance: Items spread evenly across semantic IDs instead of crowding into a few.
  • Codebook utilization: A larger share of codes holds at least one item, so the vocabulary expresses more distinctions.

Across the eight tokenizer versions we tested, we see a strong correlation between these intrinsic quality metrics and downstream ranking prediction accuracy. Tokenizer versions that scored better on these metrics also had better CTR prediction accuracy for ads models.

The Tokenization Flywheel

Tokenization maximizes the efficiency of high-volume campaigns by uncovering deeper semantic patterns across their vast product catalogs. For tail ads that accumulate fewer impressions, tokenization enables ads recommendation models to generalize across them via shared content structure, recovering cold-start performance and enabling cross-entity transfer. When a sportswear brand launches next season’s trail shoe, tokenization lets the new product and its ads build on what the model learned from last season’s shoe, even before anyone sees the new ad.

By improving tail ad prediction quality, tokenization not only lets tail ads be ranked accurately, but also improves the training data, which then improves prediction quality for all ads. Each pass through this self-reinforcing flywheel improves the quality of model predictions.

The Foundations of LLM Recommendation

Tokenizer improvements are not confined to the model they were tuned for. Optimizing codebook quality through diversity loss, dead code resets, and contrastive objectives produces measurably better downstream performance when the resulting tokens train generative recommenders. Our work on LLM-native retrieval shows how far this can go. A two-tower architecture built on a shared LLM encoder reaches state-of-the-art retrieval quality while remaining efficiently servable, matching classic two-tower performance on a fraction of the training data. Building on this, we are now extending reasoning-aware ranking on top of the same vocabulary.

The Future of GenRecs Tokenization

We are continuing to push GenRecs Tokenization toward the ROI-optimal frontier along three directions:

Deepening cold-start generalization: Tail ad inventory is where semantic tokens contribute most and where advertiser impact is largest. We are scaling the coverage of tokenization across all items to deliver better performance to advertisers.

Treating tokenizer quality as a first-class objective: Engagement-aligned training, unified cross-entity vocabulary, and codebook improvements are active areas of investment. Because intrinsic quality measures predict downstream ranking gains, we can iterate on the tokenizer without waiting on a full model training cycle.

Serving LLM-native architectures efficiently: Fully verbalized tokenization gives a model the richest view of an ad, but requires context windows that are impractical at ads scale. We are combining compacted verbalized tokens with semantic IDs to retain reasoning quality while maintaining acceptable latency.

Looking further out, we are exploring whether the same vocabulary that improves ads ranking today could unify representation across surfaces. A shared token space spanning ads content across text, image, audio, and video, would let models reason about what a person is interested in and what an advertiser has to offer with one representation, rather than stitching together separately learned embeddings. 

As recommendation systems evolve from discriminative scoring to include generative reasoning, the data foundation benefits from evolving from ephemeral IDs to stable semantic representations. GenRecs Tokenization provides the foundation, translating the complexity of Meta’s ads ecosystem into a vocabulary that generative models can learn, reason about, and generate from.

Acknowledgements

We would like to thank Weifeng Cui, Ling Leng, Luke Simon, Hadar Ohana, Jimmy Chen, Minghai Chen, Chiyu Zhang, Dinesh Ramasamy, Debajyoti Roy, Shawn Shi, Gajanan Golegaonkar, Xiao Yang, Ashkan Aleali, Anuj Gargava, Xizhou Feng, Liquan Huang, Frank Shyu, Xiaoyu Chen, Kungang Li, Chonglin Sun, Matt Steiner, Sandeep Pandey,  Santanu Kolay, Anuj Madan, Tak Yan, and the entire team behind the development and productionization of the first large scale semantic tokenization effort in Meta’s ad recommendation system.

posts.title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
posts.summary: Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Plawan Rath, Akhil Jindal, Ashwini Verma
  • Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. 
  • At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning.
  • We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents.

We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point.

When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything.

It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating.

The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists.

The Problem: More Context, Worse Results

Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives.

Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. 

The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem.

Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge.

We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one.

The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers

We split the system into two layers:

  1. A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router.
  2. Fourteen specialized subagents, each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug.

The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request:

  1. Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file.
  2. Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates).
  3. Gather required fields from the user.
  4. Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations).
  5. Reliability gate check for active warnings or required reviewers.
  6. Delegate to the subagent with full context.
  7. Handle results and surface errors, confirm success.

Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded.

What We Built: Workflow Templates, Not New Agents

One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space:

  • Column Onboarding: Schema → Validation → Population → Testing
  • Event Onboarding: Schema → Population → Validation → Testing → Event Processing
  • Pipeline Migration: Assessment → Planning → Population → Validation → Monitoring

Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability.

Each subagent follows a standardized structure:

  • Knowledge sources: which domain files to load at runtime (typically a few thousand tokens each).
  • Pre-gathering checklist: what the orchestrator must collect before delegation.
  • Step-by-step workflow: the domain-specific execution plan.
  • Discovery patterns: how to find relevant code patterns in the monorepo.
  • Troubleshooting: error-to-resolution mappings for common failures.

This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first.

Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain. When a knowledge file is updated, the next session automatically uses the latest version — no orchestrator changes required. The same knowledge files serve multiple platform implementations of our agent.

Results

Configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with our earlier config-driven system. The thin orchestrator system does it in under an hour.

For broader context: About two-thirds of the system’s changes land without significant human edits. It gets there by trading generality for deep domain knowledge, a deliberate architectural choice. The orchestrator is general; the subagents are specialists.

Why This Works (And Why Heavyweight Orchestrators Don’t)

The conventional approach is to make the orchestrator the smartest component — give it all the context and let it reason about what to do and how to do it. This works until it doesn’t, and it stops working exactly when you need it most — at scale, with complex multi-step workflows, across heterogeneous subsystems.

The thin orchestrator works because it aligns architectural boundaries with computational boundaries:

  • Deterministic decisions stay deterministic. “Which subagent handles this?” is a routing decision, not a reasoning task. Don’t use an LLM for it.
  • Context isolation prevents cross-contamination. The population agent for data source A never sees data source B’s patterns. It can’t hallucinate the wrong one.
  • Failures are contained. If a subagent fails, the orchestrator retries or escalates. The failure doesn’t corrupt the orchestrator’s state or other subagents’ contexts.
  • The system improves at every layer independently. A better model improves all 14 subagents simultaneously. A knowledge file update takes effect immediately. A new workflow template unlocks new capabilities without touching agents. No single component carries the full weight.

How to Apply This to Your AI Agents

This pattern isn’t specific to data pipelines. Any team building production AI agents can benefit:

  1. Separate routing from reasoning. If your orchestrator is making domain decisions, it’s doing too much. Routing should be deterministic: keyword matching, intent classification, field gathering. Push all domain reasoning into isolated subagents.
  2. Design subagents as structurally uniform specialists. Every subagent should have the same structure: knowledge sources, required inputs, execution steps, error handling. This makes adding new capabilities templated work rather than architecture changes.
  3. Use workflow templates, not new agents, to scale. When you need a new use case, first ask: Can I sequence existing agents differently? If you can’t reuse agents across workflows, your agents are too coupled to specific use cases.
  4. Load knowledge at runtime, not at build time. Embed knowledge in the orchestrator and every update requires redeployment. Load it on demand and updates take effect immediately, across all platforms.
  5. Draw the deterministic/probabilistic boundary explicitly. For every component, decide: Is this a routing decision (deterministic) or a reasoning task (probabilistic)? The orchestrator should be on one side, the subagents on the other. Don’t mix them.

The strongest argument for a thin orchestrator is the failure mode of the alternative. When a heavyweight orchestrator hallucinates, the error spreads to everything downstream: it routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields, or skips reliability checks. A thin orchestrator leaves little room for hallucination because its routing and reliability steps don’t rely on LLM reasoning. It follows a fixed protocol. The creativity happens downstream, in isolated, domain-scoped contexts where hallucination risk is minimized and failures are contained.

What’s Next

We’re scaling this architecture to handle an increase in data columns across new pipeline domains. The compositional thesis predicts this will work because scaling means adding workflow templates and knowledge files, not rebuilding agents. We’re also exploring how the system can continuously improve from production usage, using automated feedback loops to identify failure patterns and propose targeted improvements to subagent knowledge, with human review always gating any changes.

The counterintuitive lesson: the most important component in our AI agent system is the one that does the least work. Keep your orchestrator thin and your specialists deep, and the whole system becomes more reliable.

Acknowledgements

This work was a team effort. Some other people who contributed to this effort include:  Mani Bhushan, Rahul Maliakkal, Jae Ha, Chakrapani Kumar, Vivek Tiwari, and Amanda Yin.
