posts.title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
posts.summary: With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible. The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Kevin Lee, Yashar Bayani, Ahmed Sharif, Yee Jiun Song
  • With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible.
  • The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise  ~1 million GPUs.
  • Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently.

Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people.

Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models, including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks.

Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it.

Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind.

The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center.

The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities

Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. 

This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. 

Multiple Generations of AI Hardware

Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric.

Catalina: NVIDIA GB200

Our first platform, Catalina, leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100. It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP). 

The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We expected that imbalance to cost performance, so we opted for a configuration that delivers 800G of scale-out per GPU. This also gave us more uniformity of spec as the region expanded over time and 800G scale-out became available.


The Catalina GB200 NVL72 features:

  • 72 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with 13.4 TB of HBM3e (192 GB per GPU).
  • 720 peak PFLOPS of FP8 training compute (1,440 PFLOPS at FP4).
  • 130 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth within the domain.
  • 576 TB/s peak aggregate memory bandwidth.
  • ~120 kW total system power across the two-rack pair.

Clemente: NVIDIA GB300 NVL72

Our second platform, Clemente, moves to the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and improves on Catalina at both the GPU and the platform level. GB300 raises HBM capacity per GPU by 1.5x, from 192 GB to 288 GB, and dense FP4 throughput by a similar factor, while roughly doubling attention (softmax) acceleration. At the platform level, scale-out is no longer the constraint it was on the GB200 NVL72: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNICs deliver 800G per GPU natively, so the capability we deployed early on Ariel becomes the baseline. That, together with a 2:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio, allows Clemente to pack the full 72-GPU domain into a single rack, streamlining our physical deployment. Clemente can be deployed with our modular Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) or use Facility Liquid Cooling (FLC) in our newly designed data centers. Serviceability also improves substantially, with reduced cabling.

The Clemente GB300 NVL72 features:

  • 72 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs with 20.7 TB of HBM3e (288 GB per GPU — 50% more than the GB200).
  • Over 1 exaFLOP of peak FP4 compute.
  • 130 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth (1.8 TB/s bidirectional per GPU).
  • ~135 kW rack power.
  • 5-10% performance improvement over the GB200 NVL72.

Connecting the Supercluster

In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings.

Large pre-training jobs partition the training into data-parallel model replicas, creating a hierarchy in network usage: Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-sensitive operations concentrate within a replica, while traffic that is more tolerant of higher latency and less bandwidth is scheduled between replicas. Our network is designed to match this hierarchy, with low-latency, high-bandwidth fabrics within buildings and an aggregation network connecting the building fabrics. 

We work closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure the parallelism design, traffic patterns, and communication algorithms and software are optimized to minimize exposure of any network communication. This keeps the GPUs as busy as possible and not waiting on the network.

The Meta team has employed these networking concepts in earlier building-scale, 24K GPU clusters and our region-scale, 100K+ GPU cluster over the last several years, and we took them to a new level of scale and distance in Prometheus.

Network Fabrics

At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. Our initial design used a Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) to mitigate the network congestion caused by training collectives that typically have a small number of large, long-lived network flows that collide under traditional load-balancing techniques; it does this by utilizing sub-packet-level multipath routing and packet re-ordering in the fabric along with virtual output queues and credit-based end-to-end flow control. 

As Ethernet NIC technology advanced, enabling packet re-ordering at the endpoint, we were able to update to a Non-Scheduled Fabric (NSF) utilizing shallow-buffer 51.2T Ethernet switches, such as Minipack3 with Dynamic Load Balancing and the NVIDIA Spectrum-4 switch ASIC-based Minipack3N with NVIDIA’s Adaptive Routing on ConnectX NICs. Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale.

Aggregation

The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km. It is built with Arista 7800-series chassis running deep-buffered Broadcom Jericho3 silicon, delivering multiple Pbps of bandwidth per region pair.

Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances.

Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km.

Engineering Reliability at Every Level

At Prometheus’ scale, every component needs to be monitored for reliability. A single fault anywhere can halt an entire training job and waste valuable compute resources. 

Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic. Teams are deeply embedded at our data centers, sharing real-time telemetry and running joint triage sessions to decompose every system halt by its root cause.

This attribution-driven accountability model ensures both sides are focused on targeted improvements. While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling. This transparency eliminates ambiguity and drives faster fixes across both organizations.

The 72-GPU Failure Domain

The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.

The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.

Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale.

Fault Recovery 

Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:

Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput.

Checkpointing: When a fault blast area is larger than a data-parallel model replica, the entire job is restarted back to the last checkpoint; frequent checkpointing reduces the amount of work lost in these events. Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage. We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput.

These two fault recovery mechanisms combine with a sparing strategy that utilizes pre-allocated spare GPU trays within a rack, as well as spare racks, to minimize the time to bring up replacement hardware and reduce the amount of work lost to hardware failures

Systematic Reduction of Interruptions

When training frontier models, infrastructure reliability requires a perspective beyond simple availability. The fundamental challenge lies in maintaining training momentum without frequent system halts. Within Prometheus, we classify an interruption as any fault — from GPU silicon defects and network fabric anomalies to storage bottlenecks or thermal limits — that forces a job to pause and initiate a recovery cycle.

These interruptions introduce a large operational overhead because our workloads are tightly interdependent; a single fault within a 72-GPU domain can affect the entire cluster’s aggregate throughput. This performance loss directly impacts our engineering iteration speed, resulting in less effective compute and longer timelines for delivering advanced AI experiences to billions of people.

During the initial phase of Prometheus in mid-2025, our interruption rates reached a peak of nearly 1,000 events per 8K GPUs daily. Through a year of rigorous cross-functional engineering, we have achieved a 99% reduction in interruptions, enabling the cluster to sustain multiple training jobs of tens of thousands of GPUs in parallel.

Attaining this stability required a granular decomposition of every interruption source, followed by the deployment of targeted engineering solutions for each failure category:

NVLink Signal Integrity: initially the primary bottleneck for GB200 deployments. With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles. We implemented continuous telemetry and automated flagging, utilizing L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before production. Our classification tools distinguish transient faults from persistent signal integrity failures, guiding targeted repairs and component replacement, and we validate repaired systems before returning them to production. 

Memory Reliability (HBM and LPDDR): Memory-related faults became a major source of interruptions as we scaled GB300 with higher memory capacities. Working closely with NVIDIA, we used fleet telemetry and detailed error analysis to identify recurring failure signatures, which are mitigated via refined HBM firmware settings, memory scrubbing, an improved error correction algorithm for LPDDR, and pattern-based predictive detection to retire degrading devices before they impact job throughput. We are deploying these changes across the fleet and measuring their impact on interruption rates and hardware replacement demand.

NVLink Switch and Fabric Health: A single switch fault can compromise an entire NVL72 domain. We monitor fabric health at millisecond resolution, utilizing automated recovery paths to isolate faulty components and rebalance traffic across the remaining infrastructure without a job interruption.

posts.title: New ways for fintechs to move money and expand globally
posts.summary: We’re introducing three updates to help fintechs launch products and grow internationally more easily: simpler payout management with Stripe Global Payouts, support for stablecoin cards in more countries, and unified…
posts.content:
Many of the world’s leading fintechs use Stripe to build and scale, including 32 of the Forbes Fintech 50 (and counting). As these businesses expand into new markets, they need to deliver the same fast, reliable experience everywhere while supporting local payment methods, navigating local compliance requirements, and integrating new banking partners. 

We’re introducing three updates to help fintechs launch products and grow internationally more easily: simpler payout management with Stripe Global Payouts, support for stablecoin cards in more countries, and unified APIs for building global financial products. 

Here’s what’s new.

Send payouts to recipients in more than 160 markets

We’ve expanded Global Payouts to more markets and made it easier to set up and manage. Businesses can now send instant stablecoin payouts to recipients in 160 markets and traditional currency payouts to recipients in more than 100, directly from the Stripe Dashboard.

Fintechs can also use Global Payouts programmatically—by embedding hosted forms or integrating with flexible APIs—to enable use cases like loan disbursements, remittances, investment withdrawals, and neobank cash-outs within their products. Turo, for example, uses Global Payouts to send claims payments. The company has processed over $160 million, with a 99.5% payout success rate.

Issue stablecoin cards in more countries

Stripe is launching stablecoin card issuing in 27 EU countries, bringing availability to more than 65 countries worldwide. We plan to expand to 100 countries by the end of 2026. With stablecoin cards on Stripe Issuing, fintechs can offer cards that draw from stablecoin balances held in a custodial wallet, noncustodial wallet, or Stripe financial account. When cardholders make a purchase, Stripe automatically converts their stablecoins into the local currency at the point of sale; merchants can accept these payments just like a traditional card payment.

Fintechs can use Issuing to launch a global stablecoin card program that works across markets with one integration, rather than connecting separate providers for card issuing, currency conversion, KYC and KYB verification, fraud management, and customer support. 

Stripe Issuing already powers more than 400 million cards worldwide across commercial and consumer card programs. Stablecoin cards extend that infrastructure to fintechs and platforms building with stablecoins, enabling them to scale globally and reach a larger customer base.

Add financial capabilities with a unified stack

Stripe Treasury is the building block that connects business earnings with the tools to manage and move money.  

Stripe Treasury allows businesses to settle Stripe earnings, hold funds, convert currencies, spend with cards, and send outbound payments. Fintechs can also bring these same capabilities to their customers by embedding Treasury’s financial tools and services into their platforms.

Stripe Treasury, Global Payouts, and Issuing are all part of Stripe’s unified stack for fintechs, meaning they easily integrate with one another and KYC information can be shared, reducing compliance work and additional user verification steps. They are also compatible with Open Standard’s OUSD stablecoin and Tempo’s blockchain, helping businesses access the benefits of stablecoins while still being interoperable with fiat infrastructure.

Grow your business on Stripe

Over 1,500 fintechs on Stripe serve customers in more than 200 countries and territories. With Stripe’s unified stack, they don’t need to integrate and manage multiple vendors. Instead, they can use a single integration to build global financial products that support money movement, storage, and payment use cases while they continue to expand across markets.

Contact the team to get started.

posts.title: Advancing Generative Recommendation Inference: our collaboration with NVIDIA on TensorRT LLM
posts.summary: At Spotify, every surface and interaction is personalized to you as a user: the content on the Home page, the... The post Advancing Generative Recommendation Inference: our collaboration with NVIDIA on TensorRT LLM…
posts.content:
At Spotify, every surface and interaction is personalized to you as a user: the content on the Home page, the next song that plays, and more recently the ability to talk to Spotify. 

Traditionally, this content is provided by recommendation systems that require multiple steps for candidate retrieval and ranking, and perhaps individual systems per surface. Generative AI is fundamentally changing this. We have been exploring how to provide recommendations via a Large Personalized Language Model in real time, across multiple surfaces.

This shift, however, presents unique engineering challenges, particularly when moving from a proof of concept to a scalable, production-grade inference architecture. 

Spotify’s journey into LLM-powered recommendations

Beam search

In January 2026, Spotify introduced LLM-powered technology to its podcast recommendations. The work is grounded in recent advancements in generative recommendation architectures, specifically the foundational methods introduced in the PLUM paper . At Spotify, we have applied these concepts to build a specialized generative recommendation system for podcasts, aimed at delivering deeply personalized listening experiences. Our specialized architecture, detailed in our "Deploying Semantic ID-based Generative Retrieval for Large-Scale Podcast Discovery at Spotify" paper  employs beam search to explore multiple token sequence paths simultaneously for candidate generation. 

Beam search is a technique that allows exploration of an LLM’s output space with the goal of identifying highly probable token sequences. This technique navigates a decision tree of potential recommendations by keeping the most promising 'beams' or sequences active at each step, with the goal of identifying the highest-scoring podcasts for personalization. For this reason, these top sequences constitute semantic IDs that are then translated to catalog items to serve recommendations to users.

Our initial release relies on vLLM as an inference engine. vLLM is one of the most widely adopted open source inference engines, particularly strong at supporting modern model architectures for high-throughput  inference deployments. However vLLM’s support for beam search is limited compared to traditional completion requests – its beam search implementation doesn’t extract the maximum performance from GPU devices.

Specifically, vLLM's beam search implementation operates outside the core GPU engine, which introduces CPU-side bottlenecks and additional GPU work due to the recomputation of partially filled KV blocks.

For our January launch, these limitations meant we couldn't fully utilize high-end GPUs, so we opted for lower-tier accelerators to manage costs while keeping the system at a more optimal load point. 

Candidate scoring

Another inference technique we’ve been exploring is candidate scoring. Candidate scoring uses a model's log probabilities to evaluate and rank a set of candidates. 

A naive way to perform this type of inference is to adopt a “fan-out” approach and run inference on each candidate separately, for each request then we extract the related logprobs, before aggregating them to achieve the desired ranking operation.

This type of inference is generally available in most open source inference engines, however a more efficient technique has found its way into SGLang, thanks also to work from Linkedin’s engineering team. For this reason we’ve been utilizing SGLang as well to access this feature at inference time with an efficient candidate masking technique that allows us to score multiple candidates in a single request.

Personalization

The most important part of Spotify recommendations is our ability to personalize based on user preferences and interactions. In our traditional recommendation systems, we have used dense user embeddings to accomplish personalization at scale. As we have experimented with LLM-based recommendations, we have explored a few approaches to enable personalization in this new paradigm.

Plain User Text

This approach entails converting user listening and interaction history to text to place in the prompt for the LLM. The major issue with fully text based user history is the amount of text required to accurately represent the user. Prompts become extremely large, resulting in large inference latency that is too long for our request budget as well as higher GPU usage. Plain User Text is used sparingly, generally for smaller cases like the user’s most recent real time streams.

User Semantic Ids

Similar to the PLUM paper mentioned earlier, we explored representing user history as a semantic id. This approach extends the model vocabulary with user semantic id tokens, which are easily added to prompts using a handful of text tokens, keeping prompts short and easily servable with no custom inference requirements. The LLM was fine tuned using the user semantic id space and extended vocabulary, and at inference time, a user semantic id is added to the prompt. While early results were promising, this approach requires further experimentation and research before it's ready for production. 

Soft Tokens

The most successful method we have used for personalizing LLM requests is based on our existing user embeddings. The general approach is outlined in a white paper called Embedding to Prefix created by Spotify Research. Overall, the idea is to learn a projection from an existing embedding space into an LLM’s embedding space as a single soft token.  The LLM is fine tuned using a subset of the weights to be able to use this soft token to personalize recommendation outputs. At inference time, a user vector is projected into the LLM embedding space and inserted into the prompt before executing the initial forward pass. We have used this approach successfully for podcast recommendations and are currently integrating and evaluating it for various tasks with our internal LLM model.

Expanding LLM-powered recommendation systems

The successful rollout of our first LLM-powered recommendation system, along with continued internal experimentation, has grown into a broader effort to bring generative recommendation capabilities across Spotify, powering our listening experience across catalog offerings and driving user interactions across surfaces. As this work moves toward production, an efficient and manageable inference stack becomes increasingly important. This is where our collaboration with NVIDIA began.

Partnering with NVIDIA: Building for Feature Parity

We kicked off our collaboration with NVIDIA with a clear goal: unify the inference features that we require (efficient beam search, scoring, and user soft tokens) into a single engine. 

To address these challenges, we looked to TensorRT LLM (TRT-LLM) together with NVIDIA engineers. While TensorRT LLM offered superior hardware utilization for beam search, it initially lacked the specific "Score API" functionality available in our SGLang-based setup, as well as the ability to inject soft tokens and return sequences for multiple beams in beam search available in vLLM. With the NVIDIA engineering team—including Marek, Martin, Stefan, and Alexander—our goal was clear: close the feature gaps in TensorRT LLM.

This work resulted in several additions to the project to aid Spotify’s application of LLM in recommendation systems, specifically

  • support for returning multiple sequences in beam search (v1.2.0rc3)

  • support for out-of-tree models in trtllm-serve (v1.2.0rc4)

  • support for passing multi-modal embeddings via “image_embeds” (v1.3.0rc0)

  • support for multi-item scoring via the Python API (v1.3.0rc20)

  • general bug fixes and performance improvements

Beam search in TensorRT LLM is implemented as part of the sampler, which reduces host overheads and, combined with overlap scheduling, ensures good GPU utilization. Moreover, the C++-based sampler in TensorRT LLM has been replaced with a more flexible design relying more heavily on PyTorch. The beam search support implemented in this new sampler provided a notable performance uplift compared to the previous implementation.

With NVIDIA’s help and review, we used TensorRT LLM’s out-of-tree model support to implement a customized Qwen3 extension plugin to implement our soft token approach. The plugin enables passing user vectors via multi-modal request parameters and performs the user embedding projection and soft token replacement.

The multi-item scoring extensions to TensorRT LLM’s Python API enable functionality equivalent to SGLang’s scoring API. Currently, a custom serving layer implementing efficient tokenization and request batching is required. However, TensorRT LLM is continuously evolving and has, e.g., recently added support for serving prefill-only embeddings. Multi-item scoring is an important performance optimization, because it avoids the overhead of a single request per candidate, while retaining a computational effort linear in the number of candidates.

The efforts mentioned above have landed in recent versions of TensorRT LLM, and the following benchmarks show the performance edge that the implementation is delivering.

These performance improvements have materially translated into significant cost reduction for Spotify’s generative recommendation applications. Looking at the 1.7B variant of Qwen3 this results in up to 54% cost reduction for beam search workloads and up to 7% cost reduction for scoring workloads.

The Road Ahead

Our collaboration with NVIDIA engineers has not only helped us address immediate inference challenges but has also broadened our perspective on the opportunities for further efficiency gains. As we continue to expand the use of generative recommendation models across Spotify, optimizing inference performance and cost efficiency will remain key priorities. Looking ahead, we are excited to continue working closely with NVIDIA to explore additional optimizations, with a particular focus on quantization and NVIDIA Blackwell-specific techniques that can help us unlock even greater performance from the latest GPU architectures. Ultimately, our goal is to build an inference stack that can support increasingly sophisticated personalization capabilities at scale, while keeping latency and infrastructure costs under control.

Acknowledgments

Thank you to everyone who contributed to this collaboration, and to the authors of this post from Spotify and NVIDIA:

Ivo Senese, Reid Wilbur, Mark VanMiddlesworth, Guy Stone, Marek Pikulski, Stefan Niebler, and Alexander Young.

posts.title: How Dynata scaled AI across the development lifecycle with AI-DLC and Kiro IDE
posts.summary: Dynata reimagined its development lifecycle with AI, moving from AI-assisted coding to the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) methodology with Kiro IDE. Learn how the company reduced the development phase of…
posts.content:
When Dynata set out to compress multi-sprint feature delivery into a single sprint, the answer wasn’t simply faster coding. It was reimagining the entire development lifecycle with AI. The team progressed in deliberate stages. They began with AI-assisted coding, then connected AI with their knowledge ecosystem across Confluence, Jira, Lucidchart, GitHub, and Figma. Finally, they adopted the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) methodology from AWS using Kiro IDE, an AI-native development environment. In doing so, Dynata transformed how its cross-functional teams collaborate.

Delivering software across multiple teams is a collaborative process that produces great outcomes when it works well. Product, project management, engineering, design, quality assurance (QA), and deployment each brings essential perspective, and that coordination requires significant time. Multiple rounds of discussion and review before development begins is common. For complex features, it’s expected and healthy.

In this post, we show how Dynata reduced the development phase of features that typically spanned 3–4 sprints to approximately one sprint’s worth of time. We also share how you can bring AI into the full delivery process, not only individual developer output, giving every team earlier visibility and tighter alignment from the start.

About Dynata

Dynata is the world’s largest first-party data company, delivering precise, reliable insights that help businesses to make informed decisions at scale. Their platform empowers organizations to activate the right audiences, and measure impact with confidence through industry-leading data accuracy, commitment to continuous improvement, and operational excellence.

Across Dynata’s portfolio, multiple distributed engineering teams work in parallel. They build and evolve platform capabilities, integrate with partner ecosystems, and ship features on continuous delivery cycles. Coordinating product intent, design, engineering, and test engineering across teams at that scale while maintaining delivery velocity is the kind of challenge that rewards better process as much as better technology.

The challenge

Dynata’s engineering teams had established a solid foundation that included experienced developers, modern cloud infrastructure on AWS, clear product ownership, and a culture of continuous improvement. As the organization scaled across multiple product lines and distributed teams, the natural next ambition was to make the delivery process faster and more connected across every team involved, including product, engineering, test engineering, and project management.

The areas with the most headroom are familiar across enterprise engineering organizations. Requirements context was spread across Jira, Confluence, Lucid, and design documents, and bringing it all together into a shared, actionable picture before development started took meaningful time. Cross-functional alignment happened largely in sequence, which meant that input from test engineering, design, or deployment planning sometimes came later in the cycle than was ideal. And when scope shifted mid-sprint, absorbing the change required effort proportional to how far into implementation the team had progressed.

Dynata’s goal was clear. The team wanted to bring AI into the delivery process in a way that accelerated the whole cycle, not only individual developer output, and gave every team earlier visibility and tighter alignment from the start.

What followed was a structured, step-by-step approach starting at the code level, expanding to the knowledge ecosystem, and ultimately reaching across the full development lifecycle.

The journey: From code generation to full lifecycle AI

Dynata’s path to AI-driven development didn’t happen in a single leap. It unfolded in three deliberate steps, each one building on the confidence and lessons of the one before. The team started by bringing AI into everyday coding, then connected it to the tools and context that teams already relied on and finally adopted a methodology that brought AI into every phase of delivery. Here is how each step played out.

Step 1: AI-assisted coding

Dynata’s developers began their AI journey with Amazon Q Developer, the AI-powered coding assistant from AWS, using it for code generation, test writing, and implementation acceleration across day-to-day development work.

The productivity gains were immediate and visible. Developers moved faster on implementation, generated higher volumes of well-structured code, and spent less time on repetitive scaffolding. The experience built genuine AI fluency across the engineering team, establishing AI-assisted development as a standard part of the workflow rather than an occasional experiment.

As the team’s ambitions grew beyond code-level assistance, Dynata adopted Kiro IDE, an AI-native development environment from AWS built around spec-driven development, automated steering files, and native support for the AI-DLC workflow. Kiro gave the team the ability to connect AI to the full delivery process, from requirements through to implementation. The move was a natural progression, building on the AI fluency the team had already developed with Amazon Q Developer.

“The code generation results were great from the start. Developers were more productive, and the quality held up.”

Step 2: Connecting AI to the knowledge ecosystem

With a productive coding baseline in place, the team explored what AI could do when given access to broader project context. They integrated their AI tooling with Jira, Confluence, Lucid, and other knowledge sources, giving the AI visibility into tickets, specifications, architecture diagrams, and design documentation alongside the code base.

The value expanded significantly. Tech leads and architects began using AI not only for implementation, but for architectural decision support. They used it to review design choices against existing system context, identify potential conflicts with other components, and validate alignment with established patterns at a per-developer level.

“Once we connected AI with Jira, Confluence, and Lucid, we started using it not just for code but for architectural design at each developer level. The results were also great.”

Step 3: Discovering AI-DLC

With AI delivering value at the coding and architectural design stages, the team set its sights on a broader goal. They wanted AI to help with the entire delivery process, from requirements through to production, not just implementation alone.

The team discovered AI-DLC, the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle methodology from AWS, through AWS blog posts and published customer success stories. The methodology positions AI as a structured part of every phase of software delivery, spanning requirements capture and clarification, design, task planning, and implementation, with human review and approval at each stage. AI-DLC is powered by Amazon Bedrock, which provides the foundation model layer behind the AI analysis, generation, and clarification in Kiro.

“We were looking for solutions to include AI across the lifecycle. Then we saw the AWS AI-DLC posts and success stories and wanted to try it internally.”

Adoption: A staged approach that built confidence at every step

Dynata took a deliberate, staged adoption path. The team built expertise and refined the process before involving the broader organization. This turned out to be one of the most valuable decisions they made.

Stage 1: Internal pilot with interested developers

A small group of developers who were motivated to explore tried AI-DLC independently using Kiro IDE. Kiro implements the AI-DLC workflow natively through Specs (structured requirements-through-tasks pipelines), steering files (team coding standards injected into every AI session), and hooks (automated quality checks at defined workflow points).

What the pilot showed was qualitatively different from standard AI code generation. Rather than only producing code, AI-DLC was helping the process by guiding structured iterations, surfacing gaps and ambiguities proactively, and building confidence in the design before a line of implementation code was written.

“Instead of just generating code, it was helping the process – reviewing, identifying gaps, iterating- giving confidence that it would work at a large scale.”

The pilot also surfaced what needed to be in place before scaling. Steering files needed tuning to produce code at the team’s production standards. The person leading a team session needed solid familiarity with the AI-DLC workflow. And participants benefited from a shared understanding of what the process involved before sitting down together.

It’s worth noting that AI-DLC is IDE-agnostic. Although Kiro provides native support for the full workflow, teams at Dynata also ran AI-DLC sessions using Cursor with Claude and found the methodology worked effectively across environments. What matters is the structured process, and the tooling supports it.

Stage 2: Preparation before team sessions

Before running a full cross-functional workshop, three things needed to be in place:

Session leader readiness. The person guiding the session, typically a tech lead or senior developer, needed working familiarity with the AI-DLC methodology and the IDE being used. Not expert-level mastery, but enough to keep the team moving through each phase, handle questions, and recognize when to spend more time on a step.

Team orientation. All participants including product, project management, tech leads, and developers received a high-level briefing on what AI-DLC is, how the session would be structured, what to expect from each phase, and what their role was. This upfront alignment made sessions significantly more productive.

Input preparation. Steering files describing the team’s coding standards, naming conventions, and architectural patterns were prepared in advance. Jira epics, Confluence specifications, and design documents were gathered and accessible before the session began. The quality of AI output is directly connected to the completeness of the context it is given.

Stage 3: The three-day AI-DLC feature workshop

Figure 1: Traditional feature delivery compared to delivery with AI-DLC at Dynata

With preparation complete and pilot learnings incorporated, the team selected a feature and ran a structured three-day workshop. This is where the methodology demonstrated its full value.

The workshop brought together product, the project owner, tech leads, and developers working through the AI-DLC workflow in Kiro IDE together.

Day 1: Requirements and alignment

The AI-DLC workflow guided the team step by step through the Inception phase:

  • The AI analyzed all available context, including Jira epics, Confluence pages, design documents, and the existing code base, and generated a consolidated, structured requirements view.
  • The AI surfaced clarifying questions, such as gaps between sources, edge cases without defined behavior, and technology decisions that hadn’t been made explicit. The team worked through each question together, with answers captured directly in the IDE.
  • All stakeholders reviewed and validated the output together. This was often the first time the full team had seen a unified picture of what was being built, with role-specific documents giving each participant the level of detail relevant to their work.

By the end of the day, requirements were agreed upon, documented, and committed to the repository.

The difference came down to timing. Instead of blockers and ambiguities surfacing during implementation, when resolving them is most expensive, they surfaced during planning, when the cost of a correction is a conversation. A process that typically took days or weeks of iterative meetings across teams was completed in a single structured day.

Day 2: Design and task planning

With agreed requirements in hand, the team moved into design:

  • The AI generated component boundaries, service interfaces, data models, API contracts, and dependency maps based on the approved requirements.
  • Tech leads and senior developers reviewed the design artifacts, applied their judgment, and validated that the design reflected real system constraints.
  • When design questions connected back to requirements, the team updated the requirements documents and the AI kept the design documents consistent. Changes propagated through the artifact chain automatically.
  • Product and project management remained in the room throughout. For many, this was the first direct view into how engineering translates requirements into architecture. When design questions required a business decision, the right people were immediately available.
  • After design was approved, the AI generated a sequenced task list, each task mapped to design artifacts and requirements, with implementation detail for each.
  • The team reviewed and iterated on the task list, then distributed ownership so that each developer took responsibility for specific tasks.

The team also made one practical observation. Thoughtful task distribution upfront, accounting for component dependencies and parallel workstreams, reduces merge conflicts during development. This was something the team refined over the first one or two feature cycles and improved steadily.

Outcome. The team approved design and tasks by the end of the day, with every team member clear on what was being built and who owned what.

Day 3: Code generation and working software

With tasks distributed and owners assigned, developers worked through code generation:

  • The AI generated code grounded in the approved design documents, requirements, and user stories with steering files ensuring output conformed to the team’s coding standards from the start.
  • Before generating code for each unit, the AI produced a detailed code generation plan for the developer to review and approve, keeping developers in control of what was being built and why.
  • All documents and artifacts from Days 1 and 2 were committed to the repository, giving every developer a shared, versioned baseline to work from.

Progress was demoed to the team at regular intervals for directional feedback, keeping everyone aligned as the feature took shape.

“After a few features built using AI-DLC, the quality of the end-to-end results and the code quality showed great improvements.”

Steering files improved with each feature. As the team accumulated more experience describing their standards and conventions, code generation output became more consistent and required less adjustment, a compounding return on the investment in getting the inputs right.

Outcome. By the end of Day 3, the team had a working, demonstrable state of the feature, with the development phase completed and the full scope visible and validated. They also had a clear picture of what remained, including testing, edge case hardening, and release preparation. This isn’t the finish line. It’s a strong, confident starting point for the steps that follow. What it reduces is the uncertainty that normally exists at this stage, because requirements gaps, design misalignments, and implementation surprises are already behind the team, not ahead of them.

Beyond full workshops: Using AI-DLC selectively

After running full three-day workshops for several features, the team discovered something important about the methodology. AI-DLC is flexible, and not every situation calls for the full workflow. Teams began using individual phases of AI-DLC independently, based on what they were trying to achieve:

  • Requirements discussions between product and tech teams. Using only the Inception phase to structure a requirements conversation, surface ambiguities, and produce a shared document, without necessarily proceeding to design or code generation in the same session.
  • Design-only sessions. Working through the design phase for a well-understood feature to align on architecture before developers began implementation.
  • Code generation from existing documentation. Teams with well-documented requirements using only the construction phase to accelerate implementation.

The methodology works as a complete end-to-end workflow, and it works as a targeted tool for specific parts of the process. Teams adopted it wherever it added the most value for their situation, which is the right way to use it.

Observations and what accelerated progress

Throughout the journey, from AI-assisted coding through to full AI-DLC workshops, the Dynata team identified a set of practical observations that shaped how they adopted the methodology and what made the biggest difference. These aren’t theoretical recommendations. They come directly from what the team experienced across multiple features, teams, and sessions.

ObservationWhat the team foundWhat helpedSteering file qualityEarly code generation output needed adjustment to fully match team standardsIterative refinement of steering files across features. Quality improved steadily and compoundedSession leader readinessSessions moved best when the leader had hands-on experience with the workflowPilot developers led early team sessions. Pre-session preparation for leaders paid dividendsInput context completenessRicher input context produced better AI outputPre-session effort to gather and organize source materials consistently improved session qualityTask distribution planningParallel development on related components required thoughtful dependency planningSpending time on task distribution during the workshop, not after, reduced rework in subsequent stepsTeam orientationParticipants who understood the process upfront contributed more effectivelyA brief pre-session briefing for all participants improved engagement and session paceIDE flexibilityTeams used both Kiro and Cursor with Claude successfullyAI-DLC is IDE-agnostic. What matters is the structured process, not the specific tooling

Results

Across features where Dynata applied the full AI-DLC workflow, the results were consistent:

  • Approximately 70 percent reduction in development phase time: By Dynata’s own estimate, based on their standard sprint planning, features that would typically span about four sprints were completed in roughly 1 sprint of developer time, with working software demonstrable at the end of the structured workshop.
  • Fewer post-production iterations and bugs. By surfacing and resolving requirements gaps and design ambiguities during the planning phase, before code was written, the team saw noticeably lower post-launch rework compared to features built through traditional delivery cycles.
  • Requirements alignment in a single session.

posts.title: Sync real-time Stripe data to Postgres with Stripe Data Pipeline
posts.summary: Applications rely on current Stripe data to fulfill orders, update customer accounts, and manage access to paid features. Until now, developers have had to build and maintain custom integrations to keep application…
posts.content:
Many businesses on Stripe use Stripe data to power their applications. A subscription business relies on current plan data to update a customer’s account or grant access to paid features; an ecommerce company uses payment confirmation data to fulfill an order. 

As agents take on more tasks and businesses build more customer-facing workflows around Stripe data, applications need data they can act on immediately. Businesses on Stripe have asked us for an easier way to keep their application databases current. Developers have typically done this themselves by repeatedly calling Stripe APIs or building webhook infrastructure that copies changes into their databases. They then have to monitor the integration, handle failed or out-of-order events, and regularly check that all their stored data still matches Stripe. 

To keep databases current without requiring developers to build and maintain custom integrations, we’re launching real-time sync to Postgres through Stripe Data Pipeline. You can sync payment, customer, subscription, and other Stripe data to a Postgres database that powers your applications. Stripe handles the sync end to end.

Sync Stripe data directly to Postgres

Data Pipeline already lets businesses send Stripe data to a data warehouse or cloud storage for analytics and reporting. Anthropic uses it to accelerate month-end reconciliation, Cursor uses it to report on revenue and churn, and Lime uses it to automate financial reporting. 

The new real-time sync sends Stripe data directly to Postgres databases, including those hosted by Supabase, AWS, Neon, Databricks Lakebase, and other providers. To set up a sync, connect your Postgres database and select the Stripe tables you need. Data Pipeline backfills those tables and keeps them synchronized as the source data changes in Stripe. No code is required. 

“The value that real-time sync to Postgres creates replaces all of the other work we had to do to get our data,” said Josh Siegel, CPO and CTO at Company Sage. “It’s much easier for us to reduce our old API and webhook infrastructure and just use Stripe Data Pipeline instead.”

Keep data current automatically 

Once you set up the sync, Data Pipeline copies existing data from the selected Stripe tables into your connected Postgres database. As data changes in Stripe, Data Pipeline delivers updates to Postgres in seconds. 

Data Pipeline regularly audits the synchronized records against the source data in Stripe and resolves discrepancies. The result is a reliable, real-time copy of Stripe data in Postgres, and one fewer system for developers to build, monitor, and debug.

Get started

Postgres is the first Data Pipeline destination to support real-time syncing of Stripe data. Support for Snowflake, Google BigQuery, Amazon Redshift, Databricks, and cloud storage platforms is coming soon. 

Real-time sync to Postgres is available in public preview and free to get started. Create a pipeline in the Stripe Dashboard, or read our docs to learn more.

posts.title: How Meta Built Forum With AI-Native Engineering
posts.summary: Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups. To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Shengbo Guo, Bohou Luo, Shubhojeet Sarkar, Vivian Qu, Max (Xiangjun) Fan, Prerna Jain, Mike Plumpe, Chinmay Abhyankar, Rish Tandon
  • Meta’s newest app, Forum, is for anyone who wants to go deeper into the conversations in their Facebook groups.
  • To build Forum, Meta engineers adopted a whole new way of working by bringing an AI agent into the development cycle.
  • We’re sharing insights into what it took to build Forum with agentic AI: how we adapted the codebase, tested frameworks and internal tooling for agentic execution, what worked, and what didn’t.

Forum is a standalone Groups app that a small team built from scratch. It’s also where we tested a different way of working: treating an AI agent as a participant in the engineering process rather than a faster way to type.

That experiment needed a definition of success, and ours wasn’t code volume. We measured verified, production-ready outcomes — changes that build, pass tests, and survive review. 

From Human-In-The-Loop to Human-On-The-Loop

Pointing AI at the coding step alone doesn’t change much. Our results compounded as we extended the approach to the stages around implementation — planning, building, testing, and verification. The clearest way to see the shift is in who owns each step.

With human-in-the-loop, the engineer drives every step and the AI assists inside it by autocompleting a function, suggesting a fix, or answering a question. Each iteration advances at the pace of the person driving it.

With human-on-the-loop, the agent runs the iteration itself — plan, implement, build, test, correct, repeat — while the engineer sets the goal, watches the run, steps in when it drifts, and approves the result. The person’s job moves from executing the steps to owning the outcome and holding the quality bar. This is the target we are driving toward, not a finished state: some stages run autonomously today, while others still keep an engineer in each iteration.

When the engineer supervises, work stops being strictly sequential. Cycles that used to run one at a time can overlap, and an engineer’s time goes to direction and judgment rather than to sitting through the loop. But that only holds if what comes back can be trusted. Without verification, AI-generated code creates a familiar problem — plausible output that no one has confirmed actually works, which an engineer then has to read, debug, and often discard. Weak signals don’t remove the constraint; they move it from writing code to reviewing code that looks finished and isn’t.

So we set the bar at verification rather than compilation. Compiling isn’t the finish line — a task is complete only once automated tests and visual checks have passed. Agents check their own work before an engineer sees it, which means what reaches review is a smaller set of higher-confidence results rather than a pile of output to sift through. Less gets generated, and less gets discarded. Every shipped outcome still carries an engineer’s sign-off; our effort went into making that sign-off fast and well-evidenced, with build results, test outcomes, and recorded verification sessions attached to the change.

With the engineer outside of every cycle, the loop has to run safely on its own. Four capabilities make that possible:

Planning as technical specification: Agentic execution requires extreme precision. Ambiguity that an engineer might resolve through intuition results in agent failure. We invested in rigorous upstream decomposition and machine-readable context, which tightened the engineering loop for engineers and agents alike.

Automated verification inside the loop is the force multiplier: We integrated automated pass/fail signals — build status, unit tests, and UI spec matching — directly into the agent loop. This enabled asynchronous development producing ready-to-review pull requests with pre-populated test plans and recorded verification sessions. Verification is the hard part to get right, and how much we can safely hand to the loop is gated by how much we can trust the verifiers.

Simulated user testing with agents: We deployed navigation agents that interact with the live app exactly like a person would. These agents perform actions, read the screen, and report regressions. Navigation agents are able to run the same verification paths continuously. 

Agentic production operations: After launch, agents help automate root-cause analysis. When someone using Forum submits feedback, the agents use that feedback to investigate possible regressions. The agents then forward the analysis to engineers who decide the next course of action.  

The Operating Model

That ownership model needs machinery with five key components:

  • Rules are permanent project instructions. When the agent repeats a mistake more than twice, we encode the correction once, for everyone.
  • Skills turn team conventions into loadable steps the agent can invoke.
  • Agents automate checks that previously required a manual pass. 
  • Commands chain skills and agents into workflows. They assess complexity, reproduce a bug, plan and implement a fix, create the pull request, and run a multi-stage review.
  • Hooks are automated triggers, such as running a linter after every agent turn, checking simulator connectivity before install, and validating tests before a pull request is created.

Adapting the Environment to the Models

The biggest gains came from changing our code and tooling, not our prompts. 

Architectural legibility over inherited complexity: We worked to keep Forum’s codebase as straightforward as possible and chose to modularize key pieces of the architecture in order to get the benefits of battle-tested infrastructure while also letting the agents plug and play easily. Where we couldn’t easily do so, we rebuilt from scratch, trading reuse for agentic throughput, and it proved rewarding in development speed. Agents learn patterns from the code they read. Fix a weak pattern once and every future agent session inherits the improvement; leave it and the same shortcut shows up in everything the agent writes next. 

Give agents tools, not descriptions: Our main failure mode was the agent losing track of where it was in the app — editing the home feed when asked to change the group home screen, or guessing at screen coordinates. So instead of describing the app to the agent, we gave it tools to check: read the live view hierarchy from the simulator, list the elements actually on screen, and look up the path to a target view — all before it acts. Misdirected edits dropped sharply. We applied the same approach wherever agents touched our systems: give the agent a way to check state directly rather than a description to reason from.

Build-level isolation for safe AI prototyping: As Forum matured toward production, we wanted early-stage prototypes and agent-generated experiments to have room to run while keeping the production app strictly limited to finished, reviewed work. We wanted a stronger guarantee than feature gating alone, where prototype code still exists inside the production build. Our solution was a separate build flavor, a sandbox app that shares the exact same codebase, frameworks, and design system as production, but compiles prototype code out of the production build entirely via a plugin/socket architecture. 

This gave us three things at once: 

  • Designers and cross-functional partners could prototype freely using AI tools without needing an engineer in the loop for each change. 
  • Anything built in the sandbox could be ported directly to production with no rebuild. 
  • No prototype code could crash the production app because it physically didn’t exist in that build. 

The pattern let us keep fast AI iteration after we had real people using the app to protect.

Finding Real Bugs With AI Stress Testing

Adapting the environment did more than make the agent faster to build with — it made the agent a tester. We didn’t point it at one specific defect. Instead, we set up repeatable stress scenarios that mimic real user behavior (aggressive scrolling, random group browsing, rapid navigation, repeated media loading) and ran them routinely across builds. Because these runs produce consistent signals (crashes, memory growth, page faults, UI regressions), the agent can triage anomalies, narrow to the triggering sequence, and then investigate the root cause.

One such run surfaced a memory issue. The agent isolated a repro, proposed a fix, and verified it — all during development, before the app reached users. The fix materially reduced on-device memory growth and page faults across repeated stress sessions.

While engineers made the architectural decisions, the detection and regression monitoring were automated and repeatable; once an anomaly was detected, the agent could reproduce → isolate → propose a fix → verify with the same harness.

Applying the Same Discipline to Forum’s Feed

We applied the human-on-the-loop approach in two places:

Building the stack: Agents mapped the architectural options and trade-offs; engineers then evaluated and chose. What we deliberately kept human was the target — deciding what a good outcome looks like is a product judgment, not something the system should define for itself.

Operating the stack: Questions that used to require whichever engineer knew the relevant code path now go to an investigation agent that gathers what it needs and posts a write-up with suggested fixes. After hand-scoring a batch of real investigations we arrived at a workflow where the agent compresses the mechanical work and delivers a structured write-up to an engineer, who then validates whether a finding is a real bug or an intentional trade-off. 

What improved quality wasn’t better prompting. It was context. One recurring category of investigation came back weak until we gave the agent the same pointers to the relevant code, example queries, and design docs that we’d give any new engineer on day one. The quality of that category jumped. The difference from human onboarding is that you train once, and every future session starts from it.

Did It Work?

Beyond shipping faster, we shipped cleaner. Continuous verification surfaced systemic issues — like the memory bottleneck above — during development rather than after launch. The results show up in the performance profile:

  • Quality, found early: The autonomous stress-testing loop caught and fixed the aforementioned memory issue during development rather than post-launch, roughly halving memory use and page faults.
  • Velocity: Forum reached core feature parity with Facebook Groups in eight weeks, with AI handling much of the routine implementation so engineers could focus on architecture, product decisions, and quality.
  • Leverage that lasted: After launch, agent-driven investigation helped engineers triage and root-cause user feedback. 

The AI did more than generate code. It tightened our quality loop, helping a small team deliver a high-quality app with less ongoing rework.

What Worked, and What Did Not

Acknowledgements 

We thank Neeharika Sinha, Jane Kou, Gang Yang, Guohao Zhang, Zeya Zhang, Kinnary Jangla, andYonghui Lu for their valuable contributions.

posts.title: 2026 World Cup: Breaking Records, Spiky Charts and Reliability at Scale
posts.summary: Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record! There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let…
posts.content:
.entry-header By Syamla Bandla, Vincent Mauge, Michael Stella, Deniz Hastorun, Francois Richard, Javier Frias, Mike McCall

Every four years, the World Cup becomes the largest planned stress test of our infrastructure. This year it also set an all-time record!

There are a few moments throughout the year, like New Years Eve, that really let us see the collective impact of everything we’ve built — but none are bigger than the quadrennial World Cup tournament. The 2026 World Cup broke records across messaging, video, recommendations, and networking at the same time. 

Some highlights:

  • WhatsApp: More than 30 million messages per second during the July 19 final (Argentina vs. Spain), 1.23x the peak of New Year’s Eve 2026 and an all-time platform record. The previous record had already fallen 12 days earlier, during the Round of 16 match between Argentina and Egypt, at 29 million messages per second.
  • Messenger, Threads, and Instagram Direct: 49 million messages per minute at peak.
  • Instagram: Recommendation system traffic up to 80% higher week-over-week. Final-squad players collectively added +213.6 million activated followers — a 6.6% increase — with combined followings surging from 3.26 billion to 3.47 billion. 
  • Live video: Watch time spiked +90% on Instagram and +242% on Facebook, versus the July baseline.
  • Threads: 1.5 billion impressions on tournament-tagged posts, reaching about 15 million people daily and peaking at 25 million on July 6.
  • Facebook: 80 million posts mentioning the World Cup.

Traffic Followed the Breaks, Not the Ball 

Every World Cup match caused surges in traffic. During the final, for example, traffic surged +46% in about four minutes at the end of regular time, and +57% in about 15 minutes at the final whistle. 

But by lining game events up against global egress traffic we discovered a striking pattern – surges in sharing were primarily happening during breaks (hydration breaks, halftime, extra time, the final whistle, the awards ceremony). The end-of-regulation whistle produced the single biggest peak of the tournament.

It wasn’t the gameplay that moved our charts. It was the conversations after it. The world came to Meta to watch the game and to share what it made them feel. 

Every capacity decision below follows from that one pattern.

Layered Systems, No Manual Intervention

Those spikes were absorbed by systems built for exactly this. Taiji balanced load across datacenters, Katran and Proxygen handled L4/L7 traffic distribution, our global load balancing system routed users to the best-positioned edge, and AutoScaling provisioned capacity on demand.

Region-Specific Capacity

Months before kickoff, Meta’s edge teams analyzed network capacity and worked closely with ISP partners so that upgrades landed where they would most improve quality of experience for end users. That targeted pre-build is now permanent capacity that will keep serving demand long after the tournament.

Instagram: Preparing for 39 Consecutive Days of Surges

For Instagram, the tournament meant 39 straight days of traffic spikes as billions of fans checked scores, posted Stories, and flooded Feed during breaks. Machine learning inference, Feed serving, Stories, Explore, and data infrastructure all had to absorb it without degrading the experience.

During the final, halftime Instagram Feed traffic rose 76% above the previous day in the minute the match ended, and stayed about 21% above for the following two hours.


Our approach rested on four things, deployed incrementally as the tournament moved from group stage to final.

  1. Capacity buffers: Our products went into the tournament with sufficient capacity, which meant real buffers were available to allocate. We pre-provisioned significant additional capacity across all serving tiers so that spikes never had to wait on autoscaling to catch up. These dedicated buffers were our single most effective lever of the tournament.
  2. Country-level graceful degradation: For high-risk matches, we shed non-critical background load in the top-traffic nations (Brazil, Argentina, India, Indonesia, Spain) to protect core functionality.
  3. Cascade prevention: So spikes at the serving layer couldn’t propagate into downstream data systems.
  4. Early warning signals These alerted us before we approached capacity thresholds, rather than after.

All of this, including the phased deployment timeline and the degradation activation criteria, is now a reusable runbook for future large-scale events like the 2028 Olympics.

WhatsApp: 8.4 Billion Messages in Five Minutes

Goals and the final whistle drove WhatsApp spikes lasting four to five minutes at a time. In its single highest-traffic five-minute window, WhatsApp delivered nearly 8.4 billion messages without interruption.

That came from months of preparation. More than 100 internal services were load-tested and resized ahead of the tournament, then retested, revalidated, and resized as the bracket narrowed and demand climbed.

Two things we’d normally do, we didn’t.

We didn’t shift load between regions. For past high-traffic events, our default has been to spread demand across multiple regions, letting capacity in quieter parts of the world absorb the spike. That works when peaks land hours apart — a global New Year’s Eve, for example. This event was different. Every region peaked in the same instant, so there was no idle capacity to borrow. Instead of deriving regional demand from a global multiplier, we forecast each region’s peak on its own terms.

We didn’t freeze. The other standard playbook move for a major event is to pause continuous deployment and hold off on riskier operations like disaster recovery exercises. This time we skipped the freeze entirely, on the strength of years of reliability enhancement. Teams shipped on their normal cadence throughout the entire event window, including during the peak moment itself. 

We Stay Ready Year-Round

Enabling connection in moments like this doesn’t just happen. Powering every message sent, every follower, and every Reel shared in real time across 48 teams and 104 matches is a story of infrastructure and product working as one.

Capacity planning, load testing, traffic management, and rapid incident response come together across these teams so that billions of people can connect in the moments that matter most — like an entire continent celebrating a last-minute goal at the same second.
