posts.title: Multi-region disaster recovery for Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs
posts.summary: Learn how to build multi-region disaster recovery for Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs. This design pattern combines Amazon Route 53 DNS failover, Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables, a canary health probe, and client-side…
posts.content:
WebSocket connections power some of the most interactive experiences on the web: financial trading applications streaming live market data, collaborative editing tools where multiple users work on the same document, gaming leaderboards updating in real time, and IoT dashboards monitoring thousands of devices. These applications depend on persistent, bidirectional communication between clients and servers.

Real-time applications using WebSocket connections face a unique challenge during Regional outages. WebSocket connections are persistent and bound to a specific AWS Region. A Regional failure severs every active connection. For applications that also maintain shared state across those connections, such as a live auction or collaborative editor, users lose both their connection and their session context. This post presents a design pattern for multi-Region disaster recovery with Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs that reconnects clients and restores state automatically during failover.

In this post, you learn how to build this pattern using Amazon Route 53 for DNS-based failover, Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables for cross-Region state replication, a canary health probe for traffic-independent failure detection, and client-side reconnection logic to recover from Regional failures while preserving application state.

Solution overview

This pattern creates an active-passive multi-Region architecture where the primary Region serves WebSocket connections and automatically fails over to a secondary Region during a disaster. The core idea is separating application state from the connection itself, so the client can restore its session after reconnection.

The architecture deploys identical WebSocket API stacks in two Regions, a primary and a secondary. Both Regions share application state through DynamoDB Global Tables, so the secondary Region is consistently ready to serve traffic. A single custom domain name fronts both Regions. Amazon Route 53 failover routing policy directs traffic to the primary Region under normal conditions. When the primary becomes unhealthy, Route 53 automatically shifts DNS resolution to the secondary Region. Clients reconnect to the same domain and resume operations without changing their configuration.

Figure 1 shows the architecture and the normal operation and failover flow.

Figure 1: Multi-region WebSocket API failover architecture

  1. A user opens the application, which establishes a WebSocket connection to the application’s domain name.
  2. Amazon Route 53 resolves the domain using a failover routing policy. Under normal conditions, it returns the primary Region’s endpoint.
  3. The WebSocket connection reaches API Gateway in the primary Region, which invokes an AWS Lambda function for each connection event and message.
  4. Lambda reads and writes application state to DynamoDB. Connected clients receive updates through their open WebSocket connections.
  5. DynamoDB Global Tables replicates the application state to the secondary Region asynchronously, keeping it ready to serve traffic.
  6. Independently, an Amazon EventBridge rule triggers a canary Lambda function every minute.
  7. The canary opens a WebSocket connection to the API Gateway endpoint, sends a heartbeat, and publishes the result as a custom Amazon CloudWatch metric.
  8. A CloudWatch alarm evaluates the metric. If the canary reports consecutive failures or stops publishing, the alarm fires and the associated Route 53 health check marks the primary as unhealthy.
  9. Route 53 detects the unhealthy primary and begins resolving the domain to the secondary Region instead.
  10. Clients reconnect through the same domain, now reaching the secondary Region, and recover their application state from the local DynamoDB replica.

Prerequisites

To follow along with this post, you need:

  • An AWS account with permissions to create Amazon API Gateway, AWS Lambda, Amazon DynamoDB, Amazon CloudWatch, and Route 53 resources.
  • A domain name with a hosted zone in Amazon Route 53.
  • AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates for your domain in both the primary and secondary Regions.
  • AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI) v2 installed and configured.
  • Node.js 18.x or later (for the client application).

Deploy the solution

The complete source code and deployment instructions are available on the GitHub repo. The repository includes AWS CloudFormation templates for the WebSocket APIs, canary health probe, and a React client application with the reconnection logic described in this post.

The demo application

The sample application is a real-time auction where multiple users bid on an item simultaneously. Each bid updates a shared counter through WebSocket messages, and connected clients see the current bid in real time. The application displays which AWS Region is serving responses, making failover visible during testing. Although minimal, this pattern represents real-time workloads where multiple clients share mutable state over WebSocket connections: chat applications, collaborative editors, live dashboards, or multiplayer games.

Managing connection state across Regions

WebSocket connections are persistent, but the application state built on top of them is what matters during failover. As users interact with the application, the server builds up session data tied to their identity. When a failover occurs and the client reconnects to a different Region, that session data needs to be available for the experience to continue uninterrupted. This solution stores state in DynamoDB Global Tables, which replicates it to the secondary Region asynchronously, typically within a second. Because this replication is asynchronous, writes that occur immediately before a failure may not reach the secondary Region. For most applications, this window is small enough to be acceptable.

After failover, the client reconnects and restores its state. In this demo, the client sends a getState message after reconnection to retrieve the latest application state from the secondary Region’s DynamoDB replica.

Production applications add two considerations on reconnection. First, clients authenticate again: WebSocket APIs authenticate on the $connect route, so after failover the secondary Region re-authenticates the client through a Lambda authorizer. Deploy that authorizer in both Regions so reconnecting clients can authenticate against either one. Second, to restore state, identify the user from the validated token, such as the sub claim. Key the stored state by the user ID rather than the connection ID, which changes on every reconnect. Applications model session state in different ways, so adapt this to your design.

If your application uses a relational database, you need to set up similar cross-region state replication. For instance, Amazon Aurora Global Database provides sub-second replication latency across Regions. Note that Aurora requires promoting a read replica to primary during failover, which typically adds 1–2 minutes to the recovery process. This promotion can also be automated based on a CloudWatch alarm action.

Heartbeat

Both the client and the canary use application-level heartbeat to verify their WebSocket connections are alive. At a regular interval, they send a lightweight message and expect an acknowledgment. A missing or invalid response signals a broken connection. The client uses this to trigger reconnection. The canary uses it to drive the Route 53 health check. This mechanism is described in RFC 6455 and is the standard approach for WebSocket connection health monitoring.

The client code snippets in this post use react-use-websocket, a React library that provides built-in support for reconnection and heartbeat. You can implement the same patterns in other WebSocket client libraries or languages.

heartbeat: {
  message: JSON.stringify({ action: 'heartbeat' }),
  returnMessage: 'pong',
  timeout: 35000,   // Close connection if no message received within 35s
  interval: 30000,  // Send heartbeat every 30s
}

Detecting regional failures automatically

When the primary Region becomes unavailable, Route 53 needs to detect the failure and redirect traffic to the secondary. To do this, the solution creates a health check that actively monitors the WebSocket endpoint. A Lambda function called the canary, deployed in the primary Region, powers this health check. It probes the endpoint every minute by opening a WebSocket connection, sending a heartbeat message, and confirming it receives a valid response. The canary publishes the result as a custom CloudWatch metric (App/WebSocketHealth, dimension ApiId): 1 for healthy, 0 for unhealthy.

A CloudWatch alarm monitors this metric and treats both failures and missing data as unhealthy (TreatMissingData: breaching). After two consecutive unhealthy datapoints, the alarm fires and the associated Route 53 health check (configured with InsufficientDataHealthStatus: Unhealthy) marks the primary as down. Route 53 shifts DNS to the secondary Region.

Failback works through the same mechanism. When the primary recovers, the canary starts succeeding again, the alarm clears, and Route 53 shifts traffic back. For production workloads, consider asymmetric thresholds: use a low threshold (two datapoints) for fast failover and a higher threshold (over five) for slower failback, which helps prevent flapping if the primary is unstable during recovery. A DNS time-to-live (TTL) of 60–120 seconds provides a good balance between fast propagation and lookup efficiency.

Client reconnection strategy

When a connection drops, the client needs to reconnect without overwhelming the recovering service. The heartbeat described earlier handles detection in most cases. If no messages arrive within the timeout window, the library closes the connection. However, the backend can be degraded rather than fully unreachable. For example, API Gateway returns error responses when the Lambda function is throttled, so the connection remains technically open while the application is non-functional. To handle this, the client tracks consecutive failed heartbeats: responses that aren’t the expected pong message. After 2 consecutive failures, the client force-closes the connection and triggers reconnection. With a 30-second heartbeat interval, this detects a degraded backend within 60 seconds.

After the client identifies a broken connection, it begins reconnecting using exponential backoff with full jitter, a pattern described in the AWS Architecture Blog post Exponential Backoff And Jitter. The reconnection interval doubles with each attempt, and full jitter randomizes the actual delay within that window. This spreads reconnection attempts over time, helping prevent a thundering herd where many clients retry simultaneously and overwhelm the secondary Region the moment DNS shifts.

reconnectInterval: (attempt) => {
  // Exponential backoff with full jitter
  const expDelay = Math.min(2000 * Math.pow(2, attempt), 20000);
  return Math.random() * expDelay;
}

After each successful reconnection, the client requests the current application state from the server. Because the client reconnects to the same custom domain, Route 53 resolves it to whichever Region is currently healthy. The client doesn’t need to know which Region it’s connecting to. The server includes the Region in its response, and the application can update its UI or logging accordingly.

Failover in action

To see the full failover sequence, start the client application and connect to your WebSocket endpoint:

cd client
cp .env.example .env.local
# Edit .env.local with your custom domain URL
npm install
npm run dev

Open the application in your browser and note the serving Region displayed in the UI.

Figure 2: Client connected to the primary Region (us-east-1)

Next, simulate a failure by setting the primary Lambda function’s reserved concurrency to zero, which prevents it from processing requests:

aws lambda put-function-concurrency \
  --function-name counter-handler-us-east-1 \
  --reserved-concurrent-executions 0 \
  --region us-east-1

Within about two minutes, the canary detects the failure after two consecutive failed probes at one-minute intervals. Route 53 then marks the primary as unhealthy, and DNS begins resolving to the secondary Region.

The client detects the dropped connection and begins retrying with exponential backoff and jitter.

Figure 3: Client detecting failure and reconnecting with exponential backoff

When DNS propagation completes, the next reconnection attempt reaches the secondary Region. The client requests the current state, recovers it from DynamoDB Global Tables, and the UI updates to show the new serving Region.

Figure 4: Client after failover to the secondary Region (us-west-2) with state preserved

When the primary Region recovers, the canary confirms that it’s healthy again. After the alarm clears, Route 53 shifts DNS back and clients reconnect to the primary through the same automatic process. No manual intervention is needed for failback.

Clean up

To avoid ongoing charges, delete the resources created during this walkthrough:

  1. Delete the CloudFormation stacks: 
    aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name websocket-health-check --region us-east-1
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name websocket-counter-secondary --region us-west-2
aws cloudformation delete-stack --stack-name websocket-counter-primary --region us-east-1
  2. Delete the Route 53 failover records and API Gateway custom domain names manually from the console.

Conclusion

In this post, you learned how to build a multi-region disaster recovery pattern for API Gateway WebSocket APIs. By separating application state from the connection itself, you can restore sessions automatically after a regional failover. This pattern applies to real-time applications where WebSocket continuity matters. Adapt the health check thresholds, reconnection timing, and state recovery approach to fit your workload.

To learn more about the services used in this solution, refer to the following resources:

  • Amazon API Gateway WebSocket APIs
  • Amazon DynamoDB Global Tables
  • Configure custom health checks for DNS failover
  • Exponential Backoff And Jitter

About the authors

posts.title: How UTS established a modern curriculum data services foundation on AWS
posts.summary: The University of Technology Sydney built a modern curriculum data services foundation on AWS that treats curriculum data as a governed, reusable product, available through APIs, graph traversal, semantic search, and…
posts.content:
Students and staff experience the University of Technology Sydney (UTS) as a single institution, not as the collection of curriculum and student systems behind it. They expect the information underpinning teaching, learning, course design and institutional decision-making to be accurate, timely and coherent, irrespective of its source.

Behind that experience, UTS had reached a natural inflection point in its integration landscape. Critical teaching and learning capabilities relied upon established vendor platforms with disparate data models, interfaces, stability profiles and scaling characteristics. Although those platforms continued to perform essential operational functions, integrating and operating the surrounding estate had become progressively more intricate and costly.

UTS’s purpose remained constant: excellence in teaching, learning and the student experience. Technology exists to advance that purpose, not to supplant it. UTS Information Technology Unit (ITU) therefore sought to remove impediments between authoritative data and the people, processes and digital services that depend upon it.

UTS made that transition practical with AWS. With managed, elastic and serverless capabilities, UTS reduced undifferentiated operational effort and improved fault tolerance. This established a sustainable model for governed data services. Curriculum became the first bounded business domain in which UTS applied that model.

The challenge

UTS ITU required an architecture that could:

  • Make authoritative curriculum information available through reusable services without displacing the Curriculum Management System, a third-party software as a service (SaaS) application, as the system of record.
  • Replace tightly coupled, consumer-specific interfaces with governed contracts that insulate consumers from source schemas and implementation detail.
  • Accommodate routine change and transient high-volume activity, including complete domain reloads, without permanently provisioned capacity.
  • Support graph traversal across deeply nested and inverse curriculum relationships, exact and full-text retrieval, and semantic discovery from the same authoritative source.
  • Operate reliably and economically within finite engineering capacity whilst establishing a repeatable pattern for subsequent data domains.

Domain boundaries were non-negotiable. Curriculum describes what the university teaches and remains the responsibility of the Curriculum Management System. Preserving that bounded context prevents ownership, validation and governance from migrating into non-authoritative services.

A domain-oriented approach

UTS ITU organised the capability according to domain-driven design. Rather than aligning data services with the applications that produce or consume data, they aligned them with:

  • the business domains defined in CAUDIT’s Higher Education Reference Model (HERM).
  • the information for which those domains are accountable.

Each data product has explicit ownership, consumers, quality expectations, interface contracts and lifecycle management. Institutional data is therefore treated as a governed asset designed for reuse, not an incidental application by-product.

Declarative architecture as code provides the executable realisation of the design and a reproducible source of truth. Configuration is separated from implementation where practicable, delivery is automated and managed AWS services are preferred to bespoke infrastructure software. The discipline is “just enough code”: engineering effort focuses on building differentiated domain logic (the business rules and data services unique to higher education) rather than undifferentiated infrastructure.

Stateless execution, asynchronous communication, purpose-built persistence and independently recoverable components avoid a tightly coupled failure domain. Consumption-based services align expenditure with workload demand instead of maintaining an estate permanently sized for intermittent peaks.

Solution overview

The architecture comprises five layers: edge, ingestion, persistence, application and business logic, and interface. Each layer has discrete responsibilities, as shown in Figure 1.

Identity, encryption, network controls, observability and operational governance apply across the stack. Curriculum data services capture complete changes from the Curriculum Management System as events, preserve them in a durable event log, materialise purpose-built representations and expose governed synchronous and asynchronous services.

Figure 1: UTS curriculum data services layered architecture

The next five sections examine each layer of the realised architecture in turn.

Edge layer

The edge layer is the controlled ingress boundary between the SaaS Curriculum Management System and the curriculum domain. Its remit is deliberately narrow: receive a complete curriculum change, establish the internal event contract and submit it to the ingestion layer with minimal processing.

The source system sends change events to an Amazon API Gateway HTTP API, which invokes an AWS Lambda function acting as a technical adapter because no suitable managed connector satisfies the source system’s proprietary API contract and payload format (for example, vendor-specific REST endpoints, authentication schemes, and data structures). The adapter encapsulates the complete vendor event in a CloudEvent envelope, appends UTS operational metadata and publishes it to the appropriate Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) Serverless topic.

The edge neither reinterprets curriculum nor performs validation or consumer-specific transformation. Validation remains within the system of record. This preserves source fidelity, prevents downstream concerns from contaminating the ingress boundary and allows the stateless edge to scale automatically during complete domain reloads.

Ingestion layer

Amazon MSK Serverless forms the durable, append-only event backbone. Curriculum changes are segregated into domain-aligned topics by academic item type, retaining the complete source event whilst allowing independent consumers to progress, retry and recover without obstructing one another.

MSK Serverless scales on demand. Routine changes consume little capacity. A domain reload fans out across the event backbone and parallel processors, then contracts after completion. Model or schema changes can be accommodated through idempotent reprocessing or a complete reload, without introducing a second curriculum authority.

Persistence layer

The persistence layer uses purpose-built data services selected according to the access patterns and business questions each representation must support. Amazon Neptune Serverless stores curriculum structures and inverse relationships as a property graph, whilst Amazon OpenSearch Service stores complete source documents and indices for exact, full-text and vector retrieval.

In Neptune, programmes of learning, areas of learning and units of learning are connected academic items. Consumers can traverse from a programme to its constituent structures or begin with a unit and identify every programme and area through which it is taught. These inverse enquiries are native graph traversals rather than application-specific joins repeatedly reconstructed by consumers.

Figure 2: Curriculum structures relationships in Amazon Neptune

OpenSearch provides exact lookup, filtering and document retrieval alongside k-nearest-neighbour vector search. Selected data processors implemented as AWS Lambda functions invoke an embedding model through Amazon Bedrock and append vector representations of relevant curriculum text before persistence. Curriculum can consequently be discovered by semantic proximity rather than lexical coincidence. UTS also validated multilingual retrieval against English-language curriculum content.

Neptune and OpenSearch are independently and eventually consistent. Failure of one materialisation doesn’t block another, and neither store is exposed directly to consumers. Both are disposable projections rather than competing systems of record and can be reconstructed from the Curriculum Management System through a complete reload. Data is encrypted with a dedicated domain AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) key whose use is restricted to authorised domain services.

Applications layer

The applications layer converts those materialisations into reusable domain capabilities. Dozens of narrowly scoped Lambda-backed services query Neptune or OpenSearch, whilst persistence remains private and is exposed solely through governed contracts.

Amazon EventBridge Pipes acts as a set of transport adapters between MSK Serverless and the Lambda functions acting as processors and services consuming the event stream. Pipes provide routing and delivery, not curriculum validation, enrichment or business transformation, keeping processing responsibilities explicit, independently deployable and observable.

Stateless Lambda function execution allows services to scale with demand and recover independently through retries and re-invocation. Signature Version 4 (SigV4) authentication and fine-grained AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles provide least-privilege access to Amazon Neptune and Amazon OpenSearch Service without distributing or managing database credentials. The services provide authoritative retrieval, graph traversal and semantic discovery without transferring responsibility for curriculum validity into the data domain.

Interface layer

The interface layer provides pull-based access through REST and GraphQL and push-based delivery of domain events, whilst keeping persistence and implementation private. Amazon API Gateway supplies the REST boundary. AWS AppSync provides GraphQL access to frequently consumed capabilities with attribute-based access control at schema level. Both interfaces invoke the same governed service contracts.

Approved consumers might also receive curriculum events in the internal CloudEvent envelope. Amazon EventBridge Pipes manages last-mile delivery without bespoke routing middleware, and consumers determine which academic item events are relevant rather than UTS maintaining a filtered stream for each consumer.

Amazon Cognito authenticates approved external consumers through OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect, whilst AWS native workloads use IAM. AWS Key Management Service, AWS Secrets Manager, AWS WAF, and AWS Certificate Manager provide encryption, secrets management, perimeter protection and certificate lifecycle management. Amazon Route 53 supplies naming for a single shared vanity domain, and Amazon CloudWatch and Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) provide observability, telemetry and targeted alerting across the architecture.

Full solution architecture

The following diagram shows the complete solution architecture, including the identity, encryption, network, observability and governance controls that apply across all five layers.

Figure 3: End-to-end architecture of the curriculum data services solution

Results and measurable outcomes

The outcome isn’t a replacement for the Curriculum Management System as the system of record. It’s a governed data foundation that leaves the system of record authoritative whilst making curriculum information reusable through APIs, graph traversal, semantic search and event delivery. Since the production launch in November 2024, the domain has recorded zero production incidents.

  • Latency – Changes become available to downstream consumers in an average of 1.6 seconds from crossing the edge layer, through synchronous and asynchronous interfaces.
  • Curriculum graph – The domain models 43,794 relationships across approximately 800 programs of learning, 3,500 units of learning and 2,500 areas of learning.
  • Consumer adoption – 11 institutional consumers have adopted the services, replacing bespoke point-to-point integrations with reusable, governed contracts.
  • Operational footprint – One engineer operates the domain. Managed, serverless and self-healing components make routine intervention negligible and remove the need for dedicated Level 3 support.
  • Cost efficiency – UTS achieved a material reduction in the total cost of ownership of curriculum data integration and delivery, consolidating capabilities previously spread across commercial products, bespoke integrations, databases and multiple support teams.
  • Availability and resilience – The platform operates continuously and has maintained downstream access to trusted curriculum information when the upstream system of record was unavailable.

Collectively, these outcomes show how a small engineering contingent can operate an institutional-scale data domain using managed AWS services, whilst increasing capability, reducing operational complexity and aligning expenditure with demand.

What’s next

The curriculum domain validated the production architecture and operating model. The student data domain followed, providing a single governed point of access for student profiles, admissions, offers, enrolments and related information. UTS is now preparing the learning activities domain, a substantially larger capability built around a lifelong learner graph using Amazon Neptune and Amazon Neptune Analytics, extending the same domain-driven pattern across the teaching and learning landscape.

Each bounded context can select the AWS services appropriate to its business questions whilst retaining common controls for identity, security, observability, delivery and operational sustainability.

Conclusion

UTS’s integration landscape had reached the point at which cumulative complexity and operational overhead constrained institutional change. The response was not technology for its own sake. UTS ITU used AWS to remove the impediments between authoritative institutional data and the teaching, learning and administrative capabilities that depend upon it.

The significance of AWS extended beyond technology selection, but the outcome was principally an architectural and operating-model achievement by UTS. Curriculum data services became UTS’s first production data domain. UTS combined domain-driven design, asynchronous processing, purpose-built persistence and governed interfaces with managed AWS capabilities that made those patterns practicable at institutional scale.

The resulting service foundation supports event streaming, graph traversal, document and semantic retrieval, compute, identity, security and governed data exposure. UTS operates it without a conventional infrastructure estate. This allowed UTS ITU to convert an ambitious architectural design into a sustainable production capability whilst keeping engineering effort concentrated on domain services rather than undifferentiated infrastructure.

Curriculum data services embody the resulting transition: from a burdensome integration model to a domain-aligned data foundation that’s reusable, resilient and operationally sustainable. UTS now possesses a repeatable model through which institutional data can be treated as a strategic asset rather than a by-product of individual systems. The university will continue to operate many systems. Students and staff should never experience the boundaries between them.

For more information or support, contact the AWS Public Sector team.

About the authors

posts.title: Scope workloads and share resilience policies with AWS Resilience Hub
posts.summary: The next generation of AWS Resilience Hub adds three capabilities to keep workload scope and resilience requirements aligned with your running environment: Amazon EKS label support for service input sources, generative…
posts.content:
A resilience plan is useful only while it reflects the application you run. After a migration or deployment, a service can acquire a new dependency while its documented recovery objectives stay the same. In a shared Kubernetes cluster, even deciding which resources belong to that service can take investigation.

On September 18, 2026, the Next generation of AWS Resilience Hub introduced three capabilities to help you keep workload scope and resilience requirements aligned with your running environment:

  • Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) label support for service input sources selects Kubernetes resources using the labels that already describe your workloads.
  • Generative AI-powered Dependency Insights analyzes a service’s discovered dependencies and highlights the patterns worth reviewing.
  • Resilience policy sharing through AWS Organizations lets a central team define resilience requirements once and make them available to member accounts.

In this post, you follow a team reviewing the resilience of a sample workload named checkout on Amazon EKS, representing an online store’s checkout service. The team starts by defining which Kubernetes resources belong to checkout, using labels to distinguish it from inventory in the same namespace. This establishes the resource boundary for the resilience review.

With that boundary defined, the team examines discovered dependencies and uses Dependency Insights to prioritize findings for investigation. A cross-Region dependency becomes a concrete question about whether checkout’s recovery design accounts for the services it requires to operate. The service owner then works with a central resilience team to validate the recovery requirements and apply a shared policy. Maintaining those requirements centrally gives teams a common definition to adopt across accounts, while policy events help the central team track adoption.

You perform these steps using the console or the AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI). The workload generates synthetic traffic to demonstrate dependency discovery.

About the application model: In the Next generation of Resilience Hub, the primary unit of assessment is a service. Services can be grouped into systems, and user journeys describe paths through them. See the key changes and the overview of the new hierarchy in the Next generation of Resilience Hub.

Prerequisites

To follow the examples, you need:

  • Access to the Next generation of AWS Resilience Hub in a supported AWS Region.
  • An Amazon EKS cluster with sample, labeled workloads and permission to configure access to the cluster.
  • If you follow the CLI examples, install or update the AWS CLI using the installation and update instructions. Your installation must support the resiliencehubv2 commands. These examples use Bash.
  • An AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that Resilience Hub can assume, with the AWSResilienceHubV2AssessmentExecutionPolicy managed policy attached. The console can create this role when you create a service.
  • Kubernetes RBAC permissions and an EKS access entry that grant this role access to Kubernetes resources. The permissions guide provides the manifest and commands.
  • For policy sharing, an organization with all features enabled and access to its management account.

The examples use two accounts: a workload account containing the EKS cluster and Resilience Hub service, and a management account that owns the shared policy.

For the CLI examples, configure profiles named workload and management for the respective accounts. Replace the example cluster ARN and other placeholders with your own values, and set the Region:

export AWS_REGION=us-east-1

Each command uses --profile to select the account. Follow either the console steps or their CLI equivalents for each operation.

Amazon EKS label support for service input sources

A service input source tells Resilience Hub where to discover a service’s resources. Input sources can be AWS CloudFormation stacks, Terraform state files, resource tags, or Amazon EKS clusters. For an EKS input source, you select the namespaces to include. With this launch, you can also use Kubernetes label selectors to filter resources within those namespaces.

A namespace can contain workloads owned by different teams. With labels, you can select checkout’s resources without including inventory or reorganizing the namespace for an assessment. You use the same labels your teams already maintain.

How it works

Specify the cluster and one or more namespaces, then add label selectors to filter resources within each namespace. A selector contains a key, an operator, and values. Selectors within a namespace use AND logic: an object must match all of them. Without a selector, Resilience Hub discovers every supported object in the selected namespaces.

Checkout and inventory share the production namespace. Their resources carry app=checkout and app=inventory, respectively. Selecting production with app In checkout includes checkout’s Deployment and ReplicaSet and excludes inventory.

Figure 1: Selecting checkout resources with a Kubernetes label

The resource list also includes supporting AWS infrastructure, such as the cluster, node group, virtual private cloud (VPC), and subnets. Labels select Kubernetes objects. They don’t make that shared infrastructure exclusive to checkout.

How to use it

In the Resilience Hub console:

  1. Choose Create service and enter a name. Under Permission, choose Create default role to create an IAM role with the required AWS permissions, or choose Use another role to select an existing role.
  2. Under Service resource discovery, choose Amazon EKS cluster and enter the cluster ARN.
  3. Choose Configure namespaces, enter production, and add a label selector with key app, operator In, and value checkout.
  4. Choose Save, select Enable dependency discovery for this service, then choose Create service. Resource discovery starts automatically.

Figure 2: Scoping the checkout service to one namespace and one label

If you prefer to use the AWS CLI instead of the console, run the following commands to create the service and add its EKS input source.

Skip this block if you already created the service using the preceding console steps.

The console displays selector operators as In, NotIn, Exists, and NotExists. In the API, use IN, NOT_IN, EXISTS, and DOES_NOT_EXIST, respectively.

In the following command, replace ResilienceHubRole with your service’s IAM role name.

# Create the checkout service with dependency discovery enabled and save its ARN
SERVICE_ARN=$(aws resiliencehubv2 create-service \
  --profile workload \
  --name checkout \
  --regions "$AWS_REGION" \
  --permission-model '{"invokerRoleName": "ResilienceHubRole"}' \
  --dependency-discovery ENABLED \
  --query 'service.serviceArn' --output text)
# Add the EKS input source, selecting resources labeled app=checkout in production
aws resiliencehubv2 create-input-source \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN" \
  --resource-configuration '{
    "eks": {
      "clusterArn": "arn:aws:eks:us-east-1:111122223333:cluster/resilience-demo",
      "namespaces": ["production"],
      "labelSelector": {
        "matchExpressions": [
          {"key": "app", "operator": "IN", "values": ["checkout"]}
        ]
      }
    }
  }'

After resource discovery completes, you can use the following command to list the discovered resource types. If you created the service on the console, first set SERVICE_ARN to that service’s ARN.

# List discovered resource types after resource discovery completes
aws resiliencehubv2 list-resources \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN" \
  --query 'serviceResources[].resource.resourceType'

Generative AI-powered Dependency Insights

Dependency Insights uses generative AI to summarize discovered dependencies and highlight patterns that warrant resilience review. It provides an overview and categorized findings.

The Resources list describes the service’s components. The Dependencies list shows endpoints discovered through DNS activity, including AWS service endpoints in other Regions and external APIs. When that list grows to hundreds of entries, Dependency Insights helps you prioritize what to investigate.

How it works

Dependency Insights builds on dependency discovery, an optional, separately priced feature. Dependency discovery analyzes DNS activity through Amazon Route 53 Resolver and does not require installing an agent in your workload. It examines up to 35 days of available history and continues monitoring for changes. The dependency list shows each endpoint’s name, location, and when it was first and last seen.

Dependency Insights analyzes this list, filters out common service activity that typically does not indicate resilience risk, and highlights patterns such as these:

PatternWhat to investigateCross-Region dependenciesWhether a call to another Region is intentional, and how it affects recoveryNew dependenciesWhether an endpoint first observed within the last seven days changes the documented architectureThird-party dependenciesHow the service behaves when an external provider is unavailableUneven usageWhether activity reflects a scheduled job or a dependency used only at certain times

Figure 3: Turning dependency data into a focused review

Insights prioritize review. They don’t prescribe fixes or list every dependency. Use the full dependency list when you need detail. A new workload’s insights reflect only the history it has generated.

How to use it

In the Resilience Hub console, wait for initial dependency discovery to complete before generating insights:

  1. Open the service. On the Assessment tab, scroll to the Dependencies section to review discovered dependencies.
  2. Choose Generate insights.
  3. Read the overview and compare each finding with the intended architecture.

You can regenerate insights once every 24 hours. This limit applies whether you generate them through the console or the AWS CLI.

Figure 4: Dependency Insights for the checkout service

If you prefer the AWS CLI, use the following commands instead of the console steps. Set SERVICE_ARN to your service’s ARN.

Enable dependency discovery only if it is not already enabled. After initial discovery completes, review the dependency list and generate insights. If you already generated insights on the console, skip start-dependency-insights and use get-dependency-insights to retrieve the existing result.

Generation can complete asynchronously. Run get-dependency-insights again if the returned status is IN_PROGRESS.

# Enable dependency discovery if it is not already enabled
aws resiliencehubv2 update-service \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN" \
  --dependency-discovery ENABLED
# Review the dependency list
aws resiliencehubv2 list-dependencies \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN" \
  --query 'dependencySummaries[].[dependencyName, location, dependencyId]' \
  --output table
# Start generating dependency insights
aws resiliencehubv2 start-dependency-insights \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN"
# Retrieve insights; if status is IN_PROGRESS, run this command again later
aws resiliencehubv2 get-dependency-insights \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN"

The checkout service produced five insights across 29 dependencies. The following response shows the generated overview and all five findings:

{
    "overview": "5 insights generated for service 'checkout' across 29 dependencies, surfacing cross-region, third-party, and uneven usage patterns.",
    "insights": [
        {
            "category": "CROSS_REGION",
            "description": "DynamoDB in us-west-2 is reached cross-region with hard criticality, coupling this service's availability to a remote region. This dependency carries medium DNS query volume with consistent usage."
        },
        {
            "category": "CROSS_REGION",
            "description": "PagerDuty (api.pagerduty.com) is reached cross-region to us-west-2, creating an availability dependency on that remote region."
        },
        {
            "category": "THIRD_PARTY",
            "description": "Three third-party dependencies — example.com, example.net, and example.org — are present at medium DNS query volume with consistent usage patterns."
        },
        {
            "category": "THIRD_PARTY",
            "description": "GitHub is a third-party dependency with low DNS query volume."
        },
        {
            "category": "UNEVEN_USAGE",
            "description": "Two in-region dependencies show highly uneven daily usage: an S3 bucket (amzn-s3-demo-bucket) and an ECR registry (602401143452.dkr.ecr.us-east-1.amazonaws.com)."
        }
    ],
    "status": "COMPLETED",
    "createdAt": "2026-10-08T14:24:27.372000-05:00"
}

The first finding identifies a cross-Region Amazon DynamoDB dependency. If checkout requires that dependency to accept orders, a disruption in the remote Region could prevent it from operating even when its Amazon EKS resources remain healthy. The service owner should verify which operations require the table and review how those operations behave when it is unavailable. That review determines whether the dependency fits the recovery design or whether the architecture needs to change. DNS activity alone cannot answer that question.

The uneven-usage finding points to container image infrastructure. Image downloads during pod startup can produce bursts of DNS activity. This is a pattern to investigate, rather than evidence that your application has an outage.

Classify a dependency as hard if the service fails without it, or soft if the service degrades but keeps running. In the sample environment, we had classified the DynamoDB dependency as hard using the following command. The comment describes an illustrative failure assumption, which requires validation through testing:

# Classify the selected dependency as hard and record the reason
aws resiliencehubv2 update-dependency \
  --profile workload \
  --service-arn "$SERVICE_ARN" \
  --dependency-id "<dependency-id>" \
  --criticality HARD \
  --comment "Checkout writes orders to this table and cannot accept orders without it."

Resilience policy sharing through AWS Organizations

After reviewing checkout’s dependencies, the service owner can validate its recovery requirements with the business and the central site reliability engineering (SRE) team. Dependency findings inform that discussion. They don’t automatically determine the policy targets.

The central SRE team can codify the agreed requirements into a resilience policy, defining availability and recovery targets for critical services. The management account or a delegated administrator can share that policy across the organization so service owners can apply the centrally maintained requirements without creating separate copies.

The policy owner can review attachment and detachment events to track adoption. If a service stops using the policy, the SRE team can engage its owner to understand why and determine whether different requirements are appropriate. Application owners remain responsible for meeting the targets.

How it works

A policy can combine four target types: availability, recovery from an Availability Zone disruption, recovery from a Regional disruption, and data recovery. The recovery time objective (RTO) specifies the targeted recovery time. The recovery point objective (RPO) specifies the tolerable period of data loss.

When sharing is on, the policy appears in every member account alongside the account’s own policies, and its ARN shows which account owns it. Each service owner chooses whether to apply it. If a requirement must apply regardless of that choice, associate the policy with a system containing the relevant services instead, as described in Applying resilience policies across accounts.

The owning account can review a timeline of the services that start or stop using the policy. Turning sharing off stops evaluating member services against the policy and removes it from the services that used it, so coordinate changes with the teams involved.

Figure 5: One policy definition, shared with member accounts

How to use it

The organization integration is a one-time setup in the management account:

  1. In the Resilience Hub console, open AWS Organizations settings.
  2. Select Enable trusted access and create a service-linked role, then choose Create integration.

posts.title: Stopping business email compromise with AI-driven email security: How VIPRE protects modern enterprises on AWS
posts.summary: Learn how VIPRE Security built an AI-powered email security solution on AWS to stop business email compromise. VIPRE Integrated Email Security uses machine learning and a serverless architecture on Amazon ECS, Amazon…
posts.content:
If your organization has experienced sophisticated email impersonation attempts that bypass traditional security tools, you need advanced protection against business email compromise (BEC). This post shows you how VIPRE uses AI in its email security solution, deployed on AWS for enterprise customers. The solution identifies and stops these incidents before they reach end users, and it integrates directly with existing Microsoft 365 environments.

In this post, you will discover:

  • How AI-powered detection identifies and blocks BEC attempts.
  • Why cloud-native architecture on AWS provides stronger protection.
  • Steps to implement VIPRE IES without disrupting your email flow.

Email security challenges facing modern enterprises

BEC presents significant security challenges for your organization as you rely on email for critical business communications:

  • Sophisticated impersonation: Unlike traditional phishing that relies on fraudulent links or attachments, BEC incidents use social engineering and convincing impersonations to manipulate human behavior. According to data gathered by VIPRE Security Group, almost half of spam email messages (49 percent) are BEC scams, where criminals pretend to be someone important in a company. They usually target CEOs, HR staff, and IT departments.
  • Legacy protection gaps: Traditional Secure Email Gateways (SEGs) that rely on mail exchange (MX) record redirection are often blind to internal traffic, lateral movement, or thread hijacks. This creates security gaps that sophisticated actors can exploit.
  • Cloud collaboration issues: As you move toward zero trust architectures and cloud-native collaboration, email remains a weak link that can be exploited through various vectors.

VIPRE needed to develop a solution that could protect against these advanced incidents while integrating with modern cloud email environments such as Microsoft 365.

Solution overview

To address the challenges of sophisticated email risks, VIPRE developed Integrated Email Security (IES), a cloud-native solution built entirely on AWS. This solution uses AI-powered detection and native Microsoft 365 integration to protect against advanced BEC incidents.

The solution consists of two primary components:

  • Machine learning (ML) detection engine: VIPRE IES uses multiple ML layers that analyze the entire email structure to identify and stop sophisticated incidents. These layers include semantic similarity models that detect subtle impersonations, contextual language models that detect manipulation tactics, intent and topic analysis, and advanced dynamic behavioral analysis of embedded links and attachments.
  • Cloud-native architecture: Built on AWS services, VIPRE IES processes over half a million messages per day in production and is designed to scale to millions, with low latency and high reliability. The serverless architecture scales rapidly to meet demand fluctuations while maintaining security and performance.

This automated approach provides protection against BEC incidents without requiring MX record changes, making deployment straightforward and non-disruptive. Key features of the solution include:

  • Native integration: VIPRE IES integrates directly with Microsoft 365 through secure APIs, providing rapid, low-friction deployment.
  • Real-time analysis: Messages are analyzed in real time for impersonation attempts, unusual patterns, and deceptive content, with suspicious messages appropriately quarantined or flagged.
  • Detection capabilities: The solution looks beyond traditional indicators to catch subtle signs of manipulation, including urgency triggers, financial requests, and digital signature mismatches.
  • Unified management: A centralized dashboard provides visibility into risks, supports quarantine management, and delivers insights into incident patterns and trends.

VIPRE IES uses specific machine learning models on AWS infrastructure to identify BEC attempts while minimizing administrative overhead.

Architecture and implementation

The following diagram illustrates the solution architecture.

Figure 1: VIPRE IES architecture on AWS

VIPRE IES uses a distributed, event-driven architecture specifically designed to identify and stop business email compromise and AI-generated phishing attempts. The system combines AI and ML technologies in a cost-effective manner to analyze and neutralize email-based risks. The architecture consists of four key layers:

  • Data ingestion layer built on Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS), Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) for decoupled, elastic scaling.
  • AI and ML detection pipeline where semantic analysis and dynamic sandboxing evaluate the message’s true intent using custom BERT models on Amazon ECS with NVIDIA GPUs for high-performance email analysis.
  • Response management and remediation layer built on Amazon Managed Streaming for Apache Kafka (Amazon MSK) and Amazon ECS acts as the immediate enforcement engine based on the risk events generated by the analysis pipeline.
  • Search and analytics layer uses Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), Amazon OpenSearch Service, and Amazon MSK to provide real-time analysis and search capabilities with sub-second latency.

Data ingestion

Processing millions of email messages reliably presents significant challenges, especially with unpredictable traffic spikes. VIPRE’s ingest mechanism uses AWS services to tackle this with a highly resilient system that maintains performance and availability regardless of volume.

  • Every incoming email stream is treated as a discrete job. The raw payload is immediately committed to Amazon S3 as an object. Amazon S3 delivers 99.999999999 percent (11 9s) durability, providing a reliable foundation for email payload storage.
  • The actual processing job (a lightweight reference pointing to the Amazon S3 object) is then queued in Amazon SQS, a fully managed message queuing service. This decoupling supports reliable message handling, buffers traffic spikes, and decouples ingestion from downstream processing.
  • Stateless microservices orchestrated by Amazon ECS with AWS Fargate for serverless container management, pull Amazon SQS jobs, fetch the Amazon S3 payload, and initiate the detection pipeline.

AI and ML detection with layered intelligence

After ingesting email data, the solution performs analysis using a multi-stage workflow where multiple engines are executed in parallel and phases are coordinated using fan-in and fan-out patterns. Based on how engines operate there are roughly four kinds of analysis done:

  1. Static analysis:
    • Engines in this category look at the email as passive data.
    • Definitions, rules, signatures, heuristics and classifiers are updated using hot reload.
  2. Behavioral analysis:
    • Various artifacts extracted from the email body (links, attachments) are opened in a controlled environment (also known as a sandbox) where the execution is monitored and passed through ML classifiers and other engines to identify unexpected behavior.
    • ML classifiers are versioned and shipped along with sandbox Docker images.
    • Heuristics and rule updates are done using Amazon S3 and Amazon S3 events.
  3. Semantic analysis:
    • Email text is passed through a pipeline for text understanding which uses multiple bi-directional transformer models to perform natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as named entity recognition and coreference, intent summarization, zero-shot classification, and semantic similarity matching.
    • The models used are strongly versioned, deployed in Docker images stored in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), using PyTorch and scheduled to execute on NVIDIA GPUs.
    • Heuristics and classified embedding datasets can be updated separately through packages stored in Apache Parquet format in Amazon S3, with Amazon Managed Workflows for Apache Airflow (Amazon MWAA) orchestrating data pipeline workflows.
  4. Apply contextual intelligence:
    • Global (customer independent) and local (customer dependent) data feeds are correlated and injected during analysis for context enrichment and detection.
      • Global: artifacts extracted from the email are checked against the latest emergent risks and IoCs, and verified against reputation and classification feeds.
      • Local: sender reputation, trust lists, roles, and similar signals are injected into the analysis context.
    • Intelligence collected by the system (discovered risks, regardless of the source) is fed back into the security data lake from where it’s available for rapid identification of emerging risks. Amazon CloudWatch provides centralized monitoring and governance across the entire detection pipeline.

Response management and remediation

This layer serves as the platform’s control plane, translating detection verdicts into automated actions based on customizable VIPRE IES Action Rule Definitions. Administrators can define specific match expressions against the aggregated threat model to trigger precise remediation workflows.

In inline mode, the service acts as a final gateway so that high-severity risks, such as confirmed malware or severe BEC, are quarantined and prevented from landing in the end-user’s mailbox. This immediate intervention keeps a risk’s dwell time minimal, neutralizing the concern instantly.

The service provides granular workflows for managing quarantined messages. These include:

  • Administrator release: Admins maintain full visibility, with the ability to review audit logs, engine scores, and raw payloads to safely release false positives.
  • End-user self-release: For lower-risk categories (for example, bulk mail), users receive a secure metadata digest so they can self-release items directly from a portal. This reduces administrative overhead while ensuring all user actions remain fully audited for review.

Post-delivery remediation (clawback)

Beyond inline blocking, the system uses native API integrations with mail providers to execute programmatic clawbacks. This allows the service to instantly retract malicious messages from user inboxes post-delivery, neutralizing “time-bomb” threats and preventing lateral movement.

By balancing immediate inline enforcement with flexible release workflows, the response and remediation service maximizes protection without disrupting legitimate business communication.

Search and analytics

This layer closes the loop, transforming the continuous stream of security telemetry into actionable, real-time intelligence for security operators.

  • Every state change and verdict across the entire system is published as an event to the Amazon MSK cluster. Amazon MSK provides the highly durable, ordered, and scalable event stream necessary to handle massive data velocity.
  • Events are consumed, contextually enriched with metadata (for example, user, group profile), and committed to Amazon Relational Database Service (Amazon RDS), which provides automated backups and high availability, to serve as the long-term, auditable system of record.
  • The system delivers instant search results by using change data capture (CDC) to stream updates from Amazon RDS in real time. This low-latency pipeline populates Amazon OpenSearch Service for sub-second analytical queries across security telemetry.
  • The search and analytics service exposes a powerful API that powers VIPRE’s dashboards and interactive reports. These perform sub-second, complex analytical queries that give security teams real-time visibility into their security posture and risk. Queries and results are strictly scoped by the client’s tenant ID, enforcing multi-tenant isolation and providing data separation assurance while supporting rapid incident response.

Real-world protection: how VIPRE IES stops advanced BEC incidents

VIPRE IES’s AI-powered detection successfully identifies and blocks sophisticated BEC and other evasive incidents that traditional email security would miss. Here’s how it works in real-world scenarios:

  • The “urgent wire transfer” incident: An employee in the accounting or finance department receives an email seemingly from their CEO or CFO. The email has a sense of urgency, stating a critical business deal requires an immediate wire transfer to a new vendor. VIPRE IES’s intent-aware AI classifies the email as a financial request, detects urgency triggers in language patterns, and identifies user impersonation along with other risk indicators to automatically quarantine the message.
  • The “confidential or legal matter” incident: An employee receives an email from what appears to be a senior leader or the legal department, with a subject line such as “Confidential Legal Matter – Attorney-Client Privilege.” The email asks the employee to provide sensitive information. VIPRE IES’s semantic analysis engine flags the use of emotionally charged, high-pressure language to create a false sense of urgency and secrecy.
  • The “thread hijacking” incident: When supply chain partners’ email accounts are compromised and actors insert fraudulent payment instructions into legitimate email threads, VIPRE’s conversation thread scoring and domain analysis immediately identify these sophisticated incidents, protecting against scenarios using fake message threads.
  • The “QR code (quishing)” scenario: A QR code incident (quishing) involves an actor embedding an image of a QR code into an email, often with a sense of urgency such as a “security update” or “password expiration,” to trick the recipient into scanning the code with their mobile device, which then directs them to a phishing site. VIPRE IES addresses this evasion by using multiple layers of advanced analysis including using image analysis to decode the URL and then perform real-time behavioral analysis of the URL in an isolated cloud sandbox.

These use cases demonstrate how VIPRE IES provides protection against the full spectrum of modern BEC incidents by applying multiple AI and ML detection layers to analyze message context, sender behavior, and communication patterns.

Results and impact

When you implement VIPRE IES, the combination of its advanced detection capabilities and its native AWS architecture provides a force-multiplier effect across three critical areas:

1. Neutralizing sophisticated BEC email

By using the elasticity of AWS compute to run deep AI and ML semantic analysis at scale, VIPRE IES successfully blocks sophisticated BEC incidents that bypass traditional security tools. This significantly reduces an organization’s exposure to financial fraud and wire transfer scams by identifying malicious intent in real time.

These capabilities are proven in production. In a sample 24-hour period across VIPRE’s Europe (EU) and North America (NA) production environments, VIPRE IES scanned 517,726 messages (376,847 in EU and 140,879 in NA) and detected 5,508 BEC attempts (3,853 in EU and 1,655 in NA). BEC attempts accounted for approximately 1 percent of all scanned messages. Each of those detections represents a potential fraud attempt identified by the system. This depth of analysis also operates at speed. P95 message-processing latency (hourly average) ranges from 1.4 to 15 seconds with dynamic sandboxing disabled, and from 39 to 78 seconds with full sandbox analysis enabled. This maintains real-time protection without disrupting legitimate mail flow.

2. Operational efficiency and reduced alert fatigue

The precision of the IES detection model, supported by the high-throughput processing of Amazon SQS, Amazon MSK, and Amazon ECS, means that security teams can focus on investigating genuine risks rather than managing false positives. This minimizes alert fatigue and supports a more proactive defense posture.

3. Accelerated time-to-protection

Because the platform is built on a cloud-native, API-driven framework, deployment is remarkably fast. Without the need for MX record changes, the solution can be deployed in minutes rather than days, accelerating protection while maintaining existing email infrastructure. This agility also provides immediate visibility into internal risks that traditional gateways often miss.

Beyond the immediate technical mitigation of BEC and zero-day threats, the platform’s native integration supports stringent enterprise compliance through robust encryption, granular role-based access control (RBAC), and comprehensive audit logging. These security improvements help rebuild trust in email communications across all levels of your organization, from end users to executive leadership.

Conclusion

Modern email threats outpace conventional security tools, creating dangerous blind spots in your defenses. Built on AWS services and using advanced AI and ML capabilities, VIPRE IES provides a cloud-native solution that protects against sophisticated BEC incidents. By offloading the “heavy lifting” of infrastructure to the global reach and elasticity of the AWS Cloud, VIPRE IES delivers a security fabric that is as resilient as it is precise.

VIPRE Security and AWS worked together to create a targeted solution that addresses specific email security challenges with precision and scalability. By removing the need for MX record changes and integrating directly with Microsoft 365, VIPRE IES offers a deployment path that accelerates time-to-value.

To get started with improving your email security:

  1. Review your current email security posture to identify gaps in BEC protection.
  2. Explore VIPRE IES in the AWS Marketplace to understand deployment options.
  3. Connect with AWS and VIPRE teams to discuss your specific security requirements.

Learn more about AWS security best practices and cloud-native email protection:

  • AWS Fargate
  • Amazon MSK
  • Amazon RDS
  • Amazon OpenSearch Service
  • Amazon CloudWatch
  • Amazon ECR
  • Amazon MWAA

Learn more
