posts.title: Bulk Executor for Amazon DynamoDB, Part 2: Lessons we learned the hard way
posts.summary: In Part 2 of our Bulk Executor for Amazon DynamoDB series, we share how we built the tool: the design tradeoffs, surprises, and workarounds we hit while working with DynamoDB and AWS Glue. Consider it a travel guide for…
posts.content:
In the Introducing open source Bulk Executor for Amazon DynamoDB blog post, you learned about the purpose and usage of the Bulk Executor tool. In this Part 2 post, we share the story of how we built it: the design tradeoffs, surprises, gotchas, and eventual workarounds. Think of it as your travel guide for working with Amazon DynamoDB and AWS Glue.

Design requirements

Bulk Executor is a project designed to run actions in bulk against many or all items in a table. For example you can mass delete old items or compare two tables for equality.

Three core requirements shaped most of the decisions that follow: running a bulk command should feel like a local script (real-time output, interruptible with ^C), it should scale to hundreds of parallel workers without the user managing infrastructure, and it should be straightforward to add new commands without tight coupling to the framework.

Selecting AWS Glue

We selected AWS Glue to drive the parallel execution. It’s a serverless service where you submit jobs that get distributed across workers (compute instances), each running tasks in parallel. For more information, see Key topics in Apache Spark. Our command-line client starts a job and AWS Glue handles distributing the work across potentially hundreds of workers.

We also considered Amazon Simple Queue Service (Amazon SQS) with AWS Lambda, AWS Fargate, Amazon EMR, and Ray. We decided to use AWS Glue because it gave us both serverless parallelism and a built-in DynamoDB connector, so we got much of the hard stuff at no cost. The following short code sample shows how to read or write items:

# Read from DynamoDB into a Spark DataFrame
dataframe = (
    spark.read
    .format("dynamodb")
    .option("dynamodb.input.tableName", "source")
    .option("dynamodb.throughput.read", "40000")
    .option("dynamodb.consistentRead", "false")
    .load()
)
# Write to DynamoDB from a Spark DataFrame
(
    dataframe.write
    .format("dynamodb")
    .option("dynamodb.output.tableName", "sink")
    .option("dynamodb.throughput.write", "40000")
    .option("dynamodb.item.size.check.enabled", "true")
    .save()
)

The Spark DataFrame gave us the built-in capabilities that we needed. Specifically:

  • A where/filter that accepts a Spark SQL condition to filter the data.
  • An orderBy that sorts the data.
  • A limit that controls the number of items.

On the back of these capabilities, we built the find command as our first command with its --where, --orderby, and --limit parameters requiring almost no coding on our part. If you want to print the 100 most recent undelivered orders, you can issue a bulk command like this:

./bulk find --table orders --where "status = 'undelivered'" --orderby timestamp desc --limit 100

The count command uses the same code but counts the items instead of printing them. The delete command does the same, but after finding the items runs parallel batch delete calls to remove them.

One downside of the Spark connector is that it doesn’t fully represent the source table data types. It simplifies the data and, for example, makes no distinction between a string set and a list of strings.

Estimating costs

When working against large tables, we wanted to give a cost estimate before starting the work. Predicting the future is always hard. Here’s how we did it.

For reads, we look at the table’s metadata (updated approximately every 6 hours, so beware a table that you recently loaded can read as smaller than it really is) to learn its recent size and calculate the read request units necessary for a full scan. For on-demand tables the math is straightforward: call the Pricing API to get the cost per million read request units for the region, multiply, done.

For provisioned mode, cost depends on the provisioned level, auto scaling headroom, and job duration, making estimation harder. Our heuristic is to take two-thirds of the on-demand price (divide by 1.5). The reasoning: a table provisioned at 100 percent utilization costs about 30 percent of the equivalent on-demand throughput. However, 100 percent is rarely achievable in practice. At 50 percent utilization, the cost is about 60 percent. We use 67 percent because it’s better to quote a little high.

For the delete command, write costs depend on how many items match, which we don’t know until after scanning. So delete calculates pricing in two phases: first the read cost estimate up front, then after finding the matches, the write cost based on the size of the deletion set.

For the fill command, which mass loads synthetic data according to a custom generator, we first generate some sample items to know the approximate size of the items, then price accordingly.

We don’t estimate AWS Glue Data Processing Unit (DPU) costs for two reasons. First, knowing how much compute will be required can’t be done simply. Second, we observed that for large jobs, DPU costs tend to be a small fraction of the DynamoDB costs. This makes sense, because an AWS Glue worker running at a small hourly cost can drive a huge amount of database activity. For small jobs, DPU is a larger fraction because of the overhead of getting things started, but the absolute dollars are low. You can specify --XWaitForDPU to see actual DPU costs reported after execution.

Every --X parameter is a parameter to the Bulk Executor itself, as opposed to the command being run. We modeled this after the Java Virtual Machine convention.

Job termination (^C)

We needed a way for the caller to terminate processing, for example if the pricing estimate comes back higher than expected. Pressing ^C stops the client Python script immediately but leaves the AWS Glue job running until its timeout.

We solved this by having the Python code catch the interrupt signal programmatically. An interrupt handler sees the ^C and sets an interrupted flag. This flag gets noticed by a watcher loop that’s always running. Usually it’s watching for things like AWS Glue state changes. But when it sees the interrupt, it actively directs the AWS Glue job to stop before proceeding with a clean exit of the client-side program. Now one ^C cleanly stops both sides.

Mandating point-in-time recovery (PITR)

A command like delete has the potential to delete more than anticipated. We made the design choice to require point-in-time recovery (PITR) to be enabled on any table receiving a mutating command. That way if your --where clause doesn’t do exactly what you wanted, you have a way to roll back.

This is one reason we built out the revert-export command to undo writes in place based on a PITR-driven incremental export. See our previous blog post “Recover from accidental DynamoDB changes using Bulk Executor”.

Watching execution (CloudWatch Live Tail)

In our first version, the client polled Amazon CloudWatch Logs for AWS Glue worker output. This was inefficient and meant output appeared delayed and in chunks. Switching to Amazon CloudWatch Live Tail let job output stream to the client in near real-time.

This introduced a problem: when find returned only a small number of matches things worked fine, but with large result sets we got incomplete output. The root cause: Live Tail displays at most 500 events per second. Beyond that, it streams only a sample of matching events.

Our solution was to write large output (from find or diff) to an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and only stream the first 10 results to the terminal, plus a link to the full data set.

Live Tail had two more surprises. Events can arrive out of order, so we built a reordering layer. Also, AWS Glue jobs can complete before their final log events appear in CloudWatch (there are a few seconds of propagation delay), so we couldn’t stop listening the moment the job stopped. We implemented a “microwave popcorn monitor”: stop listening only after a few seconds of silence.

Fast and useful error handling

When an AWS Glue task hits an error, it logs an exception and by default the stack trace goes into the logs for the client to see. If the error is in only one task, that’s manageable, if a bit verbose. But if it’s something that hits every task (like a bad --where clause), you get hundreds of identical stack traces flooding the terminal. We addressed this with four patterns.

On the client side, each command validates parameters before starting the AWS Glue job. A typo gets caught locally without AWS Glue ever spinning up.

Inside AWS Glue, we create an error_accumulator that’s a Spark accumulator. Instead of letting exceptions propagate up from tasks en masse, each task adds its exception to the accumulator. The Spark driver then extracts the first error and prints only that: one clean message instead of hundreds of duplicates, followed by a graceful job shutdown.

Continuously, on the client side, the Live Tail stream of events goes through a pattern matcher looking for error patterns that will never self-resolve (like AccessDeniedException, ModuleNotFoundError, OutOfMemoryError) and can trigger an immediate job stop rather than letting every task fail with the same error.

Also, to prevent “scary” stack traces for something as simple as a typo in a --where clause, we use a special app-specific exception type that a command can choose to throw when wanting to give an error and not a stack trace. Only developer-type errors should generate stack traces.

It took a while but we developed an approach to error handling that we liked: catch errors as quickly as possible, simplify them down to show the user only what’s necessary, and have the final line of each execution indicate if the job succeeded or failed (and why). We also added color coding (red for errors, yellow for warnings) to make issues easier to spot.

DynamoDB connector compared to direct access

The AWS Glue connector reads and writes DataFrames, but it has no way to delete items. For the delete command we had no choice but to make direct DynamoDB API calls. The command logic uses the connector to first find the matching items (giving a DataFrame), then iterates over the items to perform deletes using batch writes. Here’s a simplified version:

def delete_partition(partition, table_name, keys):
    table = dynamodb_resource.Table(table_name)
    with table.batch_writer() as batch:
        for record in partition:
            item = json.loads(record)
            key = {k: item[k] for k in keys}
            batch.delete_item(Key=key)
# Distribute deletes across workers
records.toJSON().foreachPartition(
    lambda partition: delete_partition(partition, table_name, keys)
)

Each Spark partition gets a slice of the matching items, and foreachPartition() runs the delete function in parallel across workers. The batch_writer() handles batching the individual deletes into efficient batch_write_item calls under the hood.

We built fill and load-export to write items directly by using batch_writer also, instead of constructing a DataFrame.

This pattern of going direct worked so well that it inspired us to rethink how we approached the first commands we wrote. We built a scancount command to explore whether counting could be faster without the connector.

The answer: consistently faster, because of less overhead. The connector-based count has to load every item into the AWS Glue context to then filter them and count what survived the filter. With scancount, we use DynamoDB segmented scan with push-down predicates and Select: COUNT so nothing comes out of the database except the count itself with the filter already having been applied. Each worker scans its own segment of the table in parallel:

def _count(table_name, index_name, filter_expression,
             segment, total_segments, total_matched_accumulator, error_accumulator):
    table = dynamodb_resource.Table(table_name)
    scan_kwargs = {
        "Select": "COUNT",
        "Segment": segment,
        "TotalSegments": total_segments
    }
    if index_name:
        scan_kwargs["IndexName"] = index_name
    if filter_expression:
        scan_kwargs["FilterExpression"] = filter_expression
    # Error handling code removed
    local_count = 0
    while True:
        response = table.scan(**scan_kwargs)
        local_count += response.get("Count", 0)
        if "LastEvaluatedKey" not in response:
            break
        scan_kwargs["ExclusiveStartKey"] = response["LastEvaluatedKey"]
    total_matched_accumulator.add(local_count)
    return local_count
parallelize_count = 100
rdd = spark_context.parallelize(range(parallelize_count), parallelize_count)
rdd.foreach(lambda worker_id: _count(table_name, index_name,
    filter_expression, worker_id, parallelize_count,
    total_matched_accumulator, error_accumulator))

The tradeoff: scancount accepts a raw --filter-expression instead of the higher-level --where Spark SQL syntax, since there’s no DataFrame involved.

The code for diff and copy also does direct reads instead of using the connector. With these commands, it wasn’t for speed but to make sure they keep perfect data type fidelity.

A side note on diff: it was important for each task to write its subset of output directly to its own Amazon S3 object, without ever centralizing the output back to the driver, which would not scale.

Rate limiting

The connector provides built-in rate limiting. However, for our commands making direct API calls (such as delete, fill, copy, and scancount), there’s no rate limiting. With enough AWS Glue workers running loops unconstrained, it usually generates unwanted throttles.

We built a distributed rate limiter that coordinates across all workers. The approach is described in detail in Rate-limiting calls to Amazon DynamoDB using Python Boto3, Part 1 and Part 2: Distributed Coordination.

Users control this with --XMaxReadRate and --XMaxWriteRate parameters. If unspecified, we investigate the environment to infer the appropriate rates based on account and table settings and quotas.

Recently, we added a feature to issue a (yellow) warning if the max read or write rate won’t allow the work to complete within the --XTimeout (which defaults to one hour). Better to warn the user early: if even the maximum rate can’t finish within the timeout, the user can restart with a higher rate or a longer timeout.

Building a library of commands

We started with the idea that commands should be straightforward to drop in, like new Unix commands. The loose coupling has paid off in contributions from outside the original core team. So far we’ve seen:

  • The diff command contributed by Chris Gillespie.
  • The sql command contributed by John Terhune.
  • The load command contributed by Arjan Schaaf.
  • The load-export and revert-export commands contributed by Ruskin Dantra.

Each command is its own Python module loaded by name. The contract is lightweight: export a run(job, spark_context, glue_context, parsed_args) function and use the shared conventions (the error_accumulator for exceptions, the distributed rate limiter for DynamoDB calls, and a shared library to help with cost estimates).

Upgrading to new AWS Glue versions, with the help of AI

A few months ago, we migrated from AWS Glue 4 to AWS Glue 5. The benefits: faster job startup and a new DynamoDB connector that loads directly into a DataFrame (the old connector required a DynamicFrame intermediate step, adding overhead and complexity).

The migration also gave us a chance to measure the new connector against the old one. We used AI tooling to generate a suite of stress tests comparing both connectors under AWS Glue 5, varying table sizes and read/write patterns. The AI ran these tests for hours, collected the results, and produced a comparison report that gave us the confidence the upgrade was worthwhile.

This migration had been on our backlog for a while and we kept postponing it. With AI handling the test generation and execution, we finished it in one interactive working session.

Since then we’ve upgraded to AWS Glue 6, this time to capture the 30 percent lower costs for DPU-hours.

Implementing an AI linter

We noticed some things are hard to test using either unit tests or end-to-end tests. For example, we have some data that exists in three places in three different formats, and we want to make sure those three definitions do not drift apart.

First, we have a README that explains some aspects of security. You can either let us generate a new AWS Glue job role for you, or you can pass in your own custom role by name. It explains, in English prose, the minimum AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) permissions required by the AWS Glue job role if you create your own. That’s one definition.

The second definition is that when we create the role, we attach the right set of permissions on the role. The third definition is that when you provide the role we check the role’s effective permissions (partly through the IAM policy simulator and partly by reading its attached policies) to confirm that you’ve given the role the proper minimum. This follows the principle that we should error out early here if not, instead of on first execution.

It would be a bad and subtle bug if, as the permissions requirements change, any of the three differently-formatted statements of the same core facts diverge. It’s not easy to compare English prose with role-creating logic with IAM-checking logic.

Our solution was to create an AI linter. It’s a folder in the project

posts.title: The “alien” economics of AI monetization
posts.summary: As usage, costs, and customer expectations change, AI companies are moving beyond traditional SaaS pricing. Leaders at Monetize 2026 shared how they’re combining subscriptions with usage-based billing, building spend…
posts.content:
Two-thirds of the companies on the Forbes AI 50 list now use some form of usage-based pricing, reflecting AI’s variable costs and unpredictable demand. At the second annual Monetize conference last month, Metronome CEO and Cofounder Scott Woody put it more bluntly: today’s leading companies operate in ways that would seem “alien” to traditional SaaS businesses. These companies are iterating much faster on pricing, prioritizing market share over ARR, and pursuing multiple go-to-market strategies at once.

More than 300 leaders from fast-moving companies like Replit, Fin, Snowflake, and Clay came together at Monetize to trade notes on pricing, cost management, and scaling AI products as customer expectations change. Across sessions, five approaches for how companies are now approaching the economics of AI monetization came up repeatedly.

Hybrid pricing: Packaging usage with subscriptions and credits 

A year ago, it was common to expect usage-based pricing to displace subscriptions. Businesses are still using them, just in a new way. We’re seeing more companies using subscriptions to package up variable usage, often through credits.

Aisling O’Reilly, Fin’s director of product for monetization, described the evolution of her own company’s pricing models. The company evolved from a platform subscription to a hybrid model, introducing outcome-based pricing when it launched Fin AI Agent. Initially, customers paid for each support conversation resolved by the agent. As the product expanded into actions like recommending products, qualifying leads, and booking meetings, its original (and only) billable metric became an insufficient representation of customer value. Fin introduced additional billable outcomes, letting customers choose the outcome they wanted from each conversation type and pay based on its value. Customers can commit to a pool of credits, then draw down against that pool across outcomes without having to forecast each one separately.

What’s emerging for Fin and many other companies is a layered model, with subscriptions for actions and predictability, usage-based pricing for agentic work, and credits to simplify multiple usage or outcome units.

Predictability is becoming a product feature

One of the biggest challenges with usage-based billing is giving customers more predictable costs. They need to understand what drives usage, anticipate spend, set spend limits, and connect usage to value. Many companies have addressed those requirements through in-product dashboards, predictions, and other types of tooling.

Snowflake Senior Director Ryan Campbell explained how he and his team help customers monitor and control their consumption through in-product tooling like forecasting, calculators, scenario builders, and usage visibility. Similarly, Stripe’s Head of Global Pricing and Commercialization, Sam Lee, described the usage control pane, where users can see alerts, set and adjust spending controls, and manage consumption, as a new standard.

Commercial terms can also offer more predictability while keeping charges tied to usage. Annual usage buckets, discounted overages, and first-year fixed contracts with follow-on true-ups all offer customers clearer controls to manage variable bills.

As bills become more unpredictable, strong usage controls become part of what customers are paying for. Those controls help build trust in both the company and the product.

Falling AI costs and rising usage call for flexible packaging 

With advances in AI, companies are able to package the same product in different ways. Subscriptions can house lower-cost and rate-limited experiences, while usage-based billing can be used for more resource-intensive agent work. Replit uses both as model costs and agent workloads shift, said Michele Catasta, the company’s president and head of AI.

When Replit’s agents used to run for just a few minutes, the company charged 25¢ per agent checkpoint. But as runtimes grew, some jobs cost Replit several dollars while users still paid just 25¢. The company adopted usage-based billing to close the gap, aligning prices more closely with the amount of work performed by its agents. 

This move solved one problem and introduced another: unpredictable spending and abrupt paywalls for users accustomed to a straightforward monthly subscription. As inference costs fell—due in part to increasingly capable open-source models and the pressure they put on frontier-model prices—Replit introduced a rate-limited Free Mode. This gives users the ability to keep building on a simple subscription. The company changes elements of its pricing several times a month, passing savings on to customers.

This opens up more flexible packaging beyond the one-product, one-pricing-model approach. Companies can combine subscriptions and usage-based billing, then adjust the mix as the underlying economics shift. That lets them offer versions of the same product at different speeds, prices, and service levels. 

Finance’s new mandate: Proving AI value

While tokens might determine a company’s costs, it’s rare that they represent the value customers think they’re buying. In a session on how finance teams can measure AI’s value, Karan Parekh, Clay’s head of finance, said the company doesn’t want to be in the business of “upcharging and taxing tokens.” When pricing, Clay treats model tokens and third-party data as pass-through inputs, separate from the differentiated value its product provides.

Clay applies the same approach to evaluate its own internal AI investments. The sales team tracks productivity, the product team focuses on development time, and support teams measure throughput and customer satisfaction. Parekh’s team is comfortable with its own AI spending growing faster than revenue only if it’s producing something distinctive Clay couldn’t otherwise achieve. 

Attribution is difficult when multiple tools and workflow changes contribute to the same result, making token-level ROI calculations misleading. Clay’s solution is to measure AI tooling against those function-specific targets, reviewing them quarterly to track whether those AI investments prove out. For finance teams, operational outcomes are a more useful lens than focusing on input costs.

Pricing information needs to be readable by both machines and humans

Agents are already influencing how products are discovered and evaluated, even if autonomous enterprise purchasing has yet to fully emerge.

To understand how buyers might encounter pricing in AI-generated answers, Kyle Poyar, founder of Growth Unhinged, tested how six AI engines presented pricing information for companies on the Cloud 100. He analyzed 7,600 AI-generated responses. For one unnamed company, negative pricing language appeared in 88% of responses. Without accessible pricing for this organization, LLMs resorted to scouring informal sources like Reddit and reported back prices ranging from $100–$2,400 per user, per month, a 24x difference. 

Pricing information might be fully visible to humans who visit your site, but if it’s blocked from crawlers or rendered in a way agents can’t reliably interpret, it’s basically invisible. While autonomous enterprise procurement is still early, pricing now has two different audiences to serve. The person accountable for the purchase is still in the picture, but they’ve made room for the machine helping them evaluate the purchase. 

AI monetization is becoming an adaptive system

AI products, model economics, and usage patterns are changing far too quickly for pricing to stay static. Across sessions, leaders described identifying what customers value, giving them more control over spending, and adjusting pricing and packaging as products and business economics change. 

Watch the recorded sessions from Monetize 2026 for the full conversations with leaders from Replit, Fin, Snowflake, Clay, Growth Unhinged, and Stripe.

posts.title: Agentic antimicrobial resistance surveillance with AWS HealthOmics and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
posts.summary: This post presents a reference architecture that turns public sequencing data into plain-language answers about antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes. It pairs AWS HealthOmics for managed genomics processing with a…
posts.content:
Turn public sequencing data into plain-language answers about resistance genes, without writing bioinformatics code or SQL.

Bacterial antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is one of the top public health threats of our time. A systematic analysis published in The Lancet estimated that AMR was directly responsible for 1.27 million deaths in 2019 and associated with 4.95 million (Murray et al., 2022). Surveillance programs work to slow that trend by tracking which resistance genes circulate, in which organisms, and how the picture shifts over time.

The raw material for that work is already public. Sequencing archives such as the NCBI Sequence Read Archive (SRA) hold hundreds of thousands of bacterial whole-genome sequencing runs, and the data is mirrored on the Registry of Open Data on AWS. The constraint isn’t access to data. It’s the work of turning a raw sequencing run into an answer. That path normally means assembling a genome, screening it for resistance genes with specialized tools, loading the results into an analytical store, and writing SQL to explore them. Each step assumes bioinformatics skills, so the people who ask the epidemiological questions often depend on a specialist to answer them.

In this post, we present a reference architecture that shortens that path. A researcher signs in to a web application, submits a public SRA accession, and after the pipeline finishes asks, in plain language, “What AMR genes were found in Salmonella?” The system answers with the genes detected, the tool that found each one, and a confidence value taken from the data. The architecture is defined entirely in AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) and deploys into an account with a single command. This is a demonstration architecture rather than a clinical system, and the accompanying code is available for you to deploy and adapt.

How this architecture differs from variant interpretation

An earlier AWS post, Accelerating genomics variant interpretation with AWS HealthOmics and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, established a pattern that this solution shares: a genomics pipeline feeds Amazon S3 Tables, a capability of Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), in Apache Iceberg format, Amazon Athena queries the tables, and a Strands agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore turns questions into SQL. We reuse that querying pattern rather than reinvent it. What’s different here is the genomics problem and the shape of the pipeline around it.

The variant interpretation solution starts from a Variant Call Format (VCF) file, where variants have already been called, and annotates them. This solution starts a step earlier, from raw sequencing reads, and performs read quality control, de novo assembly, and gene detection before results exist to store. It adds an ingestion stage that pulls reads directly from a public archive and deduplicates work across runs, and it merges detection output into Iceberg idempotently so that reprocessing an isolate updates its rows in place. Those differences, public-data ingestion, assembly-based detection, and idempotent storage, are where the engineering effort of this architecture sits.

Solution overview

The solution is a set of loosely coupled stages, and data moves in one direction from ingestion through processing and storage to a conversational query layer. The following stages map to the numbered zones in Figure 2.

Figure 2: Solution architecture, organized as the five stages the data passes through

  1. Ingestion: An Amazon EventBridge Scheduler rule or an on-demand REST call starts an AWS Step Functions workflow. An Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS) task on AWS Fargate fetches and converts the sequencing run for the requested accession from the NCBI SRA mirror on the Registry of Open Data, and Amazon DynamoDB records processed isolates so that repeat runs skip work that’s already done.
  2. Genomics processing: AWS HealthOmics runs a single managed Nextflow workflow that chains read quality control with fastp, de novo assembly with SKESA, and resistance gene detection with AMRFinderPlus. Container images come from Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR), and the AMRFinderPlus reference database is built into the image because HealthOmics tasks run without internet access.
  3. Harmonization and storage: An AWS Lambda function normalizes the detection output into the community hAMRonization schema (a standard from PHA4GE for reporting AMR detection results), and an AWS Glue job merges it into Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables. The merge is idempotent, so rerunning an isolate updates rows rather than duplicating them.
  4. Analytical store: Amazon Athena queries the Iceberg tables through the AWS Glue Data Catalog, which gives the agent a fast SQL surface over the harmonized results.
  5. Conversational agent and web application: A Strands agent hosted on AgentCore runtime answers questions through a set of Athena-backed tools, with Amazon Bedrock Guardrails keeping responses grounded. A React single-page application on Amazon S3 and Amazon CloudFront, protected by AWS WAF and authenticated with Amazon Cognito, is the front door. Amazon API Gateway serves REST calls and streams the chat over WebSocket.

Ingesting public sequencing data

Ingestion has one job: given an accession, get the reads into the account without manual downloads or credentials. Because the SRA mirror is part of the Registry of Open Data, an anonymous Amazon S3 read is enough. A Step Functions workflow drives the process. It starts a Fargate task that downloads the sequencing run for the accession from the public bucket and converts it to paired-end FASTQ in a staging bucket, then hands off to the genomics stage.

Two design choices keep the stage predictable. A DynamoDB table records every isolate that has been processed, so a scheduled weekly run or a repeated manual submission doesn’t reprocess the same accession. Fargate runs the copy as a long-running task because fetching and converting a large sequencing run can take well beyond a few minutes. The result is a loop that runs on a schedule or on demand from the web application, without an operator in the middle.

Detecting resistance genes with AWS HealthOmics

Turning reads into a list of resistance genes is the compute-heavy part of the pipeline. AWS HealthOmics runs Nextflow workflows without a cluster to provision or scale, which suits teams that do not run a bioinformatics system of their own.

The workflow is a single HealthOmics run with three tasks connected by Nextflow channels. fastp trims adapters and low-quality bases from the raw reads. SKESA assembles the trimmed reads into contigs. AMRFinderPlus screens those contigs for known resistance genes. Combining assembly and screening in one run avoids a fragile handoff between two separate runs and matches how community AMR pipelines are structured.

Running third-party bioinformatics tools on HealthOmics calls for a few adaptations worth stating plainly:

  • HealthOmics tasks have no internet access, so the AMRFinderPlus database is baked into the container image rather than downloaded at runtime.
  • Container image URIs are passed as workflow parameters instead of hardcoded, which keeps the workflow independent of account and AWS Region and lets HealthOmics verify image access before a run starts.
  • Task outputs are published to the run output path that HealthOmics exports to Amazon S3, rather than to arbitrary locations.

Each container image is built from official tool releases with pinned versions and scanned with Amazon ECR image scanning, so the pipeline doesn’t depend on a floating latest tag.

Harmonizing and storing results

AMRFinderPlus emits a tab-separated file per isolate, which is awkward to analyze across many samples. A Lambda function first normalizes that output into the hAMRonization schema. An AWS Glue job then reshapes the harmonized data into two Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables: amr_profiles, with one row per detected gene, and isolate_metadata, with one row per isolate carrying its provenance and license.

The AWS Glue job writes with a MERGE keyed on the isolate and gene, so processing the same isolate twice updates the existing rows instead of appending duplicates. That idempotency matters for surveillance, where the same accession can arrive again through a scheduled run, and it keeps the tables consistent without a separate deduplication step. Storing the results as Iceberg gives the agent a columnar, transactional surface to query with low latency, and because Amazon S3 Tables registers the schema in the AWS Glue Data Catalog, Athena reads the same tables without extra setup. Converting per-sample files into a structured store is what makes conversational querying across the whole corpus possible.

Asking questions in natural language

The conversational layer uses the Strands Agents SDK and runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. This solution uses AgentCore runtime, its serverless agent-hosting environment. It gives each user session an isolated environment, integrates with AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), and traces the agent’s reasoning and tool calls. The team runs the agent without managing servers or scaling logic.

The agent reasons over four tools, and each one turns a natural-language request into a targeted Athena query against the Iceberg tables:

  • query_amr_profiles finds resistance genes for an organism over an optional date range.
  • get_resistance_trends summarizes how gene detections trend month over month.
  • compare_isolates compares resistance profiles across isolates.
  • lookup_gene_info returns detail on a specific resistance gene.

Grounding is enforced in two places. The system prompt requires the agent to cite the gene ID, the detecting tool, and a confidence value for every claim. It must also say plainly when no data supports an answer rather than guess. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails add a second layer, with a contextual grounding check and denied topics that keep responses tied to the returned rows and off medical or patient advice. The agent uses Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7 on Amazon Bedrock, invoked through a cross-Region inference profile, for the reasoning and synthesis those rules depend on. Model availability varies by AWS Region. See the Amazon Bedrock model support by Region documentation for current availability.

After an isolate has been processed, a researcher explores it through conversation instead of SQL. Asked “What AMR genes were found in Salmonella?”, the agent calls query_amr_profiles, retrieves the matching rows from Iceberg through Athena, and replies with the detected genes. Each gene is annotated with the detecting tool and its confidence value, along with a short reading of what the genes represent. A follow-up such as “Tell me more about mdsB” triggers lookup_gene_info without the user thinking about tables or queries.

Benefits

The architecture turns four recurring pain points into managed, repeatable steps.

ChallengeHow the architecture addresses itFetching and assembling public sequencing data by handA Step Functions workflow pulls reads from the AWS Open Data SRA mirror and runs assembly and screening on managed HealthOmics compute.Reconciling detection output across many samplesA Lambda function harmonizes results and AWS Glue merges them idempotently into Iceberg tables on Amazon S3 Tables.SQL and bioinformatics skills needed to ask a questionA Strands agent on AgentCore turns plain-language questions into Athena queries and answers with cited evidence.Reproducing the environment in another accountThe solution is defined in AWS CDK with no hardcoded identifiers, so it deploys with a single command.

Because this is a reference architecture rather than a customer deployment, its proof is that anyone can stand it up. The CDK application provisions every component described here, from the ingestion workflow to the Iceberg tables to the agent runtime and the web front end. It needs no hardcoded account identifiers or manual setup steps. Running costs depend on how many isolates you process and how often, because HealthOmics runs, AWS Glue jobs, and agent calls are billed per use. The architecture stays inexpensive when idle.

Conclusion

Pairing AWS HealthOmics for managed genomics processing with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore for grounded interpretation lets a surveillance team move from a public accession number to an answer about resistance genes in one continuous flow. Assembly, gene detection, harmonization, and storage happen without manual steps, and the analytical layer is reached through a conversation rather than a query console. The pattern reuses the S3 Tables and agent querying approach from earlier work and applies it to a different genomics problem. That problem begins at raw reads and depends on public-data ingestion and idempotent storage.

To go deeper, see the AWS HealthOmics and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore product pages, and the related post Accelerating genomics variant interpretation with AWS HealthOmics and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore.

The solution is defined entirely in AWS CDK and deploys into your own account. Explore the accompanying repository on GitHub and adapt the pattern to your own surveillance and life-sciences use cases.

posts.title: Introducing: Spotify Technology. Proven at Spotify, now yours.
posts.summary: Introducing Spotify Technology. The post Introducing: Spotify Technology. Proven at Spotify, now yours. appeared first on Spotify Engineering .
posts.content:
Today Spotify is introducing Spotify Technology - a home for everything we've built to help R&D organizations build, ship, and learn, faster. Portal. Confidence. Xirp. Spotify for Backstage. They were always designed to work as a system. Now they live under one roof, and we have more to share.

Born out of necessity

I get asked a version of this question every day: why is Spotify in the business of selling software?

The truth is, the Spotify you know and love is more than a great streaming service. Behind our consumer app are hundreds of cross-functional squads shipping products and code day in, day out. 

These squads build across music, podcasts, and books on a platform woven into the daily lives of 777 million monthly active users around the world, and at a scale and speed that demands best-in-class engineering and tools. To ensure we had the best software for the job, we built it ourselves - and now we’re making it available to others. 

This idea isn't really new to us. We open sourced Backstage in 2020. Companies have been buying Confidence since 2023, Portal by Spotify since 2024, and Xirp launched earlier this year. What's new is the identity. Spotify Technology brings these tools and future products under one brand because they work best as one system, and because we're doubling down on this rather than dabbling in it.

And it goes well beyond developer tooling. Spotify Technology covers the full product development lifecycle, from idea to impact. Alongside it sits the media technology we've built for our own needs. And, at our scale, all of it has to run cost-effectively, which is an engineering discipline in its own right.

How we build

The core DNA of The Spotify Way still holds: teams decide what to build, how to build it, and how to work together, and that sense of ownership runs through every level of the company, leadership included. 

But as we scaled, we learned firsthand that autonomy alone leads to fragmentation. So a few years ago, we pulled hard in the other direction with "One Experience," a push for one unified product rather than a federation of separately good ones. Neither extreme works on its own.

Autonomy and alignment have to hold at the same time. In practice, that means teams keep real ownership of their work, while a shared ecosystem ensures their individual choices still fit together into one product and one technology stack. Tooling that can strike that balance is rare, which is a large part of why we built our own.

Every product under Spotify Technology follows the same path. A real problem surfaces, we build something to solve it, and we prove it at scale with our own backend engineers, data scientists, ML engineers, product managers, and designers, who are very technical, very particular, and quick to tell us when something isn't working. Then we share it, either as open source or as a commercial product.

That cycle only works because we let it take time. Good tools don't fall out of pressure automatically; they come from years of building, watching things break in ways we didn't predict, and rebuilding until they hold up.

What we believe

Three principles run through the identity of Spotify Technology.

  1. We do the hard work so you don’t have to. We’ve spent years solving the infrastructure, tooling and operational challenges that come with building at Spotify’s scale. That's an effort our customers don’t have to repeat.

  2. Proven at Spotify, first. Every product we sell runs on real production workloads inside Spotify, every day. We pressure-test it at our scale and keep improving it until it earns the trust of our own teams. Then, and only then, does it reach yours.

  3. Our tools earn their place. Spotify teams choose their own tools. They can build their own or buy from anyone. Everything in Spotify Technology won out over the alternatives and proved itself in front of the toughest critics we know: our own engineers, shipping to hundreds of millions of listeners. 

The system in practice

So what does an R&D organization look like when it's running on Spotify Technology products?

It starts with the product development lifecycle. Specifically, closing the loop on it. Building and shipping is just one element of this lifecycle. The real value lies in the full circle from discovering what to build, to building and shipping it, measuring whether it worked, and deciding what to build next.

  • Portal by Spotify provides the context layer. It encodes what your organization knows - your architecture, your standards and your systems - so that every person and agent builds with that knowledge. 

  • Xirp brings that context into agentic development, so teams can work across multiple coding agents without losing state or building in silos. 

  • Confidence closes the loop, turning experimentation into a product intelligence layer where every decision about what to build next is informed by evidence. 

The connection is structural. The products share one context layer and one agent runtime, so they compound rather than just coexist. 

You start wherever you need to, whether you’re one engineer, one team, or a whole R&D organization. The pieces are designed to connect, and every cycle makes the system smarter. It's one unified system of modular products covering the full product development lifecycle, rather than a monolith that locks you in or a patchwork you stitch together yourself.

The shift

Here's what's changed. Across the industry, AI has made building faster than ever. But faster doesn't mean simpler. The complexity, the cost, and the operational surface area all grow with it.

More output means more software to secure and operate. More creation means more risks of fragmentation in how things get built and more data sprawl across models, pipelines, and artifacts that nobody has a full picture of. More usage means budgets that risk growing faster than anyone planned for. And speed makes it harder to tell whether any of it worked. Teams ship more and measure less, and end up with a growing pile of software that nobody can say is earning its keep. Shipping faster only helps if you can still tell the difference between what's working and what isn't.

There's a deeper shift happening underneath the speed. When execution gets cheap, judgment becomes the constraint. Deciding what to build matters more than ever when anything can be built. And AI makes forgetting expensive. Without shared memory, teams and agents re-learn what the organization already knows, rebuild what's already been built, and retest ideas that have already been tested, now at machine speed. 

These are problems we've been navigating for years. AI has compounded them for us, just like it has or will for everyone else. But the tooling we've built along the way, systems that help learning persist and compound, is what's allowed us to stay ahead. This isn't a framework we came up with. It's what we do every day.

What's next

With the rapid rate of innovation, it’s hard to tell what engineering organizations will look like in the future. We’re betting that software product development will still require the same base ingredients, regardless of whether a human or an agent does the work. And, that the organizations with their context organized and accessible will be the ones that benefit most from whatever new capabilities come next. 

We're making the connections between our products deeper and more seamless, and investing in agent-readiness across everything we build. 

On a longer horizon, we're building toward something bigger. Spotify Technology is becoming the R&D operating system. Not in the sense of controlling everything your teams do. In the sense of being the connective tissue that makes everything work together. The layer that captures what your organization knows, how it builds, what it's learned, and makes all of that available to every person and every agent doing the work.

We've been building this for years inside Spotify. We're excited to share it with the world.

If you want to learn more, try the products, or talk to our team, visit technology.spotify.com.

Tyson Singer is SVP of Technology and Platform at Spotify, where he oversees the teams behind Spotify Technology, including Portal by Spotify, Xirp, and Confidence.

Spotify Technology as used here refers to the brand name under which Spotify builds and externalizes our in-house made developer products. It does not refer to "Spotify Technology S.A.", the Luxembourg public limited liability company.

posts.title: Why I tried to kill token billing (and why we kept it)
posts.summary: Token billing is useful infrastructure, but usually a bad customer-facing pricing model. Your invoice should define the value your product delivers, not break down what it cost you to create it.
posts.content:
Token billing is useful infrastructure and, for almost every company, a bad customer-facing pricing model. In its simplest form, passthrough pricing charges customers for the model tokens their usage consumes, plus a markup on the underlying cost. If you’re building your pricing around that token consumption, you’re letting your costs determine your price.

That’s reflected in how our customers are using token billing today. They need it on the backend to track usage, manage markups, and protect their unit economics, but they don’t want those details defining how they price their product.

This gets at something I’ve been saying for a while: your invoice should be where you define your value to your customer.

Token-based billing has an invoice problem

This raises the obvious question: why did we build token billing in the first place? Because it’s a safeguard against runaway compute costs, and it’s easy to deploy and explain. For model providers, token usage is the product. For most other AI companies, token billing can be a useful place to start: tokens provide an obvious, countable basis for pricing. But neither subscription seats nor tokens accurately reflect the value your customer receives. 

Token billing positions your product as a commodity markup on top of an actual commodity. It shows the customer an accounting of which models were used, how many tokens were consumed, and what markup was applied. But presenting your model mix, input costs, and margins to a customer misses the point. If their invoice shows that you used 10 models with a 10% markup on one, 5% on another, and 25% on another, you’ve defined your value as the difference between your price and somebody else’s model costs. 

As those models become cheaper and more interchangeable, customers can challenge your markup or route around you entirely. Competition drives the markup, and potentially your business, toward zero.

A better model: Unified credits

Many of our customers are already using Metronome as a margin-tuning system, not just to deploy pricing models. They make model-routing decisions upstream, then send the resulting token usage to Metronome—either broken out by customer or attributed to a single aggregate customer for cost tracking. Our product then gives them visibility into token consumption so they can manage costs and tune their margins. 

That gives companies control over their internal economics, but it doesn’t solve the invoice problem. They still need a presentation layer on top of the core modeling that translates the underlying usage into something tangible for customers. More companies are turning to a unified credit model. 

A unified credit model creates a credit-based burndown. Customers draw down a common credit balance as they use different product operations, with each task consuming credits at its own rate based on the underlying token consumption. One operation might enrich a dataset, another might generate an image. In that case, the invoice can show the customer those enrichments or generated images, not the 10 models you used in the process and the markup applied to each. 

The point isn’t to eliminate complexity; it’s to keep it behind the scenes. Metronome preserves token-level metering, so companies can continue routing models upstream and tuning for margin and performance as workloads change or new models are introduced. But with a unified credit model, your customer doesn’t have to parse all that complexity. On their invoice, the customer sees credits tied to the work the product performs, not tokens tied to the model costs.

Why output-based pricing is the ideal (and outcome-based pricing is a myth)

Unified credits are a stepping stone to output-based pricing, which is the best way to align AI consumption pricing with value today. 

There are three common pricing metrics in AI. The first is an input, which is a cost, like a token. 

The second is an outcome, which could mean the customer making more money, building more pipeline, or reducing churn. Outcomes can help you orient your product around customer value, but they’re difficult to turn into defensible pricing metrics.

Outcome-based pricing only works in a very limited set of circumstances and is largely a luxury reserved for the corporate super-rich. You either need monopoly-like power—enough control over the transaction and its underlying telemetry to measure the outcome, and enough market power to make customers accept that pricing—or a very high ticket price, since only very large contracts can justify the investment required to measure outcomes. At a high enough ticket price, you can afford to instrument a workflow end-to-end and prove mathematically that you’ve made it much more efficient: it requires fewer people, work gets done faster, or inventory turns more quickly. Every quarter, you can prove that value back to the customer and charge a fee as a function of that outcome.  

For everyone else, outcome-based pricing is, for all intents and purposes, a myth. There’s a telemetry gap around what counts as the outcome, whether it occurred, and whether your product caused it. 

Say, for example, I sell you a sales agent and charge you based on the revenue it generates. I’ve immediately invited a dispute over the relative value of human labor versus automated labor. Did the agent generate the sale or was it the sales rep? Was it marketing? Would the customer have purchased anyway? The outcome might be valuable, but it can’t be objectively attributed to the product.

The third way to price is on outputs. An output is an objective, verifiable metric, like generating an image or sending an email. Fin’s pricing, based on resolved support conversations, is considered the poster child for outcome-based pricing. I would argue it’s actually an output. The outcome of customer support is happy customers; a resolved support ticket is something you can objectively count. 

All companies should do the same: define your output metric, call it an outcome, and convince the market that you’re right.

Where pricing is headed

Pricing models are slow to change because customers compare you with the rest of your competition. There’s a heavy penalty for departing from the herd.

But once a new model takes hold, the market can change very quickly. It’s Darwinian: a pricing model can look completely maladaptive, then suddenly become adaptive and spread through the category.

Three years ago, our team at Metronome predicted that hybrid pricing—some combination of seats plus usage—would become a prominent business model. We built support for it, and it went largely unused by our customers for around 18 months. Then, as of August 2026, roughly one in six (and growing) Stripe users that had crossed key revenue milestones were actively using or rolling out hybrid pricing. The model we’d been hypothesizing about for years seemed to catch on all at once.

Fin followed a similar pattern. Three years ago, almost no one in the AI customer-support category was talking about outcome-based pricing. Within a quarter of Fin introducing pricing based on resolved support conversations, all five of the leading companies in the category had committed to some version of outcome-based pricing. 

Nothing changed, then everything changed. Once the product category and its buyers reached a certain level of maturity, the preference cascaded through the market.

As agents become more involved in both buying services and doing work, I suspect we’ll see the same thing with output-based pricing. 

Subscription and seat-based pricing have been dominant thus far partly because they’re straightforward for humans to understand and compare. It’s easy to explain a fixed price per month or a fixed price per user to human buyers. An agent, on the other hand, can account for far more variables and match the price of each task more closely to its value. 

One analogy for this trajectory is high-frequency trading. Trading algorithms operate at a level of speed and complexity that humans can’t. Something similar could happen with pricing. As agents increasingly evaluate and purchase services, pricing models won’t be limited by how much complexity a human buyer can handle. Agents also make the work itself easier to measure. Each task leaves an audit trail, which makes more activities observable and verifiable without a separate monitoring system. 

As more work moves through agents, I expect the measurable outputs they produce to become pricing metrics—even if they’re still often marketed as outcomes.

posts.summary: Open USD (OUSD), a stablecoin built for global money movement, is now available across Stripe. Businesses can use OUSD to manage funds, make payments, and offer new financial services.
posts.content:
Today, support for Open USD (OUSD) launches across Stripe products. OUSD is a new stablecoin from Open Standard that is designed for global money movement at scale and enables any business to transact and build with internet-native payment rails.

Businesses can now use OUSD to receive, hold, send, and spend funds with Treasury; build and operate a global card program with Issuing; and pay recipients globally with Global Payouts. Businesses can also offer fiat-to-OUSD conversions to their customers with Crypto Onramp and accept OUSD with Payments. 

As we roll out additional support for OUSD, we will continue to make it available by default across Stripe products.

Create powerful global financial products with OUSD on Stripe

For fintechs, institutions, and global businesses building financial services at scale, OUSD is now integrated across Stripe’s stablecoin stack. It delivers the speed and utility businesses expect from a stablecoin, with low transaction fees that stay predictable even as volumes increase, and no minting or burning fees. OUSD’s benefits extend beyond costs and performance. While most businesses don’t earn rewards on stablecoin activity, businesses that join Open Standard as a partner can earn rewards based on OUSD activity—including their OUSD balances on Stripe—creating greater value as their usage increases. Businesses can join at no cost.

OUSD can also be used with Bridge and Privy. Using Bridge orchestration APIs allows businesses to easily convert between OUSD and both fiat and other stablecoins, while using Privy allows them to support OUSD in any digital wallet experience. Businesses have the flexibility to plug in these components as needed, or to use the entire stack to build powerful global financial services without stitching together separate providers for each part of the transaction flow. Finance platform Ramp will soon use Stripe to power stablecoin accounts that let users hold OUSD balances, earn rewards, and make payments anywhere in the world 24/7 with OUSD.

While OUSD on Tempo is now Stripe’s default stablecoin configuration, we continue to offer flexibility to choose the stablecoin and blockchain whose costs, settlement speed, and infrastructure best suit their product needs. OUSD is available on Base, Ethereum, Solana, and Tempo. Stripe supports several alternative stablecoins across blockchains, and won’t require Stripe users to convert their existing stablecoin balances to OUSD.

OUSD launches with the support and distribution of Open Standard’s founding companies, including Coinbase, Mastercard, Shopify, Stripe, and Visa, and more than 200 network partners.

Get started today

Read the docs or contact sales to start using OUSD on Stripe.

posts.title: Helping personal agents shop more intelligently and reliably with Link
posts.summary: As agents take on more purchases, agent builders have increasingly asked us to help agents navigate checkout and earn consumer trust. Today, we’re sharing three major improvements to support this broader set of needs.
posts.content:
The most popular personal AI agents—such as Muse, Meta’s new personal agent; Grok Bot; and Instinct—now use Link’s wallet for agents to power consumer spending. Consumers are embracing this new way to shop: over the past month, agentic purchases made with Link increased 38x.

As agents take on more purchases, agent builders have increasingly asked us to help agents navigate checkout and earn consumer trust. Today, we’re sharing three major improvements to support this broader set of needs. Link can now help agents complete more purchases with incremental authorization and guidance on how to overcome checkout obstacles; analyze consumer spending to make better product recommendations; and provide purchase protection if an agent makes a mistake.

Help agents complete more purchases

Online checkout flows are complex, and agents do not always have all the information they need at the start of a purchase. The final price may change because of taxes, shipping, or other costs added later in the process. 

Link now supports incremental authorization, which lets agents request a higher approved amount when the final price exceeds the original. For example, a consumer might ask an agent to book a flight, then add a checked bag after approving the initial fare. With Link, the agent can update the approved amount to include the baggage fee instead of restarting the purchase and placing a second hold on the consumer’s card. This helps agents account for price changes and complete more purchases with less intervention. 

When an agent encounters additional payment obstacles, Link provides specific guidance on how to proceed to increase the chances of a successful payment. For example, Link can provide a URL that the agent can send to the consumer to complete a 3D Secure challenge. Or if the original payment method was declined, the agent can ask the consumer to choose another and create a new spend request.
